A huge image cannot be imprinted in something tiny. It does not help to say that both can be divided without end. A hand cannot hold a mountain, even if both can be divided endlessly.

This objection applies only to those who say that bodily likenesses and images exist inside the powers of imagination or sense. They have not proved this with a clear and sufficient argument, as anyone who follows their claims can see. These powers may prepare the soul to see images in a greater world of images that exists apart from it. That was Suhrawardi’s view, following the ancient Persian philosophers and the Stoics. Or they may be the means by which the soul makes images in its own smaller world, as I hold.[^V01-555] In short, the objection does not apply to someone who says that sensed things have another kind of existence besides their bodily existence in the material world.

The proofs for the existence of forms known by the soul show that there is another world, and that these images and likenesses exist in another way besides the way they appear to the outer senses. Through this other existence they appear to our inner powers. The soul, freed from both these kinds of existence and higher than both worlds, may even see them with the help of its inner powers, just as it sees images with the help of the outer senses.

From what the outer senses perceive, the soul knows of the material world. From what its inner powers perceive, it knows of another world of images. And from its knowledge of itself and of realities grasped by the intellect, it knows of a third world beyond both. We remember particular people we once saw, even after they have disappeared from this world, and picture them with the same size, shape, and position. The image stands before us in its particular form. It must exist somewhere, though not in this material world, so it exists in another world.

Plato, the ancient sages, and the mystics who saw these realities taught that the beings of the imaginal world exist without a place or direction. This world lies between the world of intellect and the world of sense. Intellectual beings are entirely free from matter and from place, shape, size, color, and light. Sensible beings are immersed in these features. Images in this middle world are different from both: they do not occupy a physical place, yet they still have size and shape.

Here is the substance of Suhrawardi’s argument in *The Wisdom of Illumination*. Vision does not happen because the image of the thing seen is stamped on the eye, as Aristotle held, or because a ray leaves the eye and reaches the thing, as mathematicians said. Vision happens when a luminous object faces a healthy eye. This gives the soul direct awareness of the object, and so it sees it. The image in a mirror is not in the eye, since something large cannot be stamped into something small. Nor is the mirror image exactly the same as the person or thing seen, as some have thought.[^V01-556][^V01-557]

The image is not in the mirror or in any other body. The eye’s clear lens relates to visible things as a mirror relates to the images that appear in it. Since the mirror’s image is not in the mirror, the image perceived through the lens is not in the lens either. It appears when the soul’s direct awareness meets a luminous object and no obstacle blocks it. If the thing has an existence outside the mind, the soul sees it. If it is only an image, it needs something to show it, like a mirror.

When the eye’s lens faces a mirror in which images appear, the soul’s direct awareness reaches those images through the lens and the mirror, when the right conditions are present and obstacles are removed. Just as the large image cannot be stamped into the eye, it cannot be stamped into a place in the brain. So imagined images are not in the mind, where a large thing could not fit into a small place. They are not in the outside world either, or everyone with healthy senses would see them. Nor are they nothing, since we can imagine and distinguish them and make different true or false claims about them. They exist in another region: the imaginal world, also called the separate imagination because it is not material like the imagination joined to the soul.

This is the world whose existence was taught by ancient philosophers such as Plato, Socrates, Pythagoras, Empedocles, and other spiritual thinkers, as well as mystics from many peoples. They spoke of two worlds: the world of intellect, which includes the divine world and the worlds of intellects and souls; and the world of images, which includes sensory forms and imaginal images.[^V01-558]

Imaginal images are not Plato’s Forms. The greatest philosophers who believed in these images also believed in Plato’s Forms: great, fixed lights in the world of intellectual light. Imaginal images, by contrast, are suspended in the imaginal world. Some are dark, like the Hell that holds the suffering of the wretched; others are bright, like the gardens where the fortunate enjoy themselves. Those who are nearest to God rise to the highest level and dwell in the gardens of holiness among divine lights and sacred Forms.

Here is an insight from beyond the Throne. I believe in a world of forms and dimensions that is not material, as the greatest philosophers and mystics taught and as Suhrawardi explained so fully. But I differ from him in two respects.[^V01-559] First, I say that imagined images exist in a realm of the soul as soon as the soul forms them by its own power, using the imagination.[^V01-560] They do not exist in a world outside the soul, created by some other power, as Suhrawardi’s words seem to imply. The imagination’s random play and the ugly images it makes—unlike the work of a wise creator—belong to the small inner world. They come from the imagination’s mischief.

These images last as long as the soul attends to them and uses the imagination to form and hold them. When the soul turns away, they disappear. They do not continue to exist on their own, kept in place without the soul’s attention, as Suhrawardi thought. There is a difference between mere inattention and forgetting: when we are inattentive, the soul can still bring an image back without new sense experience. When we have forgotten it, we need a new experience or something that serves the same purpose, such as a reminder.

The second point of difference is this: Suhrawardi says that images seen in mirrors exist in the imaginal world. We say they are shadows of things we sense. They have a shadow-like existence here: they are reflections that depend on real things, not things that exist in their own right.[^V01-561] The same is true when someone sees double, or when a sound produces an echo. Neither the second image nor the echo exists on its own. Each depends on something outside it. As we have explained, everything apart from the modes of existence themselves depends on them, like a shadow or reflection depends on what it represents. A reflection is not the thing it reflects, as one mystic writes:[^V01-562] “The whole world is the echo of His song—who has ever heard an echo so long?”

A third objection is this: if things exist in the mind as you have argued, then every bodily kind and every kind of bodily quality must have an individual example that is free of matter and of its features, such as size, place, and position.[^V01-563] That example would itself be both an individual and a general kind.

The objection runs as follows.[^V01-564] On your account, every general idea we understand exists in the mind. Either it remains wholly unspecified there, without becoming an individual thing, or it becomes a particular thing. The first cannot be right, because existence always makes something particular. The idea of something existing while remaining wholly undefined makes no sense. The second means that when we understand “human being,” a particular human being—stripped of size, shape, and every other material feature—must appear in the mind. If those features remained with it,[^V01-565] it could not exist in the immaterial intellect, according to the principles you accept. But this conclusion is plainly false, and everyone agrees it is.[^V01-566] So the starting claim must be false as well.

The usual reply is that what exists in the mind is a particular quality or state of the mind. It is not an example of the substance that the idea describes, though it is the very same meaning as that substance. The same answer applies to our ideas of bodily qualities. You already know from our answer to the first objection that what the mind receives from an external substance is its meaning, not the substance itself or one of its individual examples. The mental idea is general because we consider it apart from the features that make it particular, both in the mind and outside it.[^V01-567] There is no contradiction in something being general in one respect and particular in another, especially when we compare its mental and external existence.

If someone still insists that the idea of human nature in the mind shares the reality of actual human beings and is itself a substance, while existing in the mind as a state that the mind does not need, then that person has fallen into the same difficulty we have already described.

It is strange that Mulla Dawwani insists that the mental meanings of substances are themselves substances. He says that a substance is a nature that can exist outside the mind without being in a subject. He criticizes anyone who says that the mental form of a substance is a quality, on the grounds that this would turn a substance into a quality.

Yet the change of a substance into a quality that he fears follows more directly from his own account, as careful thought will show. He can avoid this only by adding a condition to every definition of a substantial kind: “when it exists outside the mind.” If so, not only would the human being in the mind be a substance in this special sense; its ability to have dimensions, its size, growth, sensation, reason, and every feature contained in these ideas would also have to be qualified in the same way. Then there would be no real difference between saying that the mental form is truly a quality and saying, through these forced qualifications, that it is a kind of substance.

In fact, the idea of a human being, like the ideas of other kinds of independently existing things, is a feature of the mind.[^V01-568] It is human in what it means, but it is not itself an actual human being. That is the distinction between the two ways of saying what a thing is. For people who do not accept a separate intellectual world containing forms of substantial kinds—as Aristotle and his followers did—proofs of mental existence show no more than this.

But someone who believes in that higher intellectual world can say that some individual examples of a kind exist without matter, while others exist in matter. There is no clear proof or common-sense reason that this is impossible. Plato and the great philosophers before him held that every bodily kind has an individual in the world of intellect. These individuals are active causes of the bodily examples of their kinds, and care for them.[^V01-569] The argument that individuals of one kind cannot differ in how complete or perfect they are applies, if it is sound at all, only when they share the same mode of existence and the same realm. It need not apply to individuals that exist in two different modes and realms.

In truth, Plato’s view, and the view of the great philosophers before him, that there are intellectual Forms of bodily kinds is strong and well founded. Later thinkers’ objections do not stand. They arise because those thinkers did not reach the level of the earlier philosophers or understand what they meant, as we will explain later, God willing. Their conclusions rested on clear spiritual insights and sacred visions, not merely on arguments that invite doubt. One group after another has rejected the group before it.

Those great philosophers and saints did not set out a formal proof for these higher Forms. Instead, they reported clear visions they had experienced repeatedly. A person can trust what they all reported and accept that they were sure of what they saw. No one should debate them about this. If people accept the positions of the stars and the number of the heavenly spheres on the basis of observations made by Hipparchus, or a few people like him, using senses that often mislead, then it is even more fitting to accept the repeated intellectual observations of the leading philosophers, which cannot be mistaken.

A fourth objection is this: if mental existence is real, then the mind must become hot when it thinks of heat, cold when it thinks of cold, curved or straight, round, triangular, or square, a disbeliever or a believer, and even something with a location. A hot thing is something in which heat exists, a cold thing something in which cold exists, and the same applies to other descriptions. So the soul would take on the features of bodies and even opposite features. This is plainly false.

Here is the reasoning behind the objection. If the things we think about actually entered our minds, they would exist there as features of the mind. The mind would then have the very qualities it was thinking about.

There are several replies. The first is an insight from beyond the Throne. When the soul imagines these things, their images appear in a realm of the soul; they do not take up residence inside the soul. Just as the soul, a radiant, immaterial being, shines through the power of sight and directly sees what faces the eye without an image being stamped into it—as the ancient philosophers held—so it shines through the imagination and directly sees an imagined image that exists outside the soul. The image is distinct from the soul; it does not enter the soul or make the soul take on its features.[^V01-570]

Just as the soul sees and senses external images through sight and the other outer senses, it sees inner images through its inner senses. These images do not live inside the soul itself. Our experience makes no distinction between seeing while awake and seeing by day.

Second, even if imagined images exist in the soul as forms that enter it, the soul takes on a feature only when it is affected by that feature, not merely because the feature exists in it.[^V01-571] The active sources that bring events in the world into being contain knowledge of the forms of those things, yet they do not take on the bodies’ qualities. The forms are present in those higher sources through their activity and their power to bring things about, not because those sources receive or suffer the effects of the forms. We do not accept that merely existing in something makes it take on the thing’s features unless it is affected or changed by it. Whether a word such as “hot” can be applied merely because heat is present is a separate question and does not concern us here.

The second answer uses the distinction between two ways of saying that something is something else. The idea of disbelief is not itself an act or state of disbelief. Thinking about disbelief therefore does not make a person a disbeliever. The same is true of the other examples. Anyone seeking a way out of this objection should apply that distinction carefully.

A third answer, given in the standard books, is that the objection confuses real existence with the lesser, image-like existence of an idea. A body is hot because actual heat exists in it, not because the mind has an idea of heat. Heat and cold are opposites as real things, not as ideas. The same applies to the other examples. Each of these qualities means that, when it exists in a material body, it puts the body in a certain state and has effects that the senses can detect. Heat, for example, separates unlike parts of a mixture and brings like parts together. A straight line is one whose parts lie along the same direction. The same is true of curves and other shapes. If we understand these ideas and they exist as states in the immaterial soul, this means only that the soul has ideas of things that can make bodies hot, cold, straight, curved, or otherwise shaped. It does not mean that the soul itself becomes a material thing with those features.

Someone may reply that this answer fails for features that necessarily follow from what a thing is, or that we understand through a relationship. Consider evenness and oddness, necessity, causes, and parenthood. These are not external things. Nor does the answer work for features of things that do not exist, such as impossibility and nonexistence. We cannot say that the mind takes on these features only when they exist outside it, because they have no such existence. They are either ideas formed by the intellect or features of things that do not exist.

We can answer this by applying what we have already established in this book: every meaning has some share of existence.[^V01-572] Evenness, for example, exists in the sense that the thing it describes can be understood as divisible into two equal parts. That is its real mode of existence. But when the soul thinks of evenness, it does not itself become divisible into two equal parts. The same applies to other ideas. As for nonexistence and similar ideas, they have no image in the mind. The intellect actively turns some concepts into names or labels for things that cannot exist, and uses them to understand those things’ features.

A fifth objection is this: the mind exists in the world, and the things we think about exist in the mind. So those things seem to exist inside something that itself exists in the world. Anything that exists inside one thing must also exist inside whatever contains that thing—like water in a jug that is in a house.

We reply that something inside one thing is inside another only when both exist in their own right and are distinct things, like water in a jug and the jug in a house.[^V01-573] What we know in the mind is different. It is present there as an image, not as a separate thing with its own independent existence. The mind, by contrast, has its own real existence in the outside world. So the word “in” has a different meaning in these two cases.[^V01-574] The word is also used differently for being in a place or time. To exist in the outside world means to produce the effects proper to a thing; to exist in the mind means not to produce those same effects.

A sixth objection is this: the theory seems to put real examples of impossible things inside our minds, not merely ideas of them. When we judge that contradictions cannot exist together, for example, we first imagine them. That imagined contradiction then exists in the mind as a particular thing. But common sense says that contradictions cannot exist in the mind or outside it. The same problem seems to arise for absolute nonexistence and for a partner to God: if an individual example of a partner to God exists in the mind, then, by its own nature, it must also exist outside the mind.

The answer is that when we speak of things that cannot exist, our statements are not unconditional. We are saying what would follow if the idea we have named could apply to an actual example.[^V01-575] The intellect can form ideas of contradiction, a partner to God, an indivisible substance, and every other concept—including the idea of its own nonexistence, the nonexistence of its cause, nonexistence itself, and the idea of what cannot exist. It does not form these ideas as the realities of impossible things. Anything the mind forms as an idea is possible as an idea. Rather, the idea serves as a name for an impossible nature that cannot itself be pictured.

For a concept to serve as a name for a nature, its meaning must fit that nature by essential predication, even if it does not fit by ordinary predication. The intellect can form an idea and, by supposition, use it as a name for a nature that cannot exist and cannot itself be pictured. Because the idea exists in the mind and points to an impossible nature, we can correctly say that it is impossible to judge or know that nature. We can speak about that impossibility even though we cannot speak about the nature itself. The claim can be made about the idea, which can exist in the mind. It cannot be made in the same way about the impossible thing that the idea names.

The same kind of statement is made about the Necessary Being: for example, that its individuality is identical with its essence, or that its oneness differs from what we mean by “oneness.” The statement concerns the idea of the Necessary Being. But the claim that its individuality is identical with its essence concerns the reality that proof leads us to: God, the Living and Self-Subsisting, who is beyond being pictured in any mind. We can therefore see that these statements, and statements like them, are not plain, unconditional statements.[^V01-576] Although they can be restated as conditionals, they do not simply reduce to conditionals. In them, the assumption is part of the subject itself: no definite nature has been formed, not at all in the case of impossible things, or in the mind in the case of God. This is different from first taking a fully formed subject and then making a claim about it only under some added condition.

#### Chapter 4 — Further clarification and refinement

Some later thinkers could not answer all the objections to mental existence.[^V01-577] They therefore chose another view: what exists in the mind is not the thing known itself, but a shadow or image that resembles it in some way. Here is their reasoning. Proof and experience both show that when we understand something, an image of it appears in the mind. Through it, the mind becomes aware of those things, makes judgments about them, and speaks about them. But because of the objections already raised, they say that the things themselves cannot exist in the mind. The view that seems to satisfy both proof and experience is that what appears in the mind is a shadow or model of the thing known. It resembles the thing the way a spoken word or written mark resembles its meaning. But words and writing resemble meanings by agreement; mental images resemble them by nature.

We object that if the proofs for mental existence work, they show that the very things known exist in the mind—not something separate from them, as writing and spoken sounds are separate. No one says that the written name “Zayd,” or the spoken word for him, is Zayd himself.[^V01-578] But our understanding of a thing is different: we make judgments about it and describe what belongs to it, both by nature and by added features. So this proposal does not reconcile proof with experience. It sets both aside and introduces a third view.

A distinguished scholar offered a subtler answer that comes close to the truth. I shall give his argument and the objections to it, so that we can see the issue more clearly. First, he assumes that a thing’s nature follows its existence.[^V01-579] That is, unless something exists, it is not any kind of nature at all. Pure nonexistence has no nature and is nothing. Until something has become real in some way, either in the mind or outside it, it is not a nature of any kind.

Someone may ask: what is the thing that first exists and then becomes a nature?[^V01-580] Is it that very nature? Then the nature exists before it becomes itself, which is plainly impossible. Or is it a different nature? That is even worse: it would be like saying that a horse came to exist and then became a human being.

The answer is that these are not the only choices. First, this is a matter of what comes first in explanation, not what comes first in time. At one level, neither side of a contradiction need apply, as we will explain later.[^V01-581] Second, “it exists and becomes human” does not mean that a particular thing first appears and then turns into a human being. The same thing is both human and existent, but it is first real as an existing thing, and only then understood as the nature “human being.” If the objection were sound, we would also have to say that the number four cannot be prior to being even. If four existed first and only later became even, it would either already be even, making “even” prior to itself, or not be even, in which case four would first be odd and later become even. Both conclusions are obviously false.

The scholar now draws his conclusion. In this order of explanation, existence comes first. Only then can we say what kind of thing it is. If we set existence aside, there is no nature left to consider. Mental existence and external existence are truly different. So when something that exists outside the mind comes to exist in the mind, its nature may change too. Outside the mind, a thing has a nature such as substance, quantity, or one of the other basic kinds. When it exists in the mind, its nature changes and becomes a mental quality. This removes the objections, since they all assume that a thing keeps its external nature when it exists in the mind.

Someone may object that this is just the copy-and-shadow view: what exists in the mind would not be the thing itself but something that differs from it in nature.[^V01-582] The scholar replies that a thing has no fixed nature apart from its modes of existence. An external thing becomes a mental quality when it exists in the mind; a mental quality, if it exists outside the mind, becomes the very thing known. If “the thing itself exists in the mind” means that it exists there even though its nature changes with its mode of existence, then the claim is true. But if it means that the thing keeps exactly the same external nature in the mind, there is no proof for that. The proof only requires that something be present to the mind so it can make a judgment about it. The judgment is about what the thing is in itself, not about how it exists in the mind. So there must be something in the mind that, if it existed outside the mind, would have the feature named by the judgment—even if its nature changes when its mode of existence changes.

Someone may object: how could one nature turn into another unless something remained common to both—shared matter beneath the physical thing and its mental image? The philosophers compare this with prime matter, which has no definite character of its own but can become water, air, or fire when it takes on a form. They assume that there must be some shared matter behind all things. The answer is that a shared matter is needed when one feature or form changes into another, as black becomes white or an embryo develops into an animal. It is not needed when one whole nature changes into a different nature.[^V01-583] The mind may suppose an undefined common element simply to picture the change. That is the main point of this scholar’s view.

His contemporary, the well-known Mulla Dawwani, objected as follows. Anyone with ordinary good sense knows that one nature cannot turn into a different nature. What can change is matter taking on another form, or a subject taking on another quality. And anything that exists in the mind has no subject or container other than the mind, by virtue of existing in it.[^V01-584] So the mind cannot change from being a mental quality into an external substance. What, then, is this one thing that supposedly has one nature outside the mind and another inside it? If its nature changes, in what sense is it still the same thing?

It is also unclear what it means to say that existence comes before a nature. Even if that were granted, it would not allow one nature to become another. An added feature, whether it comes before or after another feature, does not change the nature it belongs to. If the nature changed, what exists in the mind would differ in kind from what exists outside it, contrary to the proof for mental existence. To say that a nature can exist in the mind either unchanged or transformed is like saying that Zayd can be in a house and either remain Zayd or turn into Amr.

It is clear that if one thing turns into another, something must remain common to both, such as matter or a general kind. If nothing remains, it is false to say that one thing has become another. Simple good sense is enough to show this.

A supporter of the copy-and-shadow view could also say that an external thing can exist in the mind only through its image or shadow. The image could become the external thing if it were to exist outside the mind; in fact, this supporter already says that the image is not the thing itself. The same problem arises for this scholar’s view. If a mental quality keeps its mental nature when it exists outside the mind, it remains a mental quality and not a substance. If a mental idea of a substance exists in the mind, it remains a substance in the mind. Nor is the mental quality hidden from external reality: as a state of the soul, it already exists in the world, like other qualities of the soul. If it remains a mental quality outside the soul, it cannot become a substance merely by being elsewhere. Indeed, a mental quality existing apart from a soul is impossible, while a substance is possible. If the scholar means that the quality becomes a substance only by changing its nature, then the copy-and-shadow view can make exactly the same claim.[^V01-585]

The strongest version of the scholar’s reply is this: each external nature has a special relation to its mental image, and the mind recognizes that relation. The image is called the mental image of that nature because, if it existed outside the mind and changed into its external nature, it would be that very nature. But this does not mean that the existence of one thing is the existence of another.[^V01-586] There is a difference between saying “If A existed outside the mind and changed into B, it would be B” and saying “If A existed outside the mind, it would be B.” In the first statement, the change from A to B is part of the claim; it is missing from the second.

Someone may object that a mental quality would remain a mental quality even if it existed outside the mind. The reply is that this misses the claim. The claim is only that it would exist outside the mind. That kind of existence itself would change its nature, because a mental nature depends on existing in the mind, while an external nature depends on existing outside it. In short, a mental thing’s existence outside the mind means that its nature changes into an external nature, or at least includes that change. This needs careful thought; there are problems with it.

There is another explanation of the scholar’s view. It is closer to the truth and avoids some of these problems. External things have essential features that bring about their proper effects. For example, a body has dimensions and occupies space; a plant form enables growth and nourishment. When these natures exist in the mind, they become qualities of the mind, while their essential features remain in some way. Their images are now mental qualities.[^V01-587]

On this account, general natures are like prime matter as the first teacher and his followers describe it: in themselves they are not yet definite or fully formed, and so do not belong to any one basic kind. They become distinct natures only when considered in relation to one of the two modes of existence. Water, for example, is a flowing, wet, heavy body when it exists outside the mind. When it exists in the mind, it becomes a mental quality. In itself, apart from either mode of existence, it is not fully defined as either a body or a mental quality.

Someone may object that this does not agree with the accepted principles, because a thing cannot lose its essential features in either mode of existence. Nor can one thing have two modes of existence. The reply is that if existence comes before nature, then apart from its mental or external existence a thing has no definite nature at all—not substance, quality, or even an undefined nature. Once it exists, its mode determines what it is. If it exists without depending on a subject, it is a substance; if it depends on a subject, it is a quality. In the same way, if it can have dimensions, it is a body; if it can grow and be nourished, it is a plant, and so on. We can draw out these essential features only by considering the thing as existing outside the mind, either actually or by supposition. If we consider it only as existing in the mind, we can draw out its mental qualities, such as knowledge and other features of the mind. If we consider it without choosing either mode of existence, we cannot point to it or assign it a definite nature.[^V01-588]

The claim that essential features remain through the change from one mode of existence to another has another meaning here.[^V01-589] The mind considers the mental image not as a quality that exists in the mind, but as a way of looking at the external nature. It can then judge the image by the features of that nature. For example, the idea of water in the mind is not itself a body, fluid, wet, or heavy. It is a mental quality. Yet the mind can consider it as water existing outside the mind and judge it by the features of external water.

When the mind sets aside what distinguishes one body of water from another, it gains a power of insight beyond the senses.[^V01-590] It sees a single reality from which particular waters arise and grasps an idea that applies to them all. The mind uses this idea as a mirror to learn about their external features and draws out their essential features as we have explained earlier. That is what we wanted to say in making sense of this scholar’s view.

Know that most later thinkers do not build their views on sound spiritual principles or on firm, inspired insights. They rely instead on what might be logically possible and on ideas accepted without proof, not on deep experience or clear demonstrations. So when they try to give a deeper explanation, they add objections and replies until their books become layers of darkness. Only a few find a way out. God has not wronged them; they have wronged themselves.

#### Chapter — A solution drawn from higher knowledge

Here is another way to answer some objections to the claim that things can exist in the mind. It avoids having to say that a thing’s nature turns into a different nature. It also avoids the view of a respected contemporary scholar, who says that calling knowledge and mental forms “qualities” is only a figure of speech or comparison. At the same time, this account preserves the principle that a thing’s essential features remain the same even when its mode of existence changes, and it treats mental forms as real qualities.[^V01-591] Here is the idea: the human soul can draw general ideas from things outside the mind, from what we imagine, and from images that are not physical things.

When the soul draws one of these ideas, it is affected by a mental quality: its knowledge of the thing. A new quality therefore arises in the soul when it understands that meaning. The philosophers say that when we look within as we think, we find only this image. So the mental quality is the image itself, present in the soul and describing it. That is why they define knowledge as an image of a thing formed in the mind. But proof shows that real things are present in the mind, not in the way they exist outside it. This made it seem that knowledge of anything in a given basic kind must itself belong to that kind. The matter became difficult, and the truth unclear. Here is the right way to understand it.[^V01-592]

Just as a particular person, such as Zayd, exists outside the mind along with his features—being white, laughing, walking, sitting, growing, an animal, and rational—so these features are real through Zayd’s existence. The Zayd we meet outside is the very person who laughs and writes, and who is an animal and rational. Zayd is a substance by his essential nature. But “substance” is not thereby essential to each way we describe him—as a writer, as someone who laughs, or as a rational being.[^V01-593]

The same is true of what exists in the mind. Universal knowledge is one of the realities found there. An instance of knowledge becomes definite when it joins with the reality of the thing known. Compare this with a body. Outside the mind, a body has size, shape and position. It may grow or remain without growth; it may be an element or a heavenly body. These features make it a particular kind of body. In the same way, knowledge becomes definite and actual by joining with the reality of what is known. Knowledge is its closest kind, while quality is a more distant kind.[^V01-594]

Knowledge becomes actual and definite only when the reality of the thing known joins with it, so that in fact they form one reality that matches the thing known. This one reality is knowledge by its closest kind, quality by a more distant kind, and belongs to the basic kind of the thing known because of what makes it definite. Just as Zayd outside the mind is an animal by his closest kind and a substance by a more distant kind, while his particular features place him under kinds such as relation, quantity, and quality. The thing known and knowledge are united as a feature is united with the thing it describes. So knowledge belongs to quality, and quality is essential to it as knowledge; in reality, however, it is the very reality of the thing known. This answers the objection: knowledge is a state of the soul, so it must belong to quality; but if the nature of the thing known exists in the mind, it must belong to the kind of that thing too. That would seem to place one reality in two kinds.

The point is that knowledge belongs to quality in its own right, because quality is its closest kind. In the mind, the idea of the thing known is one with knowledge in reality and existence, so it belongs to the kind of the known thing only indirectly. Just as Zayd is a substance in his own right, but belongs to the kind called relation when we consider him as someone’s father or son.[^V01-595] That accomplished scholar, following the earlier philosophers, holds that a quality and the description based on it refer to the same reality, though we can think of them in different ways.[^V01-596] For him, “white” and “whiteness” are one reality, though we can consider one as describing a thing and the other as whiteness in itself. As you will see later, this point is explained more fully. It clears the difficulty and removes the confusion.

### Stage Two — Further rules about existence and related questions about nonexistence

#### Chapter — What linking existence means

Someone may object: if existence is a link in a statement such as “A is B,” then B must exist in itself too.[^V01-597][^V01-598] For something to exist for another thing, the objection says, it must first exist in itself.[^V01-599] And if B’s being true of A is itself true of A, then that new link must also be true of A, and so on without end.

We can clear up this difficulty by recalling a distinction made earlier. When the word “existence” means the link in a statement, it does not mean existence in general or existence as a feature established for another thing. These two uses are easily confused. Sometimes 'existence' means no more than the link between a subject and what is said about it, like the word 'is' in a sentence. We do not treat that link as a separate thing. This is called linking existence. At other times it means that something is real, either in itself or through another thing. We can call this second sense dependent existence, to distinguish it from the link itself.

So “A is B” does not mean that B first exists on its own and then exists for A, as a color or form exists in the thing it belongs to. It means only that A has the feature B; “is” links the two. The subject can therefore be described by something that does not exist outside the mind, such as a lack or absence, while still having some standing in thought. As we have already seen, an endless series formed by our successive acts of attention and imagination is not impossible: it stops when we stop paying attention.

Unless we consider both sides of a judgment, no link forms between them for us to judge that one belongs to the other. When we say “A is B,” we understand that B belongs to A as a way of seeing what A and B are like; we do not focus on the link itself. So in making this judgment, we cannot also ask whether B’s belonging to A belongs to A, or whether it is itself linked to A. In the statement “A is B,” the link is just a link. A link, simply as a link, cannot itself be linked to something else.

But suppose we now say, 'The link between A and B has this feature.' We have stopped using that first link merely to connect the two terms and have begun thinking about it as a thing in its own right. It no longer serves only to connect the two sides; we can now treat it as one side of a new judgment and consider another link. That second link lets us consider the first, though we do not focus on the second link itself. If we then focus on it and say, “the link to the link is such-and-such,” we turn away from the original two sides and connect the second link to a subject. This creates a third link that we are not directly considering. If we then turn our attention to that link, we get a fourth, then a fifth and a sixth, and so on. The series ends when we stop making these voluntary shifts of attention.

The great philosophers of earlier times said that a predicate, simply as a predicate, has no existence of its own apart from its being true of its subject.[^V01-600] They did not mean that its existence in itself is exactly the same as its existence in its subject, as with qualities and forms. A predicate, simply as a predicate, is not a thing that first exists in itself and then belongs to a subject. They meant that it does not exist on its own; it is only true of its subject, and that is all its existence consists in.

There is a difference between saying, “A quality’s existence in itself is the same as its existence in its subject,” and saying, “Its existence in itself consists in its being true of its subject.” The first claims that the quality has an existence in itself; the second does not. This argument concerns only what a compound statement means. Whether the two sides of the judgment must, in reality, exist in some way is a separate question.

In our philosophy, every possible being exists only through its link to God's existence. I shall explain and prove this point later. It goes further than what some leading religious thinkers and great philosophers have said. They said that material natures exist in themselves in the very way they exist for their matter; that an effect, simply as an effect, exists for its cause; and that every lower being exists in the presence of the higher being that encompasses all the lower levels. On their view, all possible beings—both material things and beings free of matter—exist not for themselves but through something above them all: God, the One who must exist.

Those great thinkers could not go beyond this kind of oneness: for them, a possible being has dependent existence, but it is not itself a link. They speak of existence besides God's, and so treat possible beings as having their own distinct existence. It is connected to God and attributed to Him, and it can never be separated from that connection.[^V01-601] But through God’s grace we have proved—and will explain later—that a possible being’s existence cannot be split into an existence plus a separate link to the Creator. The being is itself a link to God: it is connected to Him in its very being, not by an added relation. In their view, a possible being has an existence that depends on God. In ours, the being is itself a link to God. We have already pointed out the difference between these meanings and the different terms for them, so they will not be confused just because the same word is used for both.

One respected scholar of a later generation tried to reach the heights attained by the mystics and the great philosophers. In a treatise called *al-Zawrāʾ*, devoted to the unity of existence, he wrote: blackness, considered as a state of a body, exists; considered as an independent thing, it does not. A garment exists as a form in cotton, but if considered a thing separate from cotton, it cannot exist in that respect.

Use this as a guide to all realities, he says, and you will understand the claim that the fixed essences have never even caught the scent of existence: they have never appeared and never will; only traces of them appear. Those are his words. He added other chapters, but none is stronger or clearer than this passage.

How can he claim to fly to the sky on such weak wings? The confusion in this account is plain to anyone who has studied these subjects closely. Has he not confused dependent existence with linking existence? When we say “the body is black,” the word “black,” as the predicate in this statement, exists only as something said of the body. But that does not prevent blackness from existing in another way, when we are not considering it simply as a predicate in a statement—even if its existence in itself is the very same existence it has for the body.

He says that blackness does not exist as an independent thing. If he means that blackness is not a substance, he is right: a quality cannot be a substance. But this is not the only way to consider blackness. We can consider it as a quality in itself, apart from its role as a feature of something. There is no doubt that its relation to a subject is not part of what blackness is when we consider it simply in itself.

If he means that blackness, considered according to its own nature, does not exist, then we cannot accept that. A quality has existence in itself, just as a substance does. The difference is that a quality’s existence in itself is the very same as its existence for the thing it belongs to. A substance exists in itself and for itself. A quality exists in itself, but not for itself; it exists for another thing. As we said earlier, to exist for itself means not to depend on another thing.[^V01-602]

#### Chapter — When existence is called a second-order concept, and what that means

Philosophers use the term 'second-order concept' in two ways. In the first sense, it refers to descriptions we form by thinking about things and the ideas from which we draw those descriptions. These include abstract nouns, features that necessarily follow from a thing’s nature, and relations between things. At other times, it means concepts studied by logic, such as “universal,” “particular,” and “kind.” These apply to concepts already in the mind, and statements made with them are themselves mental statements. These are the subject matter of logic, unlike the first group. In the first sense, the abstract idea of “existence” or “being real”—not existence itself as a reality—is a second-order concept. So are “thinghood,” possibility, necessity, and the terms derived from them. They are second-order concepts in metaphysics, not in the logical sense.[^V01-603]

More strictly, second-order concepts in logic are those that apply to first-order concepts as they exist in the mind. Their being in the mind is part of the setting for the judgment, not part of what is being described.[^V01-604] This is what philosophers mean when they say that second-order concepts depend on first-order ones. Existence, thinghood, and similar concepts do not belong to this group.

Questions about whether such concepts exist in the mind or outside it, and whether they help us reach new knowledge, belong to general philosophy. It has shown that a general concept can be a species, a broader kind, a difference, a special feature, or a common feature. When a general concept is considered as one of these and as something that can help us reach knowledge, it becomes a subject of logic. Logic then studies the features that necessarily follow from it. Necessity, impossibility, and possibility also serve as conditions under which second- and third-order concepts become subjects of logic. For example, once general philosophy establishes that a universal can be necessary, possible, or impossible—a universal considered under those conditions becomes a subject of logic. The same applies to the subjects of other sciences: a higher science establishes that they exist in the sense needed for them to be studied as subjects, while the science below it explains what they are.[^V01-605] This also suggests that a thing exists before its nature is defined, and that what a maker directly brings about is existence, not nature. This is the point we are discussing.

We can describe real things in different ways. Whiteness is a feature present in a white thing. Blindness is different: we recognise it from what the thing lacks. In either case, the description depends on the thing as it really exists. In our view, though, only existence itself is directly present outside the mind. A nature is present there only by being one with some mode of existence.[^V01-606]

Other features have no existence outside the mind in either of these ways. Their existence is only as a mental feature of something that exists in the mind, such as treating “human being” as a species or individual people as particulars.[^V01-607] When we say that Zayd is particular in reality, we do not mean that there is an external feature called “particularity” attached to him. Nor do we mean that Zayd, as he exists outside the mind, is particular in the mind’s view.[^V01-608]

In this broader sense, such concepts are not confined to statements about our thoughts. Sometimes what they describe is a nature simply as it is, not as an idea in the mind or as an object outside it. This is so with features that necessarily follow from a nature, even if the mind is where we consider them. Statements such as “a nature is possible” and “four is even” are true statements about the nature itself. Logical second-order concepts are part of this broader group, but statements made with them are only mental. By contrast, the broader, philosophical sense can be used in statements that are true of things or in statements that exist only in the mind.

Let me add a point. Some thinkers allow a thing to be truly described by a feature that does not exist in itself. One eminent scholar explains that for something to be described “outside” or “in the mind” means that the thing being described exists in that setting in a way that makes the description true of it. This requires the thing itself to exist there; the feature does not need to. It is enough for the thing to exist in a way that lets the mind draw that feature from it. The same applies to being described in the mind. For example, “human being” is universal because its existence in the mind lets the mind draw the feature of universality from it.

On this account, to say that a feature belongs to something means that the thing exists in a way that lets us recognise that feature in it. The feature need not exist separately. That was the scholar’s account.[^V01-609] It has several problems. The truth[^V01-610] is that being described is a relation between two things that differ in how they exist in that setting.[^V01-611] To say that one side exists there but the other does not is arbitrary.

Things do differ in how fully they exist, and each has its own share of existence. Every feature has a level of existence and effects of its own. This includes relations, absences, and powers or capacities. They have a weak share of existence, and a thing can be described by them only when they exist for it.[^V01-612]

This applies to every feature. If whiteness is not really present in a body, we cannot truthfully call that body white. The same applies when we say an animal is blind or the sky is above the earth. In books such as *The Healing* and *The Completion*, scholars ask: “If a feature does not exist, how can something nonexistent belong to a thing?” They mean that something with no existence in itself cannot exist for something else. But this does not disprove the claim that things can be described by relations, absences, and capacities. As we have seen, these features exist in a limited way, but they still exist. That is enough to make the descriptions true. The corresponding lack of existence prevents a thing from having that feature.

Sometimes a feature’s share in existence is stronger than that of the thing described by it. This is so when prime matter receives bodily and natural forms, and whenever matter receives a form, as we will explain later. So there is no basis for requiring the subject to exist while not requiring the feature to exist, as this scholar does. Someone could just as easily reverse the claim. Since this account does not require either side to exist, another thinker could say that being described in any setting means that the feature has a mode of existence there that lets us judge it of the subject, whether the feature is added to the subject or drawn from it. They could then argue, using the same reasoning, that the feature must exist in that setting but the subject need not.

So the distinction this scholar makes between the subject and its feature—saying that one exists and the other does not—is unsound.

Keep one point in mind. If, by God's grace, you understand that things exist at different levels of fullness and strength, you can answer a serious objection raised against the great philosophers by those whose understanding is limited. They define wisdom as knowledge of real things as they are outside the mind. Yet they also study concepts drawn from other concepts, along with seven kinds of relationships between things.

Remember that every thing has its own level of existence, with its own degree of appearance and actuality. The highest is God: self-sufficient, necessary in Himself, and dependent on nothing. He is pure actuality, free from any trace of possibility, limitation, or lack. Everything else has some degree of essential possibility and limitation. The farther a thing is from the source of existence and necessity, the more limited it is and the more possibility it has.

At the lowest level, a thing’s existence as a substance depends entirely on the form present in it. Its actuality is nothing but potentiality and readiness. Its unity as one thing is also, in one respect, a multiplicity of separate parts, and in another, a unity of connected parts. If substances can have such limited existence, how much weaker must the existence of their features be? These descend through ever weaker degrees of possibility until one feature has no reality beyond its longing and movement toward another feature—of quality, place, or position. It moves toward that other feature in stages and over time. This is the kind of existence motion has in the outside world. If first philosophy accepts motion as real, it must accept this kind of existence, which fits the world outside the mind. To claim that motion has some other, fixed kind of existence is ignorance opposed to wisdom.[^V01-613]

#### Chapter — Existence is pure good

This question[^V01-614] becomes clear once we establish that existence is more than an idea in the mind, however obvious that idea may be. Something real corresponds to it outside the mind: the reality of things actually existing.

Later thinkers treated existence as merely the act of existing, spoken of in the abstract. But here existence means what makes something real, whether we are speaking of existence itself or of a thing’s essence. Anyone who says the concept of existence has no reality outside the mind beyond this abstract idea cannot rightly claim that existence is pure good.[^V01-615]

Good is what reasonable people value, what things desire and seek, and what they are drawn to by nature, choice, and instinct. Things do not seek an abstract word or an idea that exists only in the mind. This is so clear that even the simplest mind should see it without having to reason it out.

When we see each thing’s existence as the way it appears—given by God, the One who exists necessarily, who brings natures out of the darkness of nonexistence and into the light of existence—we can see that goodness truly belongs to existence. Existence may be free of evil or mixed with it. Evil is a shortfall in a thing’s existence, or its complete absence. Evil is therefore always a kind of absence: either a thing itself is absent, or it lacks some perfection or good quality. Evil has no reality of its own.[^V01-616]

Possible essences and the fixed forms held in the mind are neither good nor evil in themselves; considered on their own, they are neither existent nor nonexistent. As we have explained, the existence attributed to them is their goodness, and their nonexistence is their evil. So existence is pure good, and nonexistence pure evil. The fuller and more complete a thing’s existence, the greater its goodness.

The greatest good in every respect is existence with no absence; full actuality with no unrealized potential; truth without falsehood; necessity rather than mere possibility; perfection without deficiency; and lastingness without change or renewal. The closer another being comes to this highest good, the greater the good it possesses. From there the order descends, step by step, to beings whose existence is weaker and less complete. This continues until we reach the lowest level: prime matter. It has no independent existence of its own; it is real only as the possibility underlying other things. It is “complete” only in its incompleteness, “noble” only in its lowliness. It acts by receiving, takes shape through its indeterminacy, and is distinguished only by its broad kind. We will prove this later. Prime matter is the source of evils and absences, the basis of deficiencies and pains. Yet it is also the net that catches rational souls—the heavenly birds held in cages made from the elements.[^V01-617]

Things remain good, both in themselves and in what follows from them, until the order of existence reaches the world of space, time, and conflict. But when this chain reaches the world of bodies and darkness, the crowded confines of material life, some forms of existence—though good in themselves and beneficial to the things they suit—are called evil in relation to what they harm, distress, or destroy. They bring about the loss of a thing itself or of one of its perfections. So evil in itself is one of these two kinds of absence. Existence, simply as existence, is not evil; as you have seen, it is pure good.

True evil is never sought in itself. Relative evil follows by accident from something truly good, which is sought in itself: existence in its own nature. What follows from a thing’s nature is not brought about separately by the one who causes it. As we have said, evils arise from the limits of individual things and from existence falling short of the fullest perfection and greatest beauty.

#### Chapter — Existence has no opposite or equal

Two opposites[^V01-618] must belong to the same kind of thing, though not to the broadest class of all. But, as we will explain, existence itself belongs to no such class. So existence, simply as existence, has no opposite. A pair of opposites must also differ as much as possible. But two existences, considered simply as existences, do not differ in that way. Nor does the general nature of existence differ from any idea that can exist. No reality is more general than existence, so that existence could fall under it together with other things and share its features. For this reason, existence itself has no equal or likeness either.

Specific existences, however, can oppose or resemble one another because they are distinguished by meanings and concepts beyond existence itself. So existence, simply as existence, has no opposite and no equal. How could it? Opposites and like things are all existents: they either differ or match. But existence exists through itself, not through something added to it. It therefore stands apart from all the realities whose opposites or likenesses are found among their members. Nothing is like it. Through existence, opposites become real and likenesses are formed. Existence itself appears in the form of opposites and shows itself in things that resemble one another, and in all other things. These differences belong only to the ways existence is limited and appears in different forms. In existence itself, all such differences fade, and all aspects come together. Every pair of opposing or similar features is absorbed into existence itself; the difference lies only in how the mind considers it.

Some raise this objection: if everything shares in existence, then even what we call its opposite or its equal must exist. That would mean opposites or equals exist together, actually or potentially, or that one could apply to the other.[^V01-619] This argument fails. We do not accept that existence applies to every idea in every sense. It does not apply to nonexistence as nonexistence, though it may apply to the idea of nonexistence as one of our thoughts.[^V01-620] If someone says existence has an opposite or equal, that opposite or equal cannot be found in existence or even imagined as existence itself; it can only be discussed as one idea among others. The rule about sharing a broad kind then does not apply, so the claim has not been proved.[^V01-621] It is not obviously absurd, in any case, to say that a feature can be attributed to the thing it opposes.

To continue: the idea of existence differs in meaning from other ideas, but it is not incompatible with them. Every idea has some reality, either outside the mind or in it. Even negative descriptions, though they refer to nonexistence, are in one respect tied to existence. Thus every distinct aspect or conflicting feature traces back in some way to the reality of existence. The fact that incompatible things do not exist together in the outside world—which is only one level of existence—does not prevent them from coming together in existence itself, considered simply as existence.

Existence is opposed to nonexistence, but not to the idea of nonexistence itself. Considered as an idea, nonexistence can be present in the mind, just like any other general idea. What existence cannot cover is not an idea but what the mind supposes the idea refers to: nonexistence, or something nonexistent, as though it were real. There is nothing to say about such a thing; it is neither a thing nor an idea. The mind invents an object for the idea of nonexistence and judges that imagined object to be false and impossible. It does not reject the idea itself, which is present in the mind. This applies to absolute nonexistence and to specific kinds of nonexistence too. There is one further point: a specific absence, like blindness, must belong to some thing, just as the corresponding capacity for sight does.

Absolute existence applies to anything real in any way. Its opposite is absolute nonexistence, which denies every kind of existence. Yet the two can be present together without being opposites, as when we imagine the idea of something absolutely nonexistent. In that thought, we have stripped it of every kind of existence. But the thought itself is still a kind of existence, and stripping it of existence is itself a relation in thought. This idea is therefore not fully stripped of thought: thinking is existence in the mind, so this imagined thing is one instance of existence. See how the light of existence reaches everywhere, even to every idea and meaning, including “nothing,” absolute nonexistence, and the impossible—when we consider them as ideas in the mind, not as actual absences.

We have already distinguished two ways of saying that something belongs to a thing: because it expresses what that thing is, or because it is a description we can truly apply to it. This distinction answers the problem of the absolutely unknown and similar cases. Here we can say that the mind can imagine every idea, even its own nonexistence, the nonexistence of nonexistence, absolute nonexistence, what does not exist in the mind, and all impossible things. It can consider the absolutely unknown, two contradictory ideas, or a word whose meaning depends on its place in a phrase. The mind can then say that the absolutely unknown cannot be described, that contradictions cannot both be true, and that such a word cannot stand alone. But the mind does not imagine the actual reality of the absolutely unknown, the actual joining of contradictions, a real instance of a preposition, a real instance of absolute nonexistence, or a partner to God.[^V01-622]

Anything the mind pictures is either a possible thing or an idea that exists in the mind. We apply a label to it only as an idea, not as a real example of what the label names. We do not say, in the ordinary sense, that any of these imagined things is a real contradiction, absolute nonexistence, or a partner to God. These ideas do not name any fixed nature in the mind or outside it. Rather, the mind supposes that some thing is an example of one of these ideas, even though such a thing would be impossible by its very nature. Because the mind pictures the idea as applying to that imagined thing, it judges that the thing cannot be described or spoken of, cannot exist, or cannot have a meaning on its own. These are not firm, direct claims. They work like conditional claims, where neither side is true.

The idea of the absolutely unknown, for example, can be described when we speak of the idea itself, even though the rule that nothing can be said applies to what the mind supposes it refers to. The same applies to absolute nonexistence and to any idea whose own nature does not appear in the mind—whether because it is empty and false, or because it is so complete and real that the mind cannot contain it. For example, when we say that God’s knowledge is identical with His essence, this claim does not apply to the idea of God in our minds, since His essence is not present to us in its full reality. The ideas we have of His true attributes are only ideas. Their unity with His essence applies not to those ideas, but to the reality that reason points to, beyond the limits of mind or imagination.

Consider first what it means to call something completely unknown. We mean that it cannot be known in any way—not even as something we are thinking about. Seen in that way, nothing can be said about it. But since this very act of considering it is a kind of knowing, the idea is mixed with knowledge even as it denies knowledge. This is why it is possible to say that nothing can be said about it, though the impossibility of describing it applies only to what the mind supposes it refers to.

The same is true of absolute nonexistence. The idea means stripping something of every kind of existence, both outside the mind and within it. That is why no claim can be made about it. Yet simply considering or imagining something—even by imagining that it is not considered or imagined—is one way it exists in the mind. In this respect, it has existence; in another, it is treated as having none. These two sides let us make a claim about it and also deny that claim. Tusi makes the same point in *Naqd al-Muhassal* (*Critique of the Summary*): “The removal of all existence, both outside the mind and within it, can be imagined as what is not established or imagined at all. We can make a claim about it as the thing we have imagined, but not as something that is not established. This is not a contradiction, because the subject is different in each case. Nor is there any bar to something being the opposite of one thing in one respect and part of it in another. For example, if we say that something is either present in the mind or not present in the mind, what is not present in the mind is the opposite of what is present there, because it is formed by adding ‘not’ to ‘present in the mind.’ Yet as an idea, it is itself part of what is present in the mind.”

#### Chapter — Nonexistence is one concept

Nonexistence, considered in itself, has one simple meaning.[^V01-623] We can distinguish one absence from another only by connecting each to something different. In reality or in imagination, there are no separate kinds of nonexistence, each belonging to a different nonexistent thing, nor are there many kinds of negation for the many things that are denied. Whatever lies in the realm of nonexistence and hidden nothingness is alike in being nonexistent. Just as something that does not exist in a given setting is nothing there, so too nonexistence itself is nothing.[^V01-624]

Differences among absences come from the things and qualities they are related to.[^V01-625] The mind pictures things or states that differ—cause and effect, a condition and what depends on it, or a pair of opposites—and connects the idea of nonexistence to them. Then the absence of a cause differs from the absence of its effect, because the first can bring about the second. The absence of a condition differs from the absence of the thing that depends on it, because without the condition that thing cannot exist. In the same way, the absence of one opposite makes room for the other. Apart from these relationships, one absence does not differ from another. There is no separate nonexistence for each thing, nor one nonexistent thing distinct from another. The imagination sees that a hand differs from a foot and wrongly concludes that the absence of one must differ from the absence of the other. If that were true, every thing would have infinitely many separate absences, piled on top of one another without end.

Some philosophers speak of an endless chain of absences, such as the absences associated with events without end. But they mean that we can always imagine another step backward. They do not mean that an infinite chain of separate absences actually exists. Whatever we actually work through is finite, though there is no one point at which we must stop.

The mind divides nonexistence by relating it to many things: the absence of this thing, then the absence of that thing. This is like dividing one continuous length into one part and another. We can imagine the parts separated and say that one comes before another in position, while the whole comes before its parts by nature. In the same way, we can speak of earlier and later absences when one is the cause of another.

An endless division of a continuous length means there is no final piece so small that we cannot imagine dividing it further. In the same way, an endless sequence of absences means there is no final absence that prevents us from imagining another one before it as its cause. It does not mean there is an actually infinite chain of separate things.[^V01-626]

Nonexistence, then, is one and has no distinct parts or form of its own. Nothing in reality is itself nonexistence. If we ask what nonexistence is, there is nothing to name; and if we ask what a thing is, nonexistence cannot be the answer. To call something nonexistent is simply to say that existence does not apply to it. When nonexistence is said of a thing, this means that existence is not said of it. The thing does not acquire a piece of nonexistence.

#### Chapter — How the absence of a cause and the absence of its effect relate to each other

Nonexistence, simply as nonexistence, cannot be understood, any more than it can exist.[^V01-627] Yet the human mind can form an idea of anything and use that idea as a label. Just as it forms ideas of the natures of things that exist outside the mind, it also forms ideas for things that have no real nature of their own.[^V01-628] These ideas apply to their supposed examples only by assumption, as we explained earlier.

Absences and things that exist only in thought become distinct through what the mind connects them with. To think of the absence of a particular thing, we must first think of that thing. Once held in thought, it can be judged in different ways, including as cause or effect.[^V01-629] So we can say that the absence of a cause causes the absence of its effect, but not that the absence of an effect causes the absence of its cause—even though we can infer from the missing effect that its cause is absent.

The key is to distinguish two ways in which the absence of a cause can be called a cause. First, because the idea of the cause’s absence is present in the mind, the mind can judge it to be a cause, even if that is not what the judgment truly refers to. What the judgment truly describes as the cause is the cause’s absence itself—not the mental picture or idea of that absence. We can make this judgment only when the idea is present in the mind.

Second, the idea of the cause’s absence in the mind itself brings about the idea of the effect’s absence there. But the absence of an effect causes the absence of its cause only in this second sense: we infer the cause’s absence from the effect’s absence. So the absence of a cause causes the absence of its effect both in reality and in thought; the absence of an effect leads us to the absence of its cause only in thought, as evidence.

As absences themselves, one is specifically the cause and the other its effect, though we judge them through the mind’s reflection of them. As mental pictures, whichever one appears first can lead to the other, so there is no circular reasoning. Just as the existence of a cause brings about the existence of its effect, while the effect’s existence gives us evidence of its cause, so the absence of a cause brings about the absence of its effect, while the effect’s absence gives us evidence that the cause is absent. If the cause is absent, its effect must be absent too. But the effect’s absence does not prove that the cause is absent. The cause may be absent along with its effect, which would explain why the effect is absent. So the effect is absent with, and because of, the cause’s absence. The cause is absent along with the effect’s absence, but not because of it.

#### Chapter — How nonexistence applies to itself

We can speak of nonexistence just as we speak of anything else. For example, we can say that nonexistence does not exist outside the mind. But this raises a puzzle. When we speak of the absence of something, we name a particular kind of absence. At the same time, that absence is the opposite of the thing whose absence it is. So if we attach it to itself—if we speak of the absence of nonexistence—does it become both a kind and an opposite at once? Those roles seem to conflict: being a kind means the idea applies to its subject, while being an opposite means it excludes what it opposes.

Keep in mind that the relation between nonexistence and the thing it is said to belong to exists only in the mind.[^V01-630] Yet the mind’s act of relating nonexistence to something shows that the thing is absent or destroyed. The thing it is said of, as pictured in the mind, gives the idea of nonexistence its limit: it makes the idea definite, and is present in thought along with it. So nonexistence tied to that thing is a particular kind of nonexistence. But when this idea names a thing that has been ruined or destroyed by nonexistence, it stands opposite to that thing.[^V01-631]

These two relations apply in different ways. Being a kind is a relation among ideas in the mind, like other logical ideas. Being opposite is a relation among things outside the mind, even though the mind can hold both opposites together as ideas. This explanation untangles the issue better than some later philosophers’ accounts.

#### Chapter — A nonexistent thing cannot be restored

Nonexistence means only that existence is absent. Since existence is a thing’s very identity, one individual can have only one identity—and therefore one existence and one nonexistence. The same individual cannot exist twice or be absent twice. This is what the mystics mean when they say that God never reveals Himself in the same form twice.[^V01-632] It follows that something which has ceased to exist cannot return as exactly the same individual. If its identity really were the same, its existence would have to be the same too. Yet the argument treats that single existence as occurring more than once. It would be both one and many, which is a contradiction. It would also mean that the beginning and the return were the same state, though they are opposites. That is impossible.

If the beginning and return are no different, then the first return cannot be distinguished from a second, or a third from a fourth, and so on. Once one return is allowed, infinitely many returns would be possible, with no reason to stop at one point rather than another. This is plainly false. The same reasoning applies to saying that one and the same thing can be absent more than once.

You might object: many events that happen in time do not exist, then exist, then cease to exist. So the same thing has two absences. If this is allowed for absence, why not allow more than one existence too? The answer is that we have already explained what it means for nonexistence to be attributed to something: the thing is wholly absent. There is no real subject that exists while nonexistence is added to it or drawn from it. The mind pictures a thing and applies the idea of nonexistence to it. So absences multiply in thought only when the things they are related to differ.[^V01-633] There is no individual thing before its existence or after it that we can call one, many, or identical. The mind simply relates absence to a nature whose existence is limited to a certain time, before or after that time.

To say that a thing did not exist before it came to be, or will not exist after it ceases, means that its existence has a limited span. Its capacity to exist does not extend into earlier or later times. Nonexistence itself is one; it is not, in itself, earlier or later. The mind’s imagination pictures a temporal event as having an endless absence before it, then existence, then a later absence—as if these were two ends with the event between them.[^V01-634]

Ordinary imagination goes further. It pictures nonexistence as something that arrives, removes a thing’s existence from reality, and wipes its identity away. They overlook that the existence of things consists in ways the True Source reveals Himself, like rays from the First Source’s light. Each of these appearances remains what it is; it does not turn into another.[^V01-635] Someone whose view is too limited to take in the whole thinks that each one disappears from existence and is replaced by another. But consider what it would mean for nonexistence to overtake something that is real. It would have to happen either at the very level and time where that thing exists, which would bring opposites together at once, or outside that level and time. Yet a thing can exist only at its own level, where it becomes real and appears. Each thing has its own mode and place in existence, with the qualities, times, and places that belong to it. These do not move from it to something else. Since each thing has only the one mode of existence its prior causes and conditions give it, there is no other state of being for nonexistence to enter and erase, or to take over in its place.
