They argued, too, that the priority of a nature to existence is not among the five familiar kinds of priority. It would have to follow if the nature itself were made. Finally, they argued that, although a thing’s denial of itself is always impossible, in contingent natures this is impossible only when we consider them as existent. We can say that a nonexistent thing is not itself, and a negative statement can be true even when its subject is absent. A contingent thing, considered in itself, does not resist nonexistence; in itself, it is not itself.[^V01-706] The divine names include “O He, O who is He, O who is no he but He.”[^V01-707] Until a thing exists, it cannot truly be said of itself. So what first and directly makes it need a cause is its being existent, not its nature.

The first argument was answered by saying that possibility is not what most people take it to be: its meaning is more precise, as we have already explained.[^V01-708] As for the second argument, it is indeed a thing’s nature that we describe as existent, but not in either of the usual ways. It is not like an essential feature, which applies when we consider the nature alone; nor is it like an accidental feature, which requires some further aspect to be added to the thing. Rather, the nature is described as existent because it has been brought about and established by its maker. This aspect lies outside what is being described, and is considered as a condition for the judgment, not as a limit on the thing itself.

In short, before a nature has been brought about by its maker, none of its essential or accidental features can be truly predicated of it. Once it has been brought about, its essential features apply—not because it was made, but simply while it is in that state. Existence, by contrast, is predicated of it because it was brought about: through its maker and at the time it was made.[^V01-709]

The third argument is answered by saying that a nature’s priority to existence is another kind of priority, established by the proof. This is priority in what something is, rather than priority in time. A thing’s defining features also come before the thing in this sense and, in another sense, by the order of nature.

The fourth argument is answered by saying that the fact that we can deny a nonexistent thing of itself does not mean that we can deny a contingent thing of itself without qualification. Not considering a thing’s existence does not mean that we are considering its nonexistence. And the fact that a thing is itself when it exists does not mean that it is itself only on the condition that it exists.

The essential features of a thing are predicated of it while it is made and exists. Existence is predicated of the Necessary Being through its own eternal reality, without any condition of time or other qualification. In this sense, only God is the absolute “He”: He is only He. Predicating existence resembles predicating a thing’s essential features in one respect, and differs from it in another.

In *al-Mutarahat*, Suhrawardi argues that natures are made by simple making. Since, on his view, existence is only a mental concept, a cause can be prior to its effect only by nature: the nature of the effect is a shadow of the nature of its cause, and the cause’s own nature comes first. A similar argument appears in another writer: we know directly that a maker’s first effect is the caused existent; but the caused existent must be a nature, since being described as existent, like other such relations, is only a mental consideration.

An even stronger version was given by our revered teacher, may God preserve his honor and standing. Since a nature itself is what makes it true to say that something exists, consider what would follow if the nature, in its own constitution, did not depend on a maker.[^V01-710] Then it would be existent in its own right and would no longer be contingent. That is impossible. So it must depend on a maker both in its basic constitution and in its being described as existent. In itself, in both respects, it is pure nonbeing, sheer negation, and pure potentiality. Its maker brings it into an established state by simple making; its existence then follows necessarily, without a separate act of making. These are our teacher’s words. We include them here as a mark of honor, in discussion with those who hold the opposing view.

Notice that all their arguments rest on treating existence as a mental concept, like “thingness” or “possibility.” We have shown that particular existences are real—indeed, they are the truest realities—and that only general existence is an abstract concept of the mind, like the general idea of animality. We have already hinted at the difference, and it will become clearer. Once their starting point is shown to be false, the rest of their argument falls with it.

Even if we grant that existence is only a mental concept, we still cannot grant that a nature itself is what “existent” applies to after the maker has brought it about.[^V01-711] If that were so, the nature would no longer depend on its maker in order to exist. This would turn a contingent nature into something necessary in itself.[^V01-712] For those thinkers, what makes something necessary in itself is that its own reality is the source of the judgment “existent.” What makes something contingent is that its own reality is not such a source. If, after its nature had been brought about, a contingent thing could itself be the source of the judgment “existent,” without our considering anything else or any other relation, then existence would belong to it by its own nature.

It does not help to say that a thing has its defining features without any reference to a cause or condition, whereas calling it “existent” requires us to consider that its maker brought it about. The nature’s being made, or its connection to its cause, must either be part of what “existent” applies to or not. If it is not, the problem remains: a contingent nature would become necessary in itself. If it is, then what “existent” applies to includes both the nature and this relation to its cause. The maker’s effect would then include both the nature and that further aspect. In the sense explained earlier, this means that the maker brings about the nature’s having existence, as Aristotle’s followers hold.[^V01-713]

It is remarkable that al-Dawani, despite being so deeply committed to the view that a nature itself is the maker’s effect, writes in one of his notes that the Necessary Being is pure existence, standing by itself, and free in itself from all limits and qualifications. It exists in itself, has its own identity, knows in itself, and has power in itself. By this he means that the basis for predicating all these attributes of it is its simple reality, which contains no multiplicity at all.

He says that other things are existent through something else: the maker brings them about in such a way that, when the mind considers them, it draws the idea of existence from them. They are existent because of the maker in this respect, not through themselves, unlike the Necessary Being.

After a passage we have left out, he says: “This general meaning, shared by all things, is an abstract idea the mind uses to describe them. In reality, it is identical with neither of them. Yet the basis for applying it to the Necessary Being is the Necessary Being itself; the basis for applying it to anything else is that thing’s nature insofar as it has been made by another. In both cases, the concept applied is added by the mind. But in contingent things, the mind draws it from an aspect they receive from their maker; in the Necessary Being, it comes from the Being itself. As we have said, the Necessary Being is existence that stands by itself. When the mind considers it, it draws the idea of existence from it, unlike everything else.” That is the end of his quotation.

In short, these thinkers say that contingent natures become existent in one of three ways. Existence may be added to them, as Aristotle’s followers are said to hold; the maker may bring about the nature itself, as Suhrawardi’s Illuminationist school is often said to hold; or the maker may make the nature related to itself, as some philosophers concerned with divine matters hold. These thinkers reject the first view, and we have shown what is wrong with the second. So they are left with the third: what is made is the nature’s relation to its maker. In other words, the maker performs a compound act, placing a relation between the nature and existence.

Here is another way to refute this view. If a nature depended on its maker in its very constitution, the maker would be part of what makes that nature what it is. The maker would therefore come before the nature in the way an essential feature comes before the thing that has it—a kind of priority these thinkers themselves accept. It would follow that we could not think of a nature without also thinking of its maker and its relation to that maker. But we can. We can sometimes grasp a nature fully[^V01-714] without considering anything else, let alone its maker, and say that a nature considered in itself is nothing but itself. This shows that natures and general kinds are not related to anything else in themselves. Their relation to something else comes from another aspect, whether that aspect is an idea drawn by the mind or something added in reality.

This does not mean that a nature can exist apart from existence outside the mind, as the Mu‘tazilites claimed, or apart from it in the mind, as some Sufis are said to claim about the “fixed archetypes.” A contingent thing that has not come to exist is not anything at all, and firm proofs show that thinghood cannot be separated from existence. The difference is this: those thinkers say that a nature depends on its maker in its very self, while depending on existence only indirectly. We say that what makes it need a cause is its being existent—that is, its becoming something that can truly be judged existent—not its nature considered in itself. Neither view requires nature and existence to come apart.

Another way to refute this view: the nature of a contingent thing is not particular in itself. If it were, it could not be general—that is, open to being applied to many things in the mind.[^V01-715] Its becoming a particular thing must therefore come from something added to it. These thinkers hold that a thing cannot exist until it is particular. Careful thinkers say that it becomes particular through its own specific existence, whether that existence is real outside the mind or an idea the mind draws from it.[^V01-716]

The same general nature has the same relation to its maker in every instance we can imagine.[^V01-717] Unless the maker determines it as one particular thing, it cannot be brought about. So what the maker brings about directly is not the general nature by itself, but that nature together with its particularity, its existence, or whatever we choose to call that further aspect. Someone might object that the maker itself makes the nature particular, without anything being added to it.

But this works only if the maker’s effect is some form of the reality of existence, not a nature.[^V01-718] A nature is a general idea that we can consider in itself, apart from its maker and everything else. If it were already particular and existent in itself, it would be necessary in itself, as we have shown. If it is not, then it is clear that it can become particular and existent in reality only by changing from what it was in itself. If it remained exactly as it was when it came to exist, it would not become particular or existent, even through another. The change must happen either by adding something, such as existence, or by newly relating the nature to something else. The first option is rejected by these thinkers; the second would mean that the nature itself turned into something else, which is impossible by its very nature.

Another problem follows for those who say that makers make natures. Since they treat existence as a mental concept, the things that affect and are affected by one another would be natures alone, with existence left out. Then made things—especially everything except the first made thing—would be necessary results of natures. But, for these thinkers, a nature’s necessary result is only a mental idea and has no reality at all. Think carefully about this.[^V01-719]

A Throne-inspired reminder: Suhrawardi and his followers, following ancient philosophers such as Agathodaemon, Empedocles, Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, held that God, the intelligences, and the souls are luminous beings. Their light and existence are not separate from what they are. So we might understand Suhrawardi’s claim that existence is a mental concept to mean that only general existence—the familiar, easy-to-grasp idea—is mental. The particular existences, which are themselves levels of light, would still be real. We might also understand his arguments against saying that a nature is existent as arguments against existence being added to a nature from outside, not against particular instances of existence being real in themselves.

But this reading raises a problem about light that belongs to another thing, rather than existing on its own. For Suhrawardi, light is one simple reality, and its different instances vary only in strength and weakness. At the highest level is the rich, self-sufficient light of the Necessary Being. At the lowest, light is only a feature of another thing, whether that thing is luminous or dark. Why could one instance of a single reality stand by itself while another depends on something else?[^V01-720]

Or perhaps Suhrawardi’s aim is to debate Aristotle’s followers, as he often does, and then quietly point toward what he himself believes. If so, his view avoids the problem that later thinkers face when they say general natures are made. For him, particular luminous beings are like the individual existences described by Aristotle’s followers: each is an individual reality that can be known only by direct awareness of it, not by forming a mental picture.

As we have said, being at a particular level is part of what each level of existence is.[^V01-721] We cannot think of one level without first considering the level before it. Each existence’s connection to what comes before it is part of its very reality; we cannot understand it as disconnected from its cause.[^V01-722] So to make such a being is simply to make its connection to the First Being. The two cannot be separated, either in reality or in thought.

This is unlike general natures. We can think of them apart from other things because they may be found in the world or in the mind, and their meanings are different from either kind of existence and from their relation to God or to anything else. Their only connections are to their own essential parts, which are also general ideas. Even ideas that describe relations are not, by their own nature, related to their maker: the thing related and the thing it is related to stand alike in this respect. For this reason, we cannot judge that a nature exists unless we consider some aspect beyond the nature itself.

For a general nature, possibility means that existence and nonexistence have equal standing for it—or that being made and not being made are equally open to it, so neither is necessary.[^V01-723] But the possibility of luminous beings means that they depend on something else: if we ignored their maker, they would be nothing at all, neither existent nor a nature. Ignoring their maker would be like ignoring what they are. This is unlike general natures, whose meanings we can grasp without considering anything else.[^V01-724]

For the Illuminationists who hold to simple making, the basis for causation is that a thing is pure existence, as *al-Talwihat* puts it, or pure light, in the language of *The Philosophy of Illumination*.[^V01-725] For them, the true maker is the Necessary Being: existence or light at its fullest, with no lack at all. As we have learned, existence is known only through direct awareness; the reality of light is grasped only through a direct connection in which it is present. If we knew any part of it only as a mental picture, its reality would be changed, as we have explained elsewhere.

So, for them, the effects that are luminous beings are real, individual results of their makers’ simple acts, not merely ideas in the mind. This does not mean that a made being is only a mental result in both its real existence and its existence in the mind. That would follow only if the natures of its makers could be present in the mind, but we have said they cannot. This shows that there are two kinds of nature and reality. One is identical with existence: it is neither general nor particular in the sense of having an added feature that makes it individual, because, as the First Teacher says, its existence and its individuality are one.[^V01-726] The other kind is different from existence and can be shared by many things. The necessary results of the first kind are real, individual beings; the necessary results of the second are only general ideas, with no existence outside the mind. The truth of this account becomes clear only after careful study of their views with a sound mind and character.

It is also strange that most people who say makers make natures reject any difference in degree among instances of the same general kind or species. Yet they treat existence as a mental concept and say, openly or by implication, that the nature of a cause comes before the nature of its effect. If the cause and effect are both kinds of substance—for example, the Active Intellect and prime matter—they must admit that the cause’s substance comes before the effect’s substance. They are reluctant to accept this.

#### Closer examination

The question of differences in degree can be examined in a way that clears away the doubts, God willing. Here is a teaching from the Throne: sound reasoning shows that existence itself is what the maker brings about through simple making. Natures themselves are not made in this way, since, considered in themselves, they have no relation to their maker. We have shown that anything insofar as it is caused is connected to its cause in some way, though the nature of this connection is hard to grasp. This is true whether existence has a nature that by itself requires a relation to another nature, with nothing between the two, or not. Someone might ask: why is the maker’s first effect not a nature’s being existent, as Aristotle’s followers commonly say—in the sense of a compound statement?[^V01-727]

I say this view is mistaken for two reasons. First, the maker’s actual effect must itself be something real. But being described as existent, however we understand that description, is only an idea. It cannot be what the maker brings about. Second, although a thing’s having a feature does not depend on that feature’s existence, it does depend on the existence of the thing that has it. So the nature must already exist before it can be described as existent. If it exists through that same existence, it comes before itself, and we end up bringing about something that already exists. If it exists through another existence, we must ask about that earlier existence and its being described as existent, and the chain goes on forever. There is a reasonable version of the view: the maker’s first and direct effect is an undivided reality that the mind can analyze into nature and existence—that is, what a compound statement expresses.[^V01-728] But once we analyze it, we see that existence itself is the direct effect, not the nature, since a nature considered in itself has no relation to anything outside it.

It is now clear that what makers bring about directly is existence, and nothing else. The mind then finds in each of these existences general features drawn from that very existence. It draws these features from the existence and applies them without considering anything outside it or beyond the level that makes it what it is. These features are called essential attributes. The mind then connects them to existence and describes them as existent. This is what the careful thinker al-Tusi means in his book *The Undoing of the Undoing*: the existence of caused things comes before their natures in reality, but the mind considers it after them. So the objection that a feature cannot come before what it describes does not apply here. What is real first and foremost is existence; the mind then draws the nature from it in itself and applies to that nature the derived description “existent,” taken from existence itself. In truth, what describes the nature is existence in this derived sense; what comes before it in itself is real existence. On our view, existence and nature stand in the opposite order from the one most people assume. Think this through carefully.

Something similar appears in the words of a careful thinker, who says that a power acts on a nature that is itself the existent thing.[^V01-729] On this view, the maker’s effect is, for example, blackness itself—the thing that exists—not its existence, not its being described as existent, and not the relation by which it is described. The mind links blackness to a maker because it exists, not simply because it is black. We say, for example, “It exists because of the maker.”

We do not say, “It is black because of him,” or “It is an accident from him.”[^V01-730] That is the end of the quotation.

This would be sound if by “the existent” he meant real existence itself, existing through itself and not through some added feature—like a relation that is related by its own nature rather than through another relation added to it, or like other things of this sort. But this thinker does not mean that. For him, “the existent” is a simple, universal idea that applies to everything and is obvious to the mind. There is no doubt that something understood in this way is not an effect of a maker, since it is only an idea.

Bahmanyar says in *The Attainment*: “When a maker gives existence, he brings about existence. Giving existence means giving its reality, not giving its existence, for existence has a reality and a nature. Every composite nature has a cause that makes it real, not a cause for the predicate ‘that nature’ to apply to it. A human being has a cause in becoming real and being constituted as a human, but no cause is needed for the statement ‘this is a human being.’ It seems that an existent with a cause must be composite, so that it can be caused. Also, a caused existent is possible in itself and therefore needs to be brought into actuality. By ‘caused,’ we mean that its reality, considered in itself, is not actual. Just as, when you think of a triangle, you necessarily think of its three lines, so when you think of a caused existence, you think of its cause.” That is the end of his words. There are several points here that support our position.[^V01-731] First, the maker’s effect, and what follows from it, is existence in its simple reality; the maker affects a nature by giving it existence. Second, he states plainly that a thing’s being predicated of itself has no cause—not a new cause, nor a cause of its existence. Third, the reality of a caused thing is constituted by the existence of its cause, so that we cannot understand it without that cause.

By “composite nature,” Bahmanyar means a contingent nature considered together with its existence, whether it is simple or composite in itself.[^V01-732]

A doubt and its answer: Someone might think that existence by itself cannot be caused, since existence is one single kind of reality. If a cause acted on existence alone, it would be a cause fit to produce every effect. For example, heat in water depends on a condition; otherwise, it would always flow from the separate source that produces it. If the condition affected only the existence of heat, and not its nature, then the condition for heat would also be a condition for cold, since cold and heat occur together in the same subject, water. So when water is present, heat would have to flow into it: its nature can receive heat, the source is ready to give it, and the condition is in place. The effect would then have to occur. This would imply that everything comes about—a claim that is plainly false, as sense and experience show.

Once you have grasped the principles we have established, you need no further effort to remove doubts of this kind. Remember this, my dear reader: take care not to misunderstand the subtle arguments and fine expressions of the philosophers, or their hints at difficult ideas. Many people heard them say, “Substance is substance by itself, and an accident is an accident by itself,” but did not understand what they meant. They thought the philosophers were saying that these things need no maker or cause at all. That is not what they meant.

The philosophers said this because, when they examined existences and their features and consequences, they found that existences are the subjects described and the things that bear those features. General meanings and ideas in the mind are all descriptions and consequences. They saw that, in thought and understanding, the differences among existent subjects come from differences in the features and descriptions that attach to them, whether essential or accidental.[^V01-733] The features themselves differ because of their own natures and existences.[^V01-734] These occupy different levels: some are more complete, others less; some are stronger, others weaker; some come first, others follow. God brought them about as distinct realities in themselves, not because of some further cause within them, but simply as they are.

For example, black things and white things differ because blackness and whiteness differ. Blackness and whiteness differ by their own natures, not because of some further cause. Anyone who thinks there must be another cause for their difference will be led on without end. Blackness and whiteness differ in themselves, not through some feature within them, but through their own natures, which are identical with their existence. This is what the philosophers mean. They do not mean that blackness, for example, was not made by a maker or produced by a cause, as many people unfamiliar with philosophy have supposed. You will understand this more clearly later.

A clarification, with a hint: An effect must be suited to its cause. We have established that the Necessary Being is existence itself and exists through its own reality. So what flows from it must be the existence of things, not their general natures, which have no likeness to Him.

Ibn Sina says in one of his treatises: “The First Good is, by its very nature, open and manifest to all beings. If this manifestation meant that something else acted upon Him,[^V01-735] then His exalted nature would have to be open to the influence of another. That is impossible. Rather, His nature is manifest through itself. Some beings, however, are unable to receive this manifestation, so He remains hidden from them. In truth, the veil is in those who are veiled: it is their limitation, weakness, and lack. His manifestation is nothing other than His own reality,[^V01-736] for what He is in Himself can mean nothing other than His very nature, as the theologians have explained. His nature is manifest to them, and for this reason the philosophers called it a form. The first being to receive this manifestation is the divine realm called the Universal Intellect. It becomes a distinct reality by receiving His manifestation, just as the image in a mirror becomes an image when the person it reflects appears. It is close to this meaning when people say that the Active Intellect is His image.[^V01-737] Be careful not to say ‘His likeness.’ This is the Necessary Being.[^V01-738]

“Everything affected by an agent is affected through an image that comes from that agent; every agent acts on what it affects through an image that comes from it. This is clear from observation.[^V01-739] Fire’s heat acts on a body by placing its image, warmth, in it. The same is true of the other powers that produce qualities. A rational soul acts on another rational soul like itself by placing its image there: an abstract form in the mind. A sword shapes a body by placing its own form there. A whetstone sharpens a knife by placing on its edge the image of what it touches: the evenness and smoothness of its parts.” That is the end of his words.

One of the mystics said that every caused thing is made up by its nature of two aspects: one that resembles and reflects its maker, and one that differs from and opposes it.[^V01-740] If it resembled its maker in every way, it would be the maker itself, not something made by it; it would be pure light. If it differed from its maker in every way, it could not come from that maker either, since a thing’s opposite cannot come from it; it would be pure darkness. The first, luminous aspect is called existence. The other, dark aspect is called nature. Nature does not come from the maker, because it is the aspect that makes the effect different from its maker. It is therefore an aspect that the maker does not possess, and nothing can come from what it does not possess. If nature came from the maker, it would be the aspect of likeness, and another aspect would then be needed to make the effect different. The effect is related to its cause like a shadow to light: it resembles the cause in its light and differs from it in its mixture with darkness.[^V01-741]

The dark aspect in a shadow does not flow from the light, nor is it part of the light, since it opposes the light and makes the shadow different from it. How, then, could it come from the light? In the same way, the aspect called nature in a caused thing does not come from its maker. This supports the view that nature is not made or given by the cause. Nature is simply what makes a thing what it is, and what distinguishes it from its maker and from everything else. It is the dark aspect we have described, which plays a role in simple things like the role matter plays in bodies.

Ibn Sina points to this kind of composition even in simple things in *The Healing*. He says: “What always exists through another is not simple in its reality, because what it has in itself is different from what it has through another. Its identity, as it exists, is made up of both. So nothing except the Necessary Being is free from what is potential and possible when considered in itself. The Necessary Being is the one true individual; everything else is a composite of two aspects.”

What a thing has in itself is its nature; what it has through another is its existence. Its reality is made up of these two aspects, as a body is made up of matter and form. For this reason, Ibn Sina ascribes potentiality and possibility to nature as he ascribes it to matter. There is still a difference between this kind of composition and the composition of a body from matter and form, just as possibility means different things in the two cases, as you will see later, God willing.[^V01-742]

Do not imagine that, by placing nature outside the realm of what is made, these philosophers have put it on the same footing as the Necessary Being and made it equally independent of a cause. Nature is unmade because it is beneath making: making requires some kind of realization, but being a nature involves no realization at all. As soon as a nature is realized in any way—even as something unrealized—it depends on a cause, because what is possible depends on its cause whether it exists or not. The Necessary Being, by contrast, is unmade because it is beyond making, through its complete reality and self-sufficiency. So how could something unmade because it falls below making be treated like something unmade because it is above making? Understand the difference.

Imam al-Razi was right when he said that the claim that natures are unmade follows from the question of absolute nature: considered in themselves, natures are neither existent nor nonexistent.

A consequence: A nature and a universal kind depend on their parts—such as broader kind and difference, or matter and form—in order to be constituted. This dependence concerns what they are in themselves, or what they are as existent. Their dependence on a maker and an end, by contrast, concerns their coming about. The first two are causes of a nature, whether considered in general or in some particular way of existing; the latter two are causes of its existence. So causation and being caused, when they mean bringing something about and coming about, apply to natures only when existence is considered together with them. This differs from causation and being constituted, which apply to a nature considered apart from whether it exists or not. This is also why knowledge involves two different tasks: judging whether a statement is true and understanding what a thing is.

Ibn Sina says in *The Healing*, at the start of the chapter on the subject of logic: “The mind cannot move from a simple idea alone to a judgment that something is true, because that idea by itself does not determine whether the thing exists or not.[^V01-743] A judgment must have a basis that brings it about, and nothing can serve as that basis whether it exists or not. So a simple idea does not suffice unless the thing’s existence or nonexistence—or some condition of it—is established. But we can often form a conception from a simple idea.”

Al-Dawani objected: “There is a problem here. First, the same point undermines conception, since the premises apply to it too. Second, the simple idea may bring about assent because it exists in the mind, without our first assenting to its existence there—just as it can bring about conception by itself. So Ibn Sina’s point is a fallacy, and it is strange to find it in a thinker like him.” That is what he says in his treatise *A Model of the Sciences*.

What we have said shows why forming an idea differs from judging that a claim is true. To judge whether a claim is true, we must first establish the reasons for it. Those reasons bring about our judgment; they are not simply parts of the idea being judged. A theoretical claim is first conceived before proof is given, without conceiving its premises or assenting to them in any way. Then, after considering the claim and its premises, the mind forms the premises that prove it and moves from them to assent. In that respect, the premises are like efficient causes of a nature’s existence, or of one of its features. Bahmanyar’s words support this: “The relation of first principles to all theoretical claims is like the relation of the agent that brings about all things to the things that exist.”[^V01-744]

A question that asks us to understand a thing—especially by defining it—depends on its near and remote principles in a different way. Its parts fit together and constitute it in meaning and nature, not by bringing it into existence. The parts of a definition stand to the thing defined in this way.[^V01-745]

This establishes the difference between accepting a claim as true and forming an idea of something. With a little thought, it also answers both objections.

#### Chapter — Can existence grow stronger or weaker?

Growth or decline in intensity is motion in quality, just as increase or decrease is motion in quantity.[^V01-746] Motion in a category means that, at each imagined moment, the changing thing is in a state of that category different—in kind, type, or some other way—from its state at another moment. Some think this means that the category itself changes in its state. That is wrong. To become blacker, for example, does not mean that one and the same blackness grows stronger. That would make blackness itself the thing moving, even though the first blackness is incomplete in itself and is not the same as the stronger one.

Nor can anyone say that the first state remains while something is added to it. If what is added is not blackness, then the blackness has not grown stronger in its blackness; another feature has appeared. If what is added is another blackness, two blacknesses would occupy one and the same thing, with no difference in their nature, place, or time. That is impossible.[^V01-747] Nor can two blacknesses become one: if both remain, they have not become one. The same is true if they both disappear and a third takes their place, or if one disappears and the other remains. So blackness grows stronger not by the first blackness remaining while another is added, but by the first ceasing to exist in the thing and a stronger blackness taking its place, while the thing remains through both states. The same reasoning applies when blackness grows weaker.

Once this is clear, we can see that existence itself does not move. This is obvious for those who treat existence as only a mental idea and say it multiplies only as the things that have it multiply. On our view, we have already seen that existence is not an extra feature attached to a nature. It is the thing’s very existence—its being existent—and, in reality, it is the thing itself. How could it change while what it is identical with remains unchanged, both in reality and in how it is brought about? Only when the mind views it in a certain way could it seem to change. Also, if existence itself moved, the thing in motion could not exist in a complete, actual way for as long as the motion lasted. At no point in that motion would it be fully settled in the very existence that was changing. A thing cannot change in what it depends on to exist, such as existence itself or the basic forms that make it what it is. There is another issue to consider here, which we will explain later, God willing.[^V01-748]

An objection, and a warning: If motion means what we have just described, someone may argue that nothing can change in any of these kinds of features. A subject can move from one instance to another only if those individual instances exist in reality. But they do not. If they did, one instant would have to follow another with nothing between them, and infinitely many ordered things would be confined between two limits.[^V01-749] We can answer that, although these instances do not exist as separate actual things, they exist as near possibilities. That is, at any imagined moment, if motion stopped then, the moving subject would be in one definite instance from among them. Someone objects that this would mean a thing moving from place to place has no actual place during its motion, and a thing changing in size has no actual size. This is plainly false.

Al-Dawani answers that, during motion, the changing thing exists only in the intermediate state between those instances. This state lies between mere possibility and full reality. It is enough to show that a body is never without those features or without this intermediate state. It is neither necessary nor proved that the body always has one of their instances in full reality; in fact, a proof may show the opposite. That is his view.

But the problem with this view is clear. Anything moving from place to place is surrounded by a body at every moment of its motion, so it must have an actual place; otherwise, there would be a void, which is impossible.[^V01-750] Also, the heavenly spheres are always in rotational motion, so this view would mean they never have a position at all.

The truth here is that the instances of the kind in which motion takes place are not limited to momentary instances. There are momentary states, which set the standard for rest, and states that unfold gradually through time across the motion as a whole.[^V01-751] Some thinkers say that the motion considered as a whole is itself one of these temporal states.[^V01-752] While motion continues without a break, the changing thing has one connected state in that category. It is not at rest. It has one identity spread continuously through time, with a measurable length, and contains all the points we imagine at separate moments, just as imagined points lie along a line. This ongoing state of the category is real; we do not need to imagine or divide it for it to exist.[^V01-753] The momentary states and the parts and limits of that ongoing state exist only because we imagine them. So the body is never without the kind of feature in which it moves. We do not need a chain of separate instants, or infinitely many actual moments between two limits: during motion, no single momentary state exists as a complete, separate thing, let alone an endless succession of such instants.

Nor can you return and say that, for existence to grow stronger or weaker, it is enough that the thing remains stable.[^V01-754] Motion requires its subject to persist, but a state that exists only in time does not persist at all—not during the time when it exists, nor beyond that time. A fuller explanation will come in our discussion of motion and time, God willing.

#### Chapter — Degrees of intensity and weakness

Perhaps you have learned in your earlier studies that two things can differ, in reality or in thought, in one of three ways.[^V01-755] They may differ in their entire essence, sharing no essential feature, as the categories do. Or they may share an essential nature but differ in one part of it: the shared nature is the broader kind, and what distinguishes each kind within it is its defining feature. Together, broader kind and defining feature make a specific nature; this is a unified kind of composition. Or they may share their whole essential nature and differ only through added accidental features. What results are individual or species-level instances, joined by those added features.

But you may have overlooked a fourth kind, proposed by the Illuminationist philosophers, that breaks this three-part division.[^V01-756] The difference may lie neither in the whole essence, nor in one part of it, nor in something added to it. Instead, one and the same nature may differ in how complete or deficient it is. It can have different levels within itself, apart from the incidental differences among the individuals that share it but also have other defining or accidental features. The two schools disagree here. Aristotle’s followers argue that this cannot be right: if the more complete thing contains nothing the less complete one lacks, the two do not differ at all. But if it does contain something the other lacks, then that feature is either part of the shared nature, in which case the two do not really share it, or an added feature, which must be either an essential defining feature or an accident.

Even setting aside the problem with accidents, this argument is very weak. It assumes what it needs to prove: two things may differ in the very respect in which they agree, rather than through something added to it.[^V01-757] Consider two instances of blackness, for example. If they differ by a defining feature, that defining feature cannot be part of the essence of blackness itself; otherwise, it would not distinguish one from the other. Rather, it would divide their shared broader kind, blackness, into two kinds. The defining feature would then lie outside the essence of that broader kind, like other accidental features. So if blackness grows stronger because of a defining feature whose meaning is not blackness, the difference lies beyond blackness itself—even though we have assumed that it lies within it.[^V01-758]

They reply that the difference among individual things belongs to a derived feature such as “black,” which is applied to things that bear blackness. Some bear an instance of blackness that is more complete at the level of its individuality; others bear a less complete one.[^V01-759] Individuality comes from features that distinguish each thing, not from the general, still-indeterminate nature itself. So what differs is the individual identity, not the nature considered in itself. By saying that degrees belong to a derived term such as “black,” they mean that this word points both to blackness and to the thing that bears it. The bearer is one of the features that makes it an individual. Their point, then, is that the difference lies in individual identity, not in the nature itself.

One might object that moving the difference to individuality does not help; it brings back the very problem they were trying to avoid. If a nature varies because of the features that make each instance an individual, the question about how the nature varies still stands. If the difference comes from the natures themselves, then the nature itself admits differences in degree. If it comes from the way the nature varies, the explanation is circular. If it comes from further individualizing features, an endless regress follows. And if individuality is existence, but existence is only a mental construct, how can it ground this difference? If existence is real, however, then it varies in itself, because the identity of an existent thing is its existence. On that view, gradation belongs to existence itself.

We reply that, according to Aristotle’s followers, a nature itself—whether a substance or a feature of something else—cannot vary by degrees. A broader kind differs among its instances through defining features. These features differ in themselves, just as distinct species differ in their essences; that is a difference between kinds, not a difference of degree. Differences of degree occur within one nature, across its more and less complete levels. If it is a specific nature that differs, the variation is explained by different matter and by features that distinguish each individual. Those, in turn, may differ because of earlier matter surrounded by other features, and so on. Aristotle’s followers allow this chain to continue indefinitely, one difference following another. This is what they mean when they say that a nature differs at the level of its individuals, and that difference through accidents is like difference through defining features: the full set of features surrounding one thing differs from the full set surrounding another. That is difference between distinct instances, not gradation.

As for the questioner's point that, if individuality is existence, existence itself must vary in its own nature, that is right; the author will establish it later. The Aristotle’s followers may mean that they deny gradation in an essence understood as what a thing is, but not in existence itself. Their reference to individuality may point to existence, since, strictly speaking, a nature becomes an individual only through a mode of existence. Their claim that a generic nature differs through defining features may point to the same thing: defining features are modes of existence, as the author will show. Existences and identities differ not through matter or material accidents, but in themselves, because existence is identity, and what distinguishes them is also what they share. Some of the Aristotle’s followers' statements about difference can be read as describing degrees of rank, as in *al-Shawāhid al-rubūbiyya*. The author's phrase “the defining features of blackness” answers the Illuminationists' objection: a defining feature is accidental to the essence of a broader kind, but not to its existence. Existence itself is one, and a broader kind is applied to a defining feature only indirectly. So a difference through defining features need not be a difference in something outside generic blackness.[^V01-760]

You can see that it is far from right to say that intense and weak blackness do not differ in their blackness, or that blackness applies to both in exactly the same way and the difference lies only between the bodies that bear them.[^V01-761] If differences between the underlying qualities make the derived word apply differently to their subjects, then those differences should also make the quality itself apply differently to its two instances. In fact, that is the more plausible conclusion.

Another argument of theirs is this: if the complete level is the essence itself, then the deficient and intermediate levels are not that same essence; and if either of those is the essence, the others are not.[^V01-762] But this does not settle the question about a specific nature. Only numerical unity cannot be shared or vary; a nature can be one in meaning while appearing at different levels. The other side can say that the specific nature is what all three levels share: the more complete, the less complete, and the intermediate.[^V01-763]

You may reply that, if the natural universal exists outside the mind, then the feature shared by all three levels also exists outside the mind, even though the mind is where we recognize them as sharing it. Once the mind strips away added and individualizing features, what remains must match the complete level or one of the less complete levels. Either way, it cannot match all of them. It would account for only one level, leaving the others to depend on something outside the shared nature. That contradicts the assumption that this nature is common to them all.

I answer that the natural universal, as you understand it, applies only to natures whose instances are alike in every essential respect. Only natures that apply in exactly the same way to every instance meet that condition. Once we set aside the added features, the nature is the same in every case, with no difference of degree. A gradable nature is different. Each level that exists in the world—in one individual or in several—would, if considered by the mind, be understood at that very level once its external features were stripped away. The same is true of every other level. These levels, taken from actual individuals and represented in the mind, are not equally complete or deficient. So none of them is universal in a way that applies to every individual across all the levels. They do share one underlying nature, but it is utterly indeterminate. It is indeterminate in its own completeness and deficiency, beyond the vagueness that comes from differences among individuals in their identities.

**A detailed clarification:** The general rule for graded difference, in all its forms, is this: a universal nature applies to its individuals with greater claim, priority, or completeness. Greater completeness includes greater intensity, size, or number.[^V01-764] The earlier Shi‘i philosophers and the Aristotle’s followers who followed Aristotle disagreed on four questions. The first is whether an essence, or an essential feature, can vary among its instances by any kind of gradation—by having a greater claim, coming earlier or later, or being more or less complete—or whether this is impossible. Some later philosophers have claimed that it is self-evident and universally agreed that essential natures cannot vary in the first two ways. This is highly doubtful. They seem to have overlooked that, for the Persian and earlier philosophers, some luminous substances are causes of others through their simple substantial nature.

The second question is whether stronger and weaker degrees must belong to different kinds. In other words, must the difference between them come from their essential features, so that they differ in species? Or can some instances share the same species, even if all do not?[^V01-765] The third question is whether differences in quality and quantity are two kinds of gradation or one, even if we use different comparative words for them. The fourth is whether strength and weakness, completeness and deficiency, occur only in quantity and quality or also in other kinds of thing, such as substance.[^V01-766] Philosophers in Aristotle’s school chose the first option in each question; the Stoics chose the second. Let us take them one by one.

As for the first question: you know by now that existence is one reality. It has no broader kind or defining feature, and it has the same meaning in all things. Its real instances do not differ through essences separate from one another, nor through identities separate from their essences; their identities are their essences. We have also seen that making and being made belong only to actual existences, not to universal natures. So conclude that the individual instances of existence, each made distinct by its own identity while sharing one reality, differ from one another in all the ways that gradation allows: one can have greater or lesser priority, come earlier or later, or be stronger or weaker.[^V01-767]

One clue is that the parts of time are alike in kind, yet one comes before another by its own nature, not because of some outside feature. The Illuminationist Shaykh offers another proof in *al-Muṭāraḥāt*. He argues that a greater and a lesser quantity do not differ because of an added accident or a defining feature that divides quantity. The difference between quantities lies in quantity itself: what one has beyond the other is not outside quantity, but belongs to the same nature they share. A longer and a shorter line differ only in how complete or incomplete they are as lines. The same is true of more and less complete blackness: they share blackness, and their difference comes from no feature outside blackness itself. It lies in blackness.

The reply is that a longer and a shorter line have one and the same nature.[^V01-768] Their difference is not in quantity itself, even though it occurs within quantity. What makes the difference is not the shared nature in which the difference occurs. Instead, each line has its own particular extent as an individual: it stretches over a certain length between set limits. This depends on differences in the matter’s readiness and its responses, so it lies outside the nature of quantity.[^V01-769] Viewed simply as lines, the longer and shorter ones are both lengths in the same sense: each is one dimension, and neither is more of a line than the other. Compared with each other, however, the longer line is longer only in relation to the shorter one, because of its particular extent. As Avicenna says in *The Categories* of *The Healing*: “I do not mean that one quantity cannot be greater or smaller than another. I mean that one cannot be more of a quantity than another quantity like it, though it can be greater in a relative sense—that is, longer in relation to the other.”

So length itself cannot be greater or less; only relative length can. The same applies to number. Avicenna also says that number is multiplicity without comparison, while being “more numerous” is a relative feature of number. The same applies to blackness and heat: their basic nature is the same across instances, and the differences come from individual features, not from the shared nature itself. True blackness cannot be stronger or weaker in itself. What is black in relation to one thing may be white in relation to another. An instance of blackness, considered on its own, is not stronger or weaker; it becomes so only when compared. In this view, the opposition between the two extremes also extends to the intermediate shades, without creating a new kind of opposition.[^V01-770]

On this account, “stronger” or “greater” means that, with help from imagination, the mind can compare one individual with another and allow for more of the same kind to be added. It does not mean that the shared nature itself grows or that its effects appear more fully in some individuals. Otherwise, many essential natures would admit degrees: people differ, for example, in how many effects their humanity produces. Aristotle’s followers say that such differences are not differences in degree within the shared nature; they only make a derived description apply differently to the things that bear the quality. In the end, they explain the difference as one thing being more fittingly described than another. They therefore say that the two instances of blackness do not themselves differ in the feature being measured. Each has its own defining feature, which makes it the kind of blackness it is. The difference lies instead between the two bodies described as deeply or faintly black: the word “black” applies more fully to one than to the other.[^V01-771]

On this account, the Illuminationist Shaykh’s objection in *al-Muṭāraḥāt* does not apply. He says that those who call stronger blackness different from weaker blackness by a defining feature must treat blackness as a broader kind that admits degrees. But they also say that no broader kind admits degrees. Their objection assumes that stronger and weaker blackness differ in kind. Our account denies that.

As for the second question, the Stoics and other early philosophers are right, for the same reasons we gave about the reality of existence. Existence is not made up of instances that differ in kind. Some instances are extremely strong and great; others, such as motion, prime matter, and number, are very weak.[^V01-772] Aristotle’s followers also accept that qualities grow stronger or weaker as a physical subject moves through different levels of heat, blackness, and other qualities. They hold that one motion is a single process, with an unbroken identity from its beginning to its end. The parts and boundaries of that continuous process belong to the same species, a point they treat as self-evident in their argument against Democritus’ account of the basic parts of bodies. It follows that the strong and weak stages of blackness, as a body grows darker, are of the same species.

An intensifying process may end in something different in kind from what it has passed through. But that new thing differs because it is where the process begins or ends, not because it is one of the levels through which the process moves. It may still have stronger and weaker levels of its own. Red, for example, lies between black and white. Common sense tells us that it is neither weak black nor weak white, yet red itself can be darker or lighter.[^V01-773][^V01-774]

As for the third question, “stronger” and “weaker” can mean what people usually mean by these words, as shown by forms such as “blacker.” The original Arabic meaning of “strong” was the power to resist; it later came to mean a greater degree of something.[^V01-775] In everyday speech, we do not say that one line is “more of a line” than another, as we say that one blackness is “blacker” than another. So, if we judge only by common usage, strength and weakness seem to apply only to qualities, not to quantities or other things. Quantities, it seems, accept only increase or decrease, more or less.

But philosophers cannot settle questions of reason by relying only on words or on everyday speech. The common-language argument is not sound even on its own terms. People may not say that one line is “more of a line” than another, but they do say that one is longer. Length is part of what it means to be a line, so strength or weakness can be found in the line itself. People also say that one line is longer or bigger than another, even though they agree that a line is a quantity.[^V01-776][^V01-777]

The same point applies to number. People may not say that one number is “more of a number” than another, but they do say that one number is greater. Since number and multiplicity are the same, being greater is a kind of strength in number; the reverse applies to being smaller. Some distinguish strength from increase by saying that strength has a limit, while length and number can always increase: no longest line or greatest number can be imagined, but blackness and heat might reach a point beyond which nothing could be stronger.[^V01-778] First, we can deny that qualities have such an absolute limit, even if every quality that exists has a finite degree. The same is true of length and number: among actual examples, there may be no longer line or greater number. So this does not distinguish them.

Second, even if we accept that some kinds have a limit and others do not, that still does not separate strength from increase. Either kind can have forms that stop at a limit and forms that do not; that is a further division, made after we have already divided things into stronger and weaker.[^V01-779] Another proposed difference is that increase applies when we can point to an equal part and an extra part, while strength and weakness do not work that way. But this fails for number. A number is made of units, not of other numbers. Four is not made of three, and three is not made of two. Each whole number is a simple kind, not a sum of lower numbers. If we split four in thought, its form disappears and another number takes its place. Which part of four matches three, and which part is extra? How can we identify what is equal and what differs between simple kinds of number?

They also say that differences in quality, length, and number deserve different names because the extra part works differently in each case. In length, we can imagine a piece of the longer line that matches the shorter line, with another piece left over. In number, the extra units belong to a whole number that differs in kind and existence from the smaller number. In a quality such as blackness, however, the whole stronger reality—not a separate piece within it—is what is greater.[^V01-780] This explanation works only if the nature shared by stronger and weaker qualities is a broader kind, and each level becomes a distinct kind through a defining feature. Then one whole nature would be stronger by its own identity, not because a separate part, real or imagined, sets it apart.[^V01-781]

Strength and weakness therefore depend on differences between the natures of things. So do “more” and “fewer,” though with the distinction already explained. Increase and decrease, by contrast, follow from differences among individual instances and their particular identities. We can grant people the usual terminology: call greater or lesser length “increase” and “decrease,” greater or smaller numbers “more” and “fewer,” and degrees in other qualities “strength” and “weakness.” All these terms share one idea: more or less completeness in the very feature being compared.

As for the fourth question, early philosophers such as Empedocles and Plato taught that the substances of this lower world are shadows of the substances in the higher world. By this they meant that the lower substances are effects of the higher ones, as an object casts a shadow. The cause comes before the effect in its reality as a substance. This follows from the principle of causation and from the view that existence is the reality things have outside the mind. A cause’s priority in its nature as a substance points to greater completeness and independence. If an effect gets its substantial nature from its cause, it cannot be equally complete in that respect; the cause must be more complete. This is what “strength” means here. So one substance can be more fully a substance than another, whether or not everyday speech has a word for it. Reality is not limited by common usage.

This is what the Illuminationist Shaykh means in *al-Talwīḥāt* when he says that all the early philosophers held that the substances of this world are shadows of those in the higher world. How, he asks, could they be equal in substantiality?

He then raises an objection: priority and strength are usually said of opposites. Substance has no opposite, so nothing can be prior or stronger in substance. He answers that necessary and higher existence is more complete and stronger than possible and caused existence.[^V01-782] By “strength” he does not mean the power to resist, but greater completeness. These levels do not take turns in one subject; they are not opposites, and they are not stages in one process.[^V01-783]

In *Ḥikmat al-Ishrāq*, he adds that philosophers define an animal as a body with a soul that senses and moves by choice. An animal whose soul has greater power to move and more senses has fuller powers of sensing and movement. Human animality, for example, is more complete than a mosquito’s. The fact that everyday speech does not call one animal “more animal” than another is no reason to deny the difference. Claims such as “this is not more watery than that” rest on everyday speech, not on proof.

Someone may object that an animal’s defining feature is not actual sensation and movement, but the powers behind them. Actual actions differ because of the animal’s organs, its readiness to act, and the presence or removal of obstacles. The power itself does not differ. In the same way, water’s defining feature is not the coldness we feel, since that can sometimes be absent, but its power to become cold when nothing prevents it.[^V01-784]

I agree that these actions and effects are signs of the powers that define the thing, and can stand in for them in a definition.[^V01-785] The effects arise from those powers, which is why we use them when defining things, just as we include building in the definition of a builder. More effects show a stronger power; fewer show a weaker one.

A definition can describe a thing in itself, describe its relation to something else, or do both in different ways. We can define a ruler or a builder by what each is, or by the kingdom each rules or the building each builds. In a definition based on relation, the kingdom or building is included; in a definition of what the person is in himself, it is not. These two kinds of definition can come apart.

The same applies to the soul. Its body and the way it governs the body are included in a definition of the soul as a manager, not in a definition of its inner nature alone. If a thing’s inner nature can be separated from its role, as with souls that do not depend on bodies, its definition by nature differs from its definition by action. But if a thing’s own being is identical with its relation or action—as with some powers and souls whose reality is to move or relate to something—then the two definitions are the same.

A definition of a power through its relation must include whatever it acts on. Just as many acts of building show that someone is a more complete builder, many acts of guidance show that a soul is more complete in its role of governing.

With this in place, consider souls and powers whose nature and actions depend on matter. Their existence in themselves is identical with their existence in relation to what they act on; neither the mind nor the world can separate the two. So their definition in one respect is also their definition in the other. Aristotle’s followers themselves admit that the actions of a power belong in its definition. As we have seen, more actions show a stronger active power. For the powers we are discussing, this active aspect is identical with their inner nature. These same powers are the essential features that make natural bodies different kinds. The bodies differ through their powers and forms, not through the bodily nature they all share. So when these powers differ in completeness as substances, the kinds of bodies differ as well. This is what we wanted to show.

**A further question and response:** philosophers in Aristotle’s school ask how their rule can stand when substances cause other substances, matter and form bring about a body, and a father causes a son, even though “substance” is a broader kind shared by all of them. The same problem appears in quantity: a body comes before a surface, and a surface before a line, even though “quantity” is a broader kind that applies to all three.

They answer that priority and posteriority within one concept can work in two ways. In the first, the thing that comes first and the feature in which it comes first are the same. For example, the existence of the Necessary Being comes before the existence of a possible being, and the existence of a substance before the existence of an accident. In the second, the thing that is prior and the feature that explains its priority are different. A human father is earlier than a human son, not in their shared humanity, but in another respect: their existence or the time of their birth. What differs is the time or existence; what accounts for the difference is their individual identity.[^V01-786][^V01-787]

With this distinction, we can see that one individual does not cause or precede another simply through its own nature, nor does it make the other an instance of the same kind by means of that nature. Cause and effect, and what is prior or later, depend on their existence, not on their essences. Existence applies first to matter and form, then to the body made from them; it also applies first to parents, then to their child. In the same way, existence applies first to substances in the higher world: they are more fully present and established than the substances in our world. But the nature “substance” applies equally to all of them. One is not more of a substance than another; one is more fully real in its existence. One existence can be naturally prior to another without any added feature. Matter and form are prior to a body in existence, not in substantial nature. The body is a substance, and so are its parts; none is more of a substance than the others. The same reasoning applies to quantity and other cases of this kind. Yet this reply faces several objections.

One objection is that this answer repeats the problem it was meant to avoid. Moving the difference from substance or quantity to existence or time does not help, because the same question then applies to existence and time.[^V01-788] If one existence is prior to another because of existence itself, then instances of one simple reality differ in priority. We have already shown that existence is one simple reality, not divided into kinds by defining features. Likewise, if parts of time come before one another because time itself is a process of renewal and passing away, then a single reality has degrees of priority and posteriority.

Another objection is that the answer conflicts with their argument against one body causing the existence of another. They say that the matter of a cause comes before the body it forms, and that body comes before the matter of its effect. But the matter in the effect is of the same kind as the matter in the cause. It would follow that the effect’s matter comes before the cause’s body, so that something comes before itself. If they accept the same kind of priority in other cases of substance, however, this argument against one body causing another no longer works.

The argument may apply to causes that bring existence about, such as an active or final cause, but not to causes that make up a thing, such as matter and form. A body’s essence is made from the essences of matter and form, not from their existence. If its parts were not substances, the whole would not be a substance. Just as bodyhood is said of a human through the animal nature, and animal nature is said of a human, we can say that substance is said of a body through its two parts. This needs a closer look.[^V01-789]

To see the point, distinguish parts of essence from parts of existence. Taken without any further condition, parts are parts of essence; taken as separate things, they are parts of existence. The first are broader kind and defining feature; the second are matter and form. If the parts of a body are taken as broader kind and defining feature, their substantiality comes before the body’s, but this is not gradation: in this respect, they are not separate kinds of substance from the body. If they are taken as matter and form, they are different from the body, but in this respect they do not make up its essence; they make up its existence. So what differs and comes first is existence, not substantiality.

Praise be to God, first and last, and blessings and peace upon Muhammad and his family. The first part of the general questions in *The Four Journeys* is complete. We did our best to correct and revise the book, comparing handwritten copies and copies corrected by experts in the field. Thanks be to God, in His greatness, the result was as accurate as we could hope. It is clear to attentive readers that few books are free of slips or errors, despite all the work and care devoted to them. We do not intend to hide mistakes made by a proofreader or printer, as some publishers do. We have marked them so readers will not misunderstand the book’s arguments. We ask that the text be corrected before it is used for reference, so that no ambiguity or confusion remains. Praise be to God, first and last, and blessings upon Muhammad and his pure family.

## Notes

[^V01-2]: The verb *kamaha* means to go blind or to develop dim vision; it can also mean that sight is covered by darkness.

[^V01-3]: The intended meaning here is astrology.

[^V01-4]: A *wathāq* is a fastening: a chain, rope, or anything else used to bind.

[^V01-5]: *Ṭawāriq* means calamities that arrive unexpectedly, as if in the night. “The blows of time” refers to life's reversals.

[^V01-6]: The verb *nazaʿa* can mean to long for or miss one's family.

[^V01-7]: *Rayʿān* means the beginning or finest period of something, as in the first flowering of youth.

[^V01-8]: *Ishāb* means speaking at length or saying too much.

[^V01-9]: *Inkabba ʿalā* means to stick close to something or devote oneself to it. One manuscript copy reads “fully engrossed.”

[^V01-10]: *Dann* here means an earthenware jar used for storing water.

[^V01-11]: That is, they were urged toward it.

[^V01-12]: Some copies read this phrase differently. A handwritten note in one manuscript gives the word as *al-jabīn*, related to cowardice.

[^V01-13]: *Arjā al-amr* means to put something off until later.

[^V01-14]: A familiar saying for returning empty-handed, with nothing to show for one's effort.

[^V01-15]: *Qidḥ* means an arrow, including one of several arrows used to draw lots.

[^V01-16]: That is, with affectionate concern.

[^V01-17]: Here it means need or strong desire.

[^V01-18]: *Rāqa al-sharāb* means to strain a drink; a *miṣfāh* is the strainer.

[^V01-19]: A *minḵal* is a sieve, used to sift one thing from another.

[^V01-20]: That is, the ordinary setbacks of the times.

[^V01-21]: *Rathāthat al-ḥāl* means a shabby or degraded condition. *Badha* can mean poor or wretched.

[^V01-22]: Some manuscript copies have a different reading of this phrase; the note gives it as *ʿāzibī al-fahm*.

[^V01-23]: *Basara wajhuhu* means “his face darkened” or “he scowled.”

[^V01-24]: To turn away from someone means to ignore or reject them.

[^V01-25]: To turn one's side away from someone means to break off with them or refuse them.

[^V01-26]: The phrase means “bringing a great deal of wealth,” by metaphor.

[^V01-27]: *Thannā al-shayʾ* means to bend or turn something back.

[^V01-28]: That is, he found rest and relief.

[^V01-29]: *Rakā al-arḍ* means to dig into the earth; for a basin it means to level it out. *Thajja al-māʾ* means the water flowed. *Zawā al-shayʾ* means to gather something together.

[^V01-30]: *Alā* means to appear and become visible; with a sword or garment, it can mean to make something flash or gleam.

[^V01-31]: *Habbat al-rīḥ* means the wind rose and began to blow.

[^V01-32]: *Ḥasira* can mean to tire or become exhausted.

[^V01-33]: *Lajlaja* means to hesitate or stumble in speech.

[^V01-34]: *Tabakhṭara* means to walk with a proud, showy gait.

[^V01-35]: That is, to become smaller and weaker.

[^V01-36]: To trouble oneself means to cause oneself pain or make oneself do something difficult.

[^V01-37]: The *maḡzā* of an expression is its intended meaning or point.

[^V01-38]: *Ḥawā al-shayʾ* means to gather or bring something together.

[^V01-39]: To critique a statement means to point out its strengths or its faults.

[^V01-40]: *Zayyafa al-dirham* means to reject or devalue a coin as counterfeit.

[^V01-41]: *Rasafa al-ḥijāra* means to fit stones tightly together.

[^V01-42]: *Shadhdha al-sikkīn* means to sharpen a knife or similar tool.

[^V01-43]: *Talaqqafa al-shayʾ* means to catch or take something quickly.

[^V01-44]: A journey is movement away from one's home or present place toward a goal, crossing stages and stopping places. There is an outward journey, which needs no explanation, and an inward journey. Those who know through direct experience describe four inward journeys.

    The first journey is from creation to God. The traveler lifts the dark and luminous veils between themselves and their own deepest reality, which has always been with them. Put another way, the traveler rises from the level of the self to the heart, from the heart to the spirit, and from the spirit to the highest goal and greatest joy: the Garden brought near to those who are mindful of God.

    The stains of the self are dark veils. The lights of the heart and the radiance of the spirit are luminous veils. These are the three main levels of the human being. The saying that a thousand veils stand between the servant and the Lord refers to these three broad levels. When the traveler reaches the goal by lifting these veils, they behold the beauty of the Real and their separate self disappears in Him. This may be called “the loss of the separate self in God’s Essence.” The secret, the hidden, and the most hidden belong here too, but they are also discussed in connection with the second journey.

    The level of the spirit may be divided further by including the intellect, since it gives a more detailed account of the realities that can be known. The seven levels then become the self, the heart, the intellect, the spirit, the secret, the hidden, and the most hidden. These names apply when the traveler has reached a lasting spiritual state. Without that stability, they are not stations. They are the levels of spiritual friendship and the lands of love that Rumi refers to:

    > Attar has crossed the seven cities of love;
    > we are still at the bend of a single alley.

    When the traveler's separate self disappears in God, the first journey ends. Their existence is then through God. They enter a state in which their separate self fades away and may speak in ecstatic words for which people judge them an unbeliever and impose a penalty.

    If divine care comes to their aid, that state passes. Clear awareness returns, and they admit their own error and servanthood after having spoken as if they shared in lordship. Abū Yazīd al-Bisṭāmī is reported to have said: “My God, if I ever say, ‘Glory be to me! How great is my majesty!’ then I am a Zoroastrian unbeliever. Break my sacred girdle, and I declare: There is no god but God, and Muḥammad is the Messenger of God.” Perhaps this discussion has already gone beyond its purpose. If it were not tiring to speak at length and tiring to listen, I would say much more about this journey. What I have set out is enough for now.

    When the first journey ends, the traveler begins the second: from God to God, through God. It takes place through God because the traveler has become a saint whose existence is through God. The traveler moves from the station of the divine Essence through its perfections, one by one, until seeing all the divine qualities except those God has kept to Himself. Their sainthood is complete. Their own essence, actions, and qualities are understood through God's essence, actions, and qualities: through Him they hear, see, walk, and act.

    The “secret” is when the separate self disappears in the Essence, the end of the first journey and the beginning of the second.
