The “hidden” is when the separate self disappears in the divine reality. The “most hidden” is passing beyond awareness of both ways the separate self disappears. In this way the circle of sainthood is completed, the second journey ends, and the traveler no longer experiences this disappearance of the separate self.

    The traveler then begins the third journey: from God to creation, through God. They travel through the levels of divine action. As this state passes, full awareness returns, and the traveler remains through God. They travel through the worlds of divine power, spirit, and human life, and witness these worlds themselves and what follows from them.

    They receive a share in prophecy: they make known what they have learned about God's essence, attributes, and acts. But theirs is not the kind of prophecy that brings religious law. They speak only of God, His attributes, and His acts, and are not called prophets. They receive religious laws and teachings from the universal Prophet and follow him.

    When the third journey ends, the traveler begins the fourth: from creation to God, through God. They study created things, their effects and implications, and learn what benefits or harms them in this life and the next. They learn how all things return to God, how they are guided or driven, and what humiliates, hinders, or helps them. They call people toward God and so become prophets through prophecy. Through the prophecy that brings religious law, they are called prophets. They announce how created things will fare, what harms and benefits them, and what makes them happy or miserable. In all this they act through God, for their existence is rooted in God. Attention to creation does not distract them from attending to Him.

[^V01-45]: This means the world of God's command, the realm of intellects and spirits. The name comes from Qur'anic expressions such as “Surely creation and command are His” and “Say: the spirit belongs to my Lord's command.” These beings are described this way because they come to exist by God's command without an intervening material process or passage of time. Their basic capacity to exist is enough for them to receive existence; they do not require the special readiness of matter. Their individual independence is also absorbed into that command, so there is no separate recipient giving orders or obeying them, only God's commands.

[^V01-46]: Anyone who considers the matter will see that what makes a thing what it is comes from its form, not its matter. The world now understood by the intellect will one day be a world directly present, as wide as the heavens and earth, when the sky is rolled up like a written scroll and the heavens are folded in God's right hand.

[^V01-47]: Doing good includes putting both outward behaviour and inner character in order, letting go of faults, taking on virtues, and ultimately letting the separate self fall away. One can describe this in four stages. First, make outward conduct clear and sound by following divine guidance. Second, remove bad qualities such as greed, envy, and pride, along with the wrongs done by tongue, appetite, and sexual desire. The Prophet is reported to have said: “Whoever is spared the evil of his *laqlaq*, *qabqab*, and *dhabdhāb* has been spared all evil.” These words mean the tongue, the belly, and the penis, respectively. Third, take on noble qualities, described here as reflecting God's names and attributes and developing qualities worthy of God. Fourth comes the loss of self-centredness, described in three degrees: one's actions cease to be regarded as independent of God's action; one's qualities cease to be independent of God's qualities; and one's very existence is understood as having no independence from God's existence.

[^V01-48]: “Pattern” here means a model or style. To say that something follows a certain pattern means that it is made or ordered in the same way.

[^V01-49]: The first “where” asks about our origin: “God was, and nothing was with Him.” The third asks about our final destination: “To your Lord is the return,” and “Everything passes away except His face.” The first points to the downward arc of creation: “Go down from here, all of you.” The third points to the upward journey: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord.” The first can also point to the withdrawal or concealment of divine light: God is said to be hidden from created eyes by His radiance, and a tradition speaks of seventy thousand veils of light and seventy thousand of darkness. The verses about the Night of Decree describe the angels and spirit descending by God's permission until dawn. The third direction points to the appearance of light: “God is the light of the heavens and earth.” Another verse speaks of the angels and the spirit ascending to Him on a day measured as fifty thousand years. The second “where” concerns our present life, the time of traveling through the world, looking carefully at it and reflecting on God's signs: “Travel through the earth and see,” and “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that He is the Truth.” God speaks the truth.

[^V01-50]: Someone might object: “A thing cannot be described as many unless we treat it mathematically, because few and many are properties of number. We call time many only because it can be divided into days and hours. Being many is like being equal or unequal; all depend on quantity.”

    The answer is that we call something many once we consider it as a number. But number is not studied only in mathematics. It can be considered in two ways, as the author will explain later. That is why he calls this one way of considering it “mathematical.” In any case, multiplicity has no existence beyond the weak existence it has as a number. As the author will say repeatedly, existence goes together with unity—or may even be one and the same as unity.

[^V01-51]: The study of nature was divided into eight branches. It studies natural bodies as they change. It may study them in general, in what is called physics or the study of nature. The name of this branch means the first thing one hears when studying nature. It examines such basic matters as time, place, boundaries, movement, and rest.

    Natural philosophy may study simple bodies as a whole. This branch is called the study of the heavens and the world. It examines the simple bodies and the wisdom behind how they are made and arranged. Or it may study how simple bodies change into one another. This is the study of things coming into being and passing away. It explains how things are produced and how they reproduce, and how God's care allows earthly bodies to benefit from the rays of the heavens as they grow and live. It also explains how kinds of things continue even though individual things perish through the movements of the heavens.

    Another branch studies what happens in the upper air, such as clouds, rain, snow, thunder, lightning, rainbows, and halos. The remaining branches study minerals, plants, animals, and the soul. Minerals are mixed bodies that do not grow or perceive. Plants grow but do not perceive. Animals grow and perceive but do not reason. The soul has all these powers, including reason. Books also list branches of the highest philosophy and of mathematics and the study of nature.

[^V01-52]: The author sometimes says “existence” and sometimes “existent” to mean the same thing, because what truly exists is existence itself.

[^V01-53]: The author follows an earlier way of dividing questions, but that division does not simply sort them into “yes” and “no.” Nor is he pointing to the reason for asking a question or its nearest cause.

    A clearer way to make the point is this. First, we must answer the skeptic who doubts or denies reality itself by establishing that something exists. Once we do that, we accept that many things exist. We also know that we can make mistakes: we may take something nonexistent to be real, or fail to recognize something that is real. So our first need is to tell what exists from what does not, and to build our thinking and knowledge on that distinction.

    We can do this only by studying what can be said about existence as a whole: both the features it shares generally and those that belong to particular kinds of things. For example, we may say that existence itself is real, while a thing's nature is not existence; that existence has different degrees of strength; and that a thing that exists may either have to exist or may depend on something else. What depends on something else may be a substance (a thing in its own right) or a quality.

    What does not exist has no place among real things. So the divisions of what exists, and the rules that apply to those divisions, all belong to existence as a whole. The claims made in each science describe features of the things it studies; in the end, those claims are rooted in existence itself. In truth, these inquiries return to the divisions of existence and to the features of its different forms.

    That is why first philosophy studies the primary divisions of existence, such as what must exist and what may exist, and what is one or many. It also studies the next divisions, including the subjects of other sciences, considered as things that exist. This also shows why other sciences depend on first philosophy to establish that their subjects exist, unless that is already clear. — ط مد

[^V01-54]: Someone may ask: If the concepts “existence” and “thing” are shared features that apply to existing realities, why can’t existence itself be defined by description? By “description,” the commentator means a logical description: defining something through an incidental feature drawn from the realm of essences. Clearly, existence has no description of that kind. Also, reality itself can enter the mind only through a concept, so this would amount to defining a thing by itself. The concept of “thing” is just as familiar—or unfamiliar—as the thing it names, while a definition must be clearer than what it defines. — س ره

[^V01-55]: Someone may object that lacking a definition means lacking a cause that makes a thing what it is, but does not mean lacking a cause of its existence. And the absence of a proof depends on the absence of all four kinds of cause. The answer is that the author has already said that everything except God has a composite structure of matter and form. Lacking a cause that makes it what it is—even if that cause is matter and form in the mind—therefore means lacking a cause of its existence too. When he says in *The Beginning and the Return*, “Since it has no definition and no cause, it has no proof,” he is reinforcing this answer to the objection. It is also enough simply to deny that existence has a definition; there is no contradiction.

    A second objection appeals to the real existence of a possible thing: existence itself has no definition, yet the existence of a possible thing can be proved because it is caused in its very nature. The answer is that if we mean existence simply as existence, it has neither definition nor proof. If we mean existence with a qualification, then it can have both.

    A third objection asks: If what has no definition cannot be proved, how can one thing be proved by another when neither causes the other? For example: every human can laugh, and everyone who can laugh can write. Laughter and writing are not causes of one another; both result from a third cause. The answer is that philosophers who study the divine use “proof” in a strict sense for proof from cause to effect. Avicenna says in the *Metaphysics* of *The Healing*: “It has no definition and no proof; rather, it is the proof of everything, though clear signs point to it.” That is why they say things with causes can be known only through their causes. If a logician also uses “proof” for reasoning from an effect, that is a broader use of the word. And in the case where two effects share a third cause, we really reason from one effect to that cause, then from the cause to the other effect we want to establish. In the example, we move from laughter to the rational soul, then from the rational soul to the human capacity to write. The proof thus ultimately proceeds through a cause. — س ره

[^V01-56]: In a definition, “parts” means the elements that make it up. In a proof, it means the middle steps that connect the premises to the conclusion. Their correspondence is considered in light of the material being discussed. — ه ره

[^V01-57]: A thing’s being itself is necessary. But we still need to distinguish the concept of the thing from the thing itself, as we do in a definition and what it defines; otherwise, we would end up predicating a thing of itself. — س ره

[^V01-58]: There is a strict sense of “related,” in which it means the relation itself, and a looser, common sense, in which it means the thing that has a relation. The same distinction applies to “universal.” Strictly speaking, the real existent is existence itself; in common usage, “existent” means the essence to which existence belongs. — ه ره

[^V01-59]: That is, the feature belongs to existence without needing any additional qualifying condition. This is also what it means for existence to be suited, in itself, to receive that feature. Nothing can come between the subject and its feature, not even something equal to the subject, and the feature must apply to the whole subject. If it applied only to a narrower kind, the subject would need an added qualification before it could receive that feature. If it applied more broadly, the qualification would serve no purpose. This also shows why the division must cover every case: otherwise, one of its branches would be narrower than the subject and would not be an essential feature of it. — ط

[^V01-60]: As explained above, if a feature belongs essentially to a subject, the division must cover every case. The reverse is true only in some cases: a complete division does not always mean that its members are essential features. — ط

[^V01-61]: As explained above, shared features must be defined as features that apply to existence as a whole, either by themselves or together with their opposite in a complete division. Here, “opposite” means the alternatives that result when something is divided. This resolves the objections the author has raised. — ط

[^V01-62]: Limiting each science to the study of the essential features of its subject is not just a matter of convention. It is required by proof in sciences that rely on proof, as explained in the logical study of demonstration.

    A proof aims to give certainty, so its premises must be certain. Certainty means knowing that something is so and that it cannot be otherwise. A certain premise must therefore be necessary in truth, even if it is possible in the modal sense; otherwise its opposite would remain possible and there would be no certainty. It must be true at every time; otherwise it might be false at some time, leaving the opposite possible. It must be universal across circumstances; otherwise it might be false in some cases, again leaving the opposite possible. Its predicate must also belong to its subject itself: when the subject is affirmed, the predicate is affirmed with it, and when the subject is denied, the predicate is denied, setting everything else aside. This is why an essential predicate must be equal in scope to its subject. If it were narrower—for example, being prone to wonder in relation to animal—simply being an animal would not be enough for that feature to apply. If it were broader, as walking is in relation to human, the qualification “human” would add nothing to the feature’s application.

    Because an essential predicate belongs to its subject necessarily, the subject helps explain why the predicate exists. It must therefore appear in the full definition of that predicate. This is the rule for recognizing an essential feature. If a predicate has another predicate, and that predicate has one more, the original subject must appear in the definition of each, all the way down the chain. Each feature is essential to the original subject as well as to the subject of its own proposition. For example, a human being is capable of wonder, can laugh, and shows the teeth when laughing. The same rule applies in the other direction: if a subject has a subject, that first subject must be included in the definitions all the way back. For example, blackness is a visible quality; visible quality is a sensible quality; sensible quality is a quality; quality belongs to essence; and essence is something that exists.

    If a predicate is narrower than its subject, that predicate and its opposite in a complete division together form one essential predicate of the broader subject. Each side is essential to the corresponding part of that subject. For example, what exists is divided into what must exist and what may exist. In the definition of either part, the broader subject is included; in the definition of the combined division, the broader subject itself is included. A science, then, is a set of propositions whose subjects share one subject, which appears in the definitions of the subjects and predicates of its questions. This chain begins with a proposition about the science’s broad subject and ends with a proposition whose predicate no longer includes that subject in its definition. The highest branch of philosophy studies body as something that exists; the study of nature begins with body as a natural kind, not merely as something that exists. Likewise, philosophy studies the circle as something that exists, while mathematics studies it as a geometric shape.

    These points establish eight things. First, a science is a collection of propositions about one subject, which appears in the definitions of the subjects and predicates of its questions. Second, every science must have a subject shared by its propositions. Third, that subject is what the science examines through its essential features. Fourth, an essential feature belongs to a thing in itself and can be recognized because the thing appears in its definition. Sometimes the subject and predicate are reversed, so the rule is that either the subject appears in the predicate’s definition or the predicate appears in the subject’s definition. For example, what exists is divided into one and many; and what must exist exists. Fifth, an essential predicate does not apply through an intermediary feature—whether that intermediary is broader, narrower, or equal in scope. An intermediary here means something included in the predicate’s definition without the subject itself being included. For example, blackness belongs to a crow through its feathers. Sixth, the predicate must match the subject in scope: it cannot be broader or narrower. Seventh, the predicate in any question must be essential both to the subject of that question and to the subject of the science as a whole. Eighth, sciences differ according to their subjects.

    These rules apply to sciences that prove their claims. There is no reason to suppose they apply in the same way to conventional disciplines whose subjects are constructed ideas rather than things that exist in reality. — ط

[^V01-63]: This note explains the statement that a science studies the essential features of its subject. An essential feature truly belongs to a thing, without metaphor or error. In Arabic grammar, it is a description of the thing itself, not a description of something merely related to it. Put another way, it has no intermediary in how it belongs to the thing. There are different kinds of intermediary, however. A ship’s motion, for example, is an intermediary for the motion of someone sitting on it; not every kind of intermediary works this way. The author discusses these distinctions later, in connection with the primacy of existence.

    The features of a distinguishing feature are also features of its general kind because, when the general kind is considered without restriction, it is united with that distinguishing feature. Their features are therefore the same in reality. The features of the intellects, for example, truly belong to existence as existence when existence is considered without qualification. This differs from the features of a body considered as changing: matter and motion are what make it a subject for the study of nature. A body considered simply as something that exists, or as composed of matter and form, is instead a subject for the highest branch of philosophy.

    Many later scholars found this difficult. Al-Khwansari, for example, wrote in his notes on *The Healing* that discussing something narrower than a science’s subject is done only for convenience, because the narrower thing is one kind or class of it. Remember, though, that the older definition of an essential feature—as an external predicate that belongs to something in itself or through something equal to it—can be understood correctly. “In itself” does not mean that the thing causes the feature or necessitates it; that reading would make it hard to explain features of narrower kinds. It means that no intermediary stands between the thing and the feature, and that the feature belongs to the thing itself rather than to something merely related to it.

    An equal thing here means a concept equal to the subject in the respect under discussion, even if the two concepts differ. Unity and existence, for example, are different concepts but apply to the same reality. If indivisibility belongs to existence because of unity, it is still an essential feature. Likewise, if existence cannot be truly applied to many things because of individuality, that too is an essential feature. But two things may be equal in what exists while belonging to different qualifying aspects. If one feature belongs to a subject only through another aspect attached to it, it is incidental, just as a feature that belongs through something narrower would be. That is why earlier thinkers spoke broadly of a property beyond a thing’s definition, including properties considered with an added qualification. Otherwise, unity, being a thing, possibility, and other features grasped by reason would be left out. — س ره

[^V01-64]: Here are examples from the study of nature. An essential feature of its main subject is that every body has a natural shape. An essential feature of one kind is that one element changes into another. A general feature of a kind is that an element is in motion. An essential feature of a kind of essential feature is that the lights of the heavens stimulate plant life. A general feature of that kind is that the lights of the heavens, especially the sun, warm the world of the elements. In the last two examples, the feature stays within the scope of the subject of the science. — س ره

[^V01-65]: The statement made from a general kind and its distinguishing feature is a particular claim: “Some animals are rational.” This shows that the distinguishing feature belongs to the relevant share of the general kind, not to the general kind as such. The claim that a kind’s essential or incidental features belong to its general kind is rejected, for the reasons already given. — ط مد

[^V01-66]: A careful reader should see that a feature attached to something narrower—such as a particular subject in a science narrower than the highest branch of philosophy—can in one respect be essential to the broader subject and in another respect incidental. The reason is that a general kind has its own reality at the level of the concept and its reality in the world, and these are far apart. When the broader subject and narrower subject are one in the world but not at the level of the concept, a feature of the narrower subject is incidental to the broader concept but essential to the broader thing in reality. This resolves the difficulty. What matters for a feature to be essential is that no intermediary lies between it and its subject. But we may consider the subject as it is at the level of a concept or as it is in reality, and the judgment changes accordingly. This creates no contradiction for a clear-minded reader. — ن ره

[^V01-67]: The argument shows that existing things differ in degree. It does not show that the parts we imagine within the *concept* of existence differ in degree. Strictly speaking, it is real existence that has degrees; its concept does so only indirectly. This is what is meant when the author says that existence is a general concept applied to things by degrees. — ط

[^V01-68]: Be aware—may God guide us both—that Aristotle's followers, philosophers of illumination, and other careful thinkers do not seriously disagree that the natural universal exists. Philosophers call it “essence”; mystical writers call it the “fixed reality”; different schools use other names for it. By “natural universal,” I do not mean an essence considered without restriction, whose existence is only in the mind and is a mental construct. I mean the underlying essence that can be considered as absolute, combined with conditions, or separate from matter. This underlying essence is even harder to grasp than “absolute essence,” one of its divisions. How could it fail to exist if the combined essence is one of its divisions? That alone is enough to establish the point.

    There is no need to use the older argument that the natural universal exists because it is a part of a composite essence. An essence considered without restriction is not literally a part of an essence considered together with a condition; only an essence considered specifically apart from other conditions is a part. If Avicenna meant by “without restriction” the essence as it exists within what is considered apart from other conditions, his part-and-whole argument would work: it would establish the general essence from matter itself. But the argument I have given from the combined essence is already enough. There is also no need for Lahiji's explanation that the “part” in this argument is merely a part in thought.

    The real dispute is whether, once a cause brings an essence about, the essence exists in its own right and existence is what lets us affirm it, or whether the essence is called existent only because existence is a feature that belongs to it. There are three kinds of such attribution. First, something may be described as moving only because something connected to it moves, as when we say a passenger moves because the ship moves; in truth, the passenger is not the source of that motion. Second, a subject may truly have a feature, as when a body is black because of its blackness. Both the body and blackness exist, and the body is genuinely black, though it can exist without being black. Third, a general kind and its distinguishing feature may form one reality: the general kind cannot exist without the distinguishing feature.

    The view that existence is fundamental is not like the first case, since the natural universal truly exists; its existence is not merely figurative. Nor is it exactly like the second, since a body can exist without blackness, while an essence has no actual existence apart from existence. It is closer to the third case, though with a difference: the existence of a species is attributed to its general kind, its distinguishing feature, and the complete species made from both; the relation between essence and existence is more like that between a shadow and what casts it.

    Both sides agree that when we say an essence exists, we must explain what makes it real and in what respect we are calling it existent. An essence by itself is open to both existence and nonexistence. If the only qualifying factor were the mental idea of existence, or a merely conceptual relation to the cause—as those who have not seen this clearly claim—then the essence would still not be real. Adding one mental concept to another does not create an existing thing. The concept of existence is itself just an idea; it is “existence” by its definition, not because it exists as a separate thing in the world. The same applies to the idea of “necessary existence.” By contrast, the illuminating relation is itself the light of existence, just as real bringing-into-existence is actual existence. In that light, the different expressions point to one reality. This shows why accusing the author of assuming what he is trying to prove is mistaken.

    There is another reason the accusation fails. The author's point is that reality is an essence taken together with existence. Without existence, an essence is not yet real. So how could existence itself fail to be real when it is what makes an essence real? — س ره

[^V01-69]: The author means that the outside world is where the existence of existence is found, not that the outside world is a container for existence itself; that latter question is not at issue here. We infer that external things are where existence's own existence is found. If existence is present in something else because it is received in it, then it is even more fitting for it to be present in itself, since nothing can be separate from itself. — ن ره

[^V01-70]: In a proof, “existent” means whatever has existence, whether a thing's being itself—which means it cannot be separated from itself—or its being something else. This is what “existent” and similar derived words mean in the language of reasoned proof, which aims to grasp things as they are in reality, whether or not everyday language uses the words in exactly the same way. It is simply a matter of terminology. — ن ره

[^V01-71]: The passage quoted here from *The Healing* was confused in places, so we have reproduced it from the original source.

[^V01-72]: If we included the kind of thing described in the distinguishing feature itself, the species would become part of its own distinguishing feature. This is an even stronger objection than the one given afterward. Someone could challenge that later objection by saying that it is not really a case of a thing being affirmed of itself. But this would not affect the claim that a merely possible statement would become necessary: its logical status would still be necessity.

    Here is the point. In the statement, the predicate may be the whole qualified expression, “human,” with the qualification outside it but included in the way the predicate is restricted. Then “human” is what is directly being said of the subject, and the statement is necessary. Or the predicate may be “human” with the qualification included in it. In that case the qualification is considered only indirectly; the main point is still that the subject is human. Compare “Zayd is in the house,” where his location is the point, with “Zayd is standing in the house,” where the location is secondary. The statement “a human is a human who can laugh” contains two claims: “a human is a human,” which is necessary, and “a human can laugh,” which is possible. This is like the way philosophers analyze the subject phrase in a statement: Avicenna treats it as unrestricted, while al-Farabi treats it as possible. It is also established that before we know a description, it functions as a report; once we know it, a report can function as a description.

    Another argument that the thing itself is not built into a derived adjective is that describing a cloth as white does not repeat the subject, either generally or in a narrower sense. If the word “white” included the thing it describes, the subject would be repeated. — س ره

[^V01-73]: A derived adjective has one simple descriptive meaning; it is not made up of the adjective plus the thing it describes. Because it is descriptive, however, it needs a link to its subject, supplied by the pronoun. — ن ره

[^V01-74]: The commentator gives two reasons for the view that a feature and the thing described by it are one. First, when we see something white, what we directly perceive is whiteness. Before considering the theory that whiteness is a feature that cannot exist on its own, we naturally call it both whiteness and white. If whiteness and “white” were not one in reality, we could not make that judgment so readily. Second, Aristotle and the translators of his work use derived adjectives to name the categories. If those adjectives were not one with the things they describe in reality, this usage and these examples would require an awkward explanation: we would have to say that the adjectives merely point to the underlying features. — س ره

[^V01-75]: The soul is pure being because what lies above it, and the goal of its perfection, are pure being too. It also has no fixed limit at which it stops. And each concept, such as “immaterial substance,” is itself, not an “I.” — س ره

[^V01-76]: Here “essence” means what makes a thing what it is, as the words that follow show. The source uses the noun where a pronoun would normally appear. — س ره

[^V01-77]: Someone might say that this argument assumes what it is trying to prove. The answer is that it leaves out a step: otherwise, the essential features would not differ. That is the difficulty the author is pointing to. — س ره

[^V01-78]: The view that limits the rule to cases other than simple claims of existence is Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's. Replacing “depends on” with “implies” is the view of Jalal al-Din al-Dawani. The claim that existence is not attributed to an essence even in the mind, and has no individual instance until it belongs to an essence, is held by a later scholar known as the meticulous Sayyid. This resembles the author's claim that the concept of “human” is united with a human being's own particular reality, even though the concept itself is not what exists outside the mind. The Sayyid reverses the claim: for him, the concept of existence has nothing corresponding to it in reality. To say that a thing is united with a concept means that the thing itself, without qualification, is represented by and drawn from that concept. — س ره

[^V01-79]: By “its own reality,” the author means existence without limiting it to one particular degree. He does not mean only the highest degree. Existence has levels. Imagine them rising from weak to strong, then from strong to stronger still. Each lower level is limited because it lacks some of what the next higher level possesses. The higher level, in turn, contains the completeness of the lower. Yet each higher level is itself limited in relation to one above it. This continues until we reach a level with no limit at all—its only limit is that it has none. This is pure reality taken with the condition that it be considered apart from other levels, making it one level among them. Taken without that condition, it would include all the levels and would not be one level opposed to the rest. — ط

[^V01-80]: The author chooses “particularization” here instead of “individuality,” as he also does in *The Divine Witnesses*, to point to a subtle idea: existence is one reality that unfolds through different forms and states. In a hierarchy of levels, existences are distinct through their own priority or posteriority. Being prior is part of what an existence is, though not in the way a part belongs to a whole. The concept “priority,” by contrast, is a relation and does not make up the existence itself. In a series of things at the same level, that concept necessarily follows and does not arise later than existence. A thing may also be distinguished by material features when it exists in matter.

    To see how features can make a thing distinct, consider the difference between an adjective and the underlying feature named by it. When “black” is considered as a description of a subject, it is an adjective that applies to the subject. When “blackness” is considered on its own, it is a feature that the subject bears. The difference depends on how we consider them. A similar distinction applies when we consider a body without qualification or as something set apart from what belongs to it. Features distinguish a thing in the first sense because they share one existence with their subject; a thing becomes distinct through its particular way of existing. In the second sense, the feature is not predicated of the subject in the same way and does not share its existence. The feature exists for the subject, rather than being the subject’s own existence, so it comes after the subject exists. How could it make the subject distinct before that? We may still call such features signs of distinctness. In the first sense they are necessary consequences of the thing; in the second, their being necessary while separate from the subject is harder to explain. That is why philosophers treated certain quantities, qualities, and positions as necessary features.

[^V01-81]: The alternatives here rule out only the possibility that neither applies; they need not exclude one another. Another possibility is that the intellects have no essence. The earlier either-or should be understood in the same way. This is why the second division has two branches: in the different degrees of existence, what makes them distinct is also what they share. — س ره

[^V01-82]: The point is that existence is one reality, one kind, whose degrees and essences differ without being separated by distinct essential features, as different universal essences are. Across these degrees, what makes existences different is the same as what makes them one. This reveals the meaning of Imam Ali's saying: “His unity is His distinction from His creation; distinction means a difference in quality, not separation into isolation.” The absence of isolating separation is the secret of existence as one reality. Understand this, if you are ready for it: here lies the highest aim. — ن ره

[^V01-83]: Someone may ask: How can essences distinguish existences if essences are not established before existence? On the view that existence is fundamental, existences themselves have no prior independent reality either. The first answer is that essences need not come before existence or be fundamental in their own right. It is enough for different essences to arise together with existence. An essence is real only in a secondary sense, because existence is real; it is made only in a secondary sense, because existence is what is made. Think of colored light appearing at the same time as colored glass is formed. Second, essences may be prior in what they are. Third, they may have earlier forms of existence, so their differences in an earlier realm can distinguish existences in a later one. Ultimately, the explanation reaches the fixed realities linked to God's names and attributes at the level of divine oneness. These are not made, and neither are their differences; this is where the question of what caused the differences comes to an end. — س ره

[^V01-84]: The self-evident general idea of existence is a mental construct; it has no existence outside the mind. It is not like “human,” which exists in the world and also has a mental form. If the concept of existence existed in both ways, then its essence would move between external and mental existence, and actual existence could be in the mind—something the author has already ruled out. As for how the mind can draw this idea from the reality of existence, even though that reality cannot enter the mind and the mind cannot move into the outside world, the author will explain later. This is what he means by saying that the general, self-evident idea of existence then follows in the mind: the mind contains the idea, not the individual realities together with the idea. — ط مد

[^V01-85]: The question is whether the reality of existence is made from a general kind and a distinguishing feature, as the argument supposes. The author does not discuss the possibility that it is made from something still broader and the third element of a three-part division, since that would obviously lead to an endless chain. Nor can the general kind be broader than both the first and third elements: in the third case, the general kind would not become one of the parts that make up the whole. By “something else,” the author means a species.

    In the first case, a distinguishing feature, considered on its own, brings the general kind into actuality. The two then stand as matter and form, with form acting alongside matter to make the whole. Some commentators say that a distinguishing feature causes only certain qualities of a general kind, such as its ability to exist in a particular form or to be definite. But since the general kind also causes some qualities of the distinguishing feature, the argument instead makes the feature a cause of the very essence of the general kind. That would contradict the assumption that existence's reality is their composite whole.

    In the second case, what makes broader kind and species the same in reality would also have to be what makes them different. General kind, distinguishing feature, and species are different ideas but one reality, as predication requires. Here, however, the idea of the distinguishing feature and the idea of the species are both identical with the reality of existence. So none of them could really be a broader kind, a feature that distinguishes it, or a species. Existence could not be composed of them. This reasoning establishes both that existences are simple realities and that existence itself is not a general kind. — س ره

[^V01-86]: What makes the elements one would have to be the very thing that makes them different. — ن ره

[^V01-87]: This argument takes an unnecessarily long route. If existence were a general kind, its species would either be a kind of existence, in which case everything in question is already existence, or an essence of some other kind. In the first case, there is no need to prove from the general kind that the species or its distinguishing feature is existence. In the second, what needs to be shown is that the species is existence. The author's wording suggests that he thinks the opponent is claiming that the general kind “existence” is predicated of its distinguishing feature. Perhaps that is what the opponent means. If the argument said “general kind” where it says “distinguishing feature,” the difficulty would be even clearer. A general kind is indeterminate by nature, while a distinguishing feature and a species are definite. Form is what makes a thing what it is, just as a distinguishing feature is what makes a species what it is. But this brings us back to the first argument given by the author and by Avicenna in the *Metaphysics* of *The Healing*. — س ره

[^V01-88]: If the distinguishing feature is predicated of its general kind, as in “some animals are rational,” then one might have to say “some existence is not existence.” The author gives this as a counterexample. The answer is that a general kind is a broad feature in relation to its distinguishing feature, just as the distinguishing feature is a specific feature in relation to the general kind. A feature that distinguishes existence could itself be called existence without becoming a species under existence; the predication is incidental. — س ره

[^V01-89]: They fall under substance only incidentally, just as a thing can be classed under a necessary property it implies, even though that property is not part of what the thing is. — ه ره

[^V01-90]: See Stage Four, in the chapter on how the general kind is taken from matter and the distinguishing feature from form. — ه ره

[^V01-91]: The relation between an individual and its species is like the relation between a distinguishing feature and its general kind. — ه ره

[^V01-92]: This means a species considered under its general kind. The author begins with species rather than general kind to show that a part of a general kind needs a distinguishing feature. The general idea of a species relates to its particular instances as parents relate to their children—not as one parent relates to all the children. — س ره

[^V01-93]: You may think the author should say that the other three kinds of universal idea reduce only to species, or else add “distinguishing feature” as well. If he means universals that apply to many things with the same underlying nature, they reduce to species. If he follows the common account, in which a shared feature reduces to a general kind and a defining feature to a distinguishing feature, then “distinguishing feature” should be added. The answer may be that he follows the second account but does not name the distinguishing feature because it is only part of a complete nature; the whole nature is the species, so naming the species is enough. The general kind, too, is only an incomplete part, but its breadth makes it relevant when discussing shared features. More likely, the author follows the first account: the other three universal ideas are all treated as species because they are complete. A distinguishing feature is only part of a nature, though the species becomes what it is through that feature. As Avicenna says, “A thing's form is its reality, that by which it is what it is.” The other three kinds of universal apply to many individual things with the same underlying nature. A general kind, by contrast, is only an indeterminate part of a nature. In reality, it is an open choice among distinguishing features, an ambiguity that moves among species. What the mind pictures as a complete, definite thing is actually matter considered apart from its form, not a general kind. It has no individual cases sharing one complete nature—especially at the highest levels of general kinds, and in the highest general kinds of qualities, which are simple realities. This is why the author does not reduce it to a species. — س ره

[^V01-94]: This is like a general kind and distinguishing feature, considered as what is still vague and what makes it definite; or like existence and nonexistence, as in complete, separate intellects. Dividing a thing into parts in either way makes it dependent on those parts. Consider this carefully. — ن ره

[^V01-95]: The relation here is like a shadow to what casts it, or a reflection to the surface that reflects it—not like one independent thing attaching to another. Existence is not one item in a series that could be followed by another existence. If we imagine a second existence alongside pure existence, that second would be the same as the first. Existence is light, and things are its rays; existence is the root, and everything else is a branch of it. — ن ره

[^V01-96]: The author says the resulting identity is “distinct from” the First, rather than merely saying its concept differs from the concept of existence, to point to a subtle idea: existence is the very act of proceeding from the First and being related to it. Dependence on another is part of what dependent existence is, as explained earlier. — س ره

[^V01-97]: What necessarily follows from something is made real through the very act that makes its basis real; it is not made by a second act. The same applies to what is not made. The scholar's statement therefore clearly supports the view that existence is what is made real. This truth even appears in the writing of a determined defender of the view that essences are fundamental, al-Lahiji. In the twenty-seventh question of *The Dawning Lights*, he says that calling essence what is made means only that we should not imagine essences fixed in nonexistence before they are made, with existence or the condition of existing added afterward. Once that mistaken idea is removed, there is no problem in saying that existence—or the fact that something exists—is what is made, since no essence exists before it is made. — س ره

[^V01-98]: Even if essences detached from all existence could somehow exist, the nature of a general kind would still come before the nature of a species. That is priority in the very nature of a thing. — س ره

[^V01-99]: The point is that considering an essence stripped of every kind of existence and every other feature does not, by itself, give it existence. It removes all existence and all features from it. Only when we add a second thought—that this very stripping is itself a kind of mental existence—does the question of existence arise. Even then, there is no problem or endless chain: the sequence ends when the mind stops considering it. We can also say that stripping essence is itself a kind of “mixing” with the idea of stripping, not with actual existence, so no further act of stripping is needed. This is like saying that prime matter is the potential for form and other things in a body. If we then ask whether this potential itself has actual existence, we might imagine an endless series of potentials and actualities. The answer is that the actuality of the potential is the potential itself, not something added to it—just as parts of time do not need another time in order to be earlier or later. In short, essence is stripped of existence when considered in its primary sense; it is mixed with existence only in the common, expanded sense. In the first sense, it is not described as existing, so the question of how it can be described that way does not arise. The author says it is described as existing under one consideration only to grant the objection for the sake of argument. — س ره

[^V01-100]: A statement can be analyzed into three parts—the subject, the idea of the predicate, and the predicate's being affirmed of the subject—when we examine its concepts. That does not mean these three parts all exist in reality. In “Zayd is Zayd,” we can distinguish three conceptual parts, but the reality of the statement is just the subject itself. The author has another answer in one of his treatises. Existence exists through itself, while an essence exists through existence. So “the human being exists” means that existence is what makes the idea of humanity true in the outside world. In reality, the idea of “human” is affirmed of this existence and depends on it, as a shadow depends on what casts it. This applies when we mean a particular reality. If we mean the general concept of existence, it works like other mental features: they apply to things once those things are established or distinguished in the mind. But the broad mental idea of existence is not what makes an essence real and removes nonexistence from it; like other mental concepts, it is outside the essence of everything. — س ره

[^V01-101]: That is, there is an immense difference between this relation and the other relations discussed. Words are used for general meanings even when the levels they cover differ greatly. — س ره

[^V01-102]: Put another way, after carefully considering essence apart from every kind of existence, essence is not “existence” in the strict, primary sense, even though in broader usage it is called existence. — ه ره

[^V01-103]: Some copies say “the concept of existence”; the meaning is the same. The abstract noun “existence” means existence considered on its own, while “existent” means existence without restriction. The difference is like that between a feature and an adjective made from it: “whiteness” considered on its own is not predicated of a subject, while “white” is; they differ only in form, just as unrestricted whiteness and “white” differ in how they are used in a sentence. The commentator then says that the different meanings under discussion may be features either in reality or in thought. Existence as a separate abstract noun cannot be a feature in reality or thought. Once essence is considered in itself, it is not described by that isolated idea of existence, but by “existent” or by existence in its ordinary meaning. The Sayyid does not hold that the underlying feature must literally inhere in the subject for an adjective to apply. The other two meanings may be features in thought, but not in reality. — س ره

[^V01-104]: “Far apart are dust and the Lord of lords, water and a mirage, darkness and light!” The author says that essence disappears into existence and that, in reality, essence is its own being. The Sayyid says instead that existence disappears into essence and that essence is its being. Both reject a real division between the two. But what makes it true to predicate the idea of existence of an essence? The Sayyid does not say that existence is a feature inhering in essence, either outside the mind or in thought, nor that it is connected to essence by some other relation. If so, there would be no difference between a true and a false statement. He does say that things exist by being united with the idea of existence, as he explains later. But what makes that union true? It must already be established. — س ره

[^V01-105]: This conflicts with what the same author says later: no one disputes that essence and existence differ in thought, not in the outside world. Consider this carefully. — س ره

[^V01-106]: One can reply that to doubt something is to picture it as an open question. What exists outside the mind cannot be pictured in that way; whatever we picture is an abstract idea. At most, this proves a difference in thought, not in reality. It therefore defeats Suhrawardi's claim that existence itself needs another existence and also the Aristotelian claim that existence is added to essence in the outside world. It does not, however, defeat the claim that a possible thing's existence is added to its essence in thought, which both sides accept. The commentator also suggests another reading: the author may mean that his answer to Suhrawardi's argument for existence being fundamental also applies to the Aristotelian proof that existence is added to essence in thought. A note the author wrote while discussing this argument in *The Philosophy of Illumination* supports that reading: the same response works whether the argument is used against the Aristotelian proof that existence is added to essence or as proof that nothing exists whose essence is existence itself. — س ره

[^V01-107]: The cases where existence differs from substance and quality include God's existence; the cases where substance or quality differs from existence include the four kinds of quality. You might object that whenever the four qualities exist, existence exists too, since an essence cannot be established without existence. If you consider only what those natures are in themselves, they count as qualities in the strict, defining sense, not as actual instances of the general kind “quality”; quality itself is not an instance of itself. For them to count as actual qualities that are not instances of existence, there would have to be a real case of quality that is not a real case of existence. Yet, as al-Lahiji says, the cases that distinguish two concepts must differ in their realities, not merely in how we think about them. We reply that only on your view—where individuality is existence—is the essence of quality an instance of existence. The Shaykh holds that a thing becomes an individual through its own essence after it is made, even if that view is mistaken in reality. If existences are real, they are like accidents that belong to subjects after those subjects are already complete in their own natures. On his view, the particular existence of each quality would be like a particular quality belonging to another particular quality, as an accident belongs to its subject. — س ره

[^V01-108]: Careful thought shows that this is a proof, not merely an argument designed to corner the other side. — س ره

[^V01-109]: That is, real existence lies outside both essence and the general idea of existence, and differs from them as a standing person differs from a shadow, or a shadow from the person who casts it. Yet it is united with essence as something not yet fully determined is united with what makes it definite. “Accidental,” in the sense of a feature predicated of things from outside their definition, applies to the general concept of existence, as the author says below. — س ره

[^V01-110]: The claim that the reality of light is not universal or particular applies to a meaning broad enough to include God, immaterial beings, and sensory light. But visible light, which the eye perceives, is certainly one of the kinds of things that have an essence and can be considered universal or particular, like anything else. — ط مد

[^V01-111]: Do not take “unfolding” or “descent” to mean literal movement from one place to another. For something to flow from a source does not mean that the source leaves its place or loses any of its levels. It means that the source casts a shadow or reflection: something proceeds from it without reducing its perfection. If that manifestation returns to it, it adds nothing to its perfection. The true Giver has a reality in which His manifestations have no share, while none of them has any reality apart from Him. A familiar example is light reflected from the sun to the moon, from the moon to a mirror, from the mirror to water, and from the water to a wall. — س ره

[^V01-112]: The author pictures spiritual light and darkness as two cones pointing in opposite directions. The cone of light has its broad base in the world of intellect and its tip in the material world; the cone of darkness has its tip in the world of intellect and its broad base in the material world. — س ره

[^V01-113]: It is called existence as a predicate because it is what we affirm in simple statements such as “X exists.” In the predicate position, what matters is the concept; what that concept refers to is what is affirmed of all actual things and even of illusory essences. Another explanation is that the mind knows how things are connected to the reality named by this concept and can affirm that connection. But as for what that reality is in itself, none knows it except He. — س ره

[^V01-114]: Since the simple statement “X exists” comes before the compound statement “X is such-and-such,” we are now concerned with existence as what makes something real, not with its unity, which already presupposes that reality. The view that all existences depend on God is the special understanding of divine oneness. The fitting religious way to express this is that all existences are wholly dependent and needy before the One who is utterly self-sufficient: “You are the ones in need of God, while God is the Self-Sufficient.” True monotheists mean nothing else by their oneness. Woe to a doctrine of oneness that means something other than this, and to a claim of singleness that misses this point. — س ره

[^V01-115]: “Being” expresses a relation. When real existence is attributed to itself, the relation is like a thing's relation to itself. When being is attributed to an essence, the relation is like a thing's relation to something else. — ن ره

[^V01-116]: *The Dawning Lights* by al-Lahiji suggests that the first view belongs to al-Dawani. The meticulous Sayyid, however, says that existence is prior to essence because it is more truly entitled to reality. Perhaps, then, the author means al-Dawani by “some careful scholars.” I do not have their books at hand to check. — س ره

[^V01-117]: This does not work for a statement in which subject and predicate mean exactly the same thing, because such a statement says they are one in meaning. But in *The Book of Insights*, the author argues that without the primacy of existence we could not make ordinary true statements, only definitions. Here he goes further: without it, no statement would be possible at all. Even in a statement where subject and predicate are one in meaning, what makes them one is existence—not existence as something contained in a thing, but existence as the link between them. The earlier argument in *The Book of Insights* is a concession to a less exact way of speaking. — س ره

[^V01-118]: The author calls the human being's union with existence a unity in reality, although existence is an added feature of the human essence when we consider the human being's thinghood. This follows from its union with the human being's actual existence, which is itself the reality of the human being. — س ره

[^V01-119]: This may sound as though the real existence of whiteness were the very existence attributed to the human being. That cannot be right, since one existence would then have to be both a substance and an accident. The answer is that when the existence of whiteness is considered without restriction, it is one level of the human being's existence: it belongs to the human being in its own right, but only indirectly to the idea of whiteness or to “what is white.” — س ره

[^V01-120]: In the first example, one of the two is an idea drawn from reality; in the remaining examples, the other—or both—are. — س ره

[^V01-121]: The author restates his point as a choice between two possibilities: two fully real things cannot be one, but a mental idea and a real thing can be united. Otherwise, once we establish that what makes them one is real and that one or both sides is only an idea drawn from reality, there is no remaining question to settle. — س ره

[^V01-122]: Calling real existence a “concept” means that some aspect of it appears in the mind. A thing's aspect is, in a way, the thing itself, so we can describe the reality through what appears of it—as we speak of a universal nature even though its universality exists only in the mind. Or perhaps “concept” is being used to mean “reality,” as it often is among those who know through direct insight. As the verse says: “All are words, but you are the meaning, you who draw hearts to yourself.” If real existence is said to be shared among essences because they share one general concept, that would be impossible: one concept cannot be drawn from different realities precisely as different. We discussed this when treating the shared meaning of existence. Real existence is shared among essences because their possible features and effects appear through it. Its different levels are shared in one respect, since what makes them alike is also what makes each distinct; in another respect they are distinct, since what makes them distinct is also what they share. Understand this and hold to it. — س ره

[^V01-123]: There seems to be a copying error here. I think the correct wording is: “Both real existence and the abstract concept of existence are shared among essences.” There is no need for the elaborate explanation offered by Mullā Hādī Sabzawārī.

[^V01-124]: This points to the realm of existence as a mirror that reveals the realities of things and their states. The words “If existence did not shine within the things that are, and reveal itself through them” point to the reverse as well: things and their realities are mirrors that reveal the reality of existence, its attributes, and its names. This is a profound secret to those who know. — ن ره

[^V01-125]: People who speak of God's oneness take four positions. (1) They may accept that both existences and existent things are many, while professing God's oneness aloud and holding to it in a general way. Most people are at this level; this is ordinary monotheism. (2) They may say that both existence and what exists are one. This is the view of some Sufis; it is the most special form of monotheism. (3) They may say that existence is one but existent things are many. This is the position attributed to the spiritual insight of the divine philosophers; it is special monotheism. (4) They may say that existence and what exists are one within their very multiplicity. This is the author's view and the view of the highest mystics; it is the highest form of monotheism. Another classification divides monotheism into oneness of effects, acts, attributes, and essence.

    The difference between the author's way and the view attributed to the divine philosophers is this. The author accepts many existences and many existent things, while also affirming unity within that multiplicity. Think of one person standing before many mirrors. The person appears many times, and each reflection has the form of a human being. There are many images, and yet, because each image is only a reflection and has no independent reality, they are one in the very midst of their multiplicity. If you attend to the person who is reflected, the images become ways of seeing that person. If you treat the images as independent things, you lose sight of what they are. The same relation can hold through a hierarchy of levels or across levels that are far apart, as when the same face appears tiny in ice, dimly in muddy water, or clearly in a mirror.

    The presence of the one who is reflected is like a thread that strings together the many different images, connects them, gathers what is scattered, and joins opposites. In the same way, when we see existences as dependent manifestations of God—as flashes of His light—they are never wholly separate from His own appearing. But if we take them as independent things, we misunderstand their reality, because dependence belongs to them by their very nature. For the author, existence is one reality with levels that differ in strength and weakness. The very feature that makes the levels different is also what they share, and this confirms their unity: the more fully reality is affirmed and found, the wider its scope and the less it is marked by absence and loss. This is why he calls the multiplicity of existences luminous, while the multiplicity of essences is dark.

    Particular contingent existences are real, but they are rays of the sun of reality and pure relations of dependence; they are not separate things that happen to have a relation to God. The author will soon criticize the claim, made in a treatise called *al-Zawrāʾ*, that the existence of things is a relation to God rather than a relation that itself exists.

    By contrast, the other group's view is that real existence is one individual, with no multiplicity in any way, while the many existent things are essences. They exist by being related to real existence, not through distinct contingent existences understood as need and dependence. They allow the derived word “existent” to apply more broadly than something in which the source meaning of the word inheres: it can also apply to what is merely related to that source, and even to the source itself. They say that the realities of things cannot be established by ordinary language, so there is no problem in saying that an essence is “existent” simply because it is related to existence. Arabic usage allows similar words, such as names for someone who sells milk, dates, or iron. They also hold that essences are real; if essences were only ideas drawn from something else, they would have to be drawn from God's existence, since they recognize no other existence.

    The author rejects this view for three reasons. First, how can one and the same real existence belong to itself and to other things—making it both a substance and an accident, and both prior and later—when things with the same essence, such as human beings, do not differ in their essence or admit degrees? Second, if the relation to God is a real, illuminating connection, it would itself have to be another existence beyond God's one existence, which this view denies. The relation must therefore be an ordinary relation that depends on both things already existing. But essence is not simply identical with dependence: the essence whose existence we question is not the same as its relation to God. This objection does not apply in the same way to the author's view, because existence cannot be grasped as a concept apart from the realities we encounter; still, such a relation of identity does not fit the other group's view. They treat essences as fully real in themselves, whereas identity through relation can hold only between what is not yet fully determined and what makes it definite—not between two already complete realities, as will be explained later.

    Third, if existence is simply what makes things existent, then those relations must themselves be many existences. How, then, can this view count as special monotheism or as belief in one existence? It becomes ordinary monotheism, like the view that both existence and existent things are many. By treating essences as primary realities distinct in their very nature from existence, they end up affirming a second reality alongside existence. So they do not escape a subtle form of associating others with God. May God make us among His sincere servants—indeed, among those made wholly sincere for Him. The author, by contrast, treats what is related to God as existence too. There is nothing in the house but existence.

    The first and third objections may seem inconsistent. The first assumes that God's necessary existence is the existence of things; the third assumes that their existences are many mental relations. We can answer that the proponents of this view express it in different ways: sometimes they say that what makes things existent is their relation to God; at other times, they say that Zayd's existence serves as a means of presenting Zayd. One objection addresses the first version and the other the second. Consider this carefully. — س ره

[^V01-126]: If “thing” means something whose existence is in question—that is, an essence, as in the author's earlier distinction between the familiar names for kinds of thing and the unfamiliar names for kinds of existence—then saying that thinghood and existence go together means that they are realized together. Wherever an essence is realized, its particular existence is realized too, and the two move together. Otherwise, the claim means that they are one in reality. To explain this: as we have seen, existence has a reality of its own. It is one reality that differs in strength and weakness, necessity and possibility, and other ways. Its highest level, complete in every respect and without any deficiency, is the Necessary Existence, which has no essence apart from its existence. Every level below it has a limit and a deficiency. The definition of a human being as a rational animal, for example, tells us about the limits of that person's existence; the definition of an animal as a body that grows and moves by sensation and will tells us about the limits of an animal's existence. A deficiency depends on the existence it limits; it cannot be real without it. This also clarifies a further dispute: does existence become real before essence is established, or does essence become established first? Some people argue that a nonexistent thing must still be a thing because it is necessary for something to be itself, and impossible for it not to be itself. We reply that a thing is itself by its very nature, not because it has existed from eternity. It can fail to be itself when it does not exist, because then there is no thing at all—only nonexistence. This view is extremely weak, unless its supporters mean to defend God's eternal knowledge. But in eternity a nonexistent thing is sheer nothing: it has no disclosure or distinction by which it is known, and it has neither external nor mental existence. Otherwise there would be multiplicity in God's essence and things would be eternal alongside Him. Still, we do not need to say that things have a fixed reality detached from every kind of existence. Their reality follows from God's own existence, as the Sufis hold. — س ره

[^V01-127]: This argument, and the final point made by the Illuminationist philosopher, rest on the view common among those thinkers: most held that essences are established even in nonexistence and that “states” are also fixed. As al-Kātibī says, they treated being a substance as a state, even though it belongs to an essence whether it exists or not. As Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi says, they explained differences among nonexistent essences by means of states. For them, a state is a feature of a thing that is neither existent nor nonexistent. But under the familiar definition—a feature of something existent that is itself neither existent nor nonexistent—a state would be like the abstract features of existing things. Existence itself would then be a state belonging to something that already exists, not a feature of an essence while it is nonexistent. Otherwise it would not be a feature of something existent. — س ره

[^V01-128]: The either-or question is meant to force the other side to answer. In their own account, a state is fixed because it is a feature. It cannot be existent, or the features themselves would need further features without end; it cannot be nonexistent either, or the thing would have a feature opposed to its own nature. — س ره

[^V01-129]: “Thinghood” faces the same problem as possibility. We call thinghood fixed because it is a feature. If they refuse to let a thing be described by what is fixed of it, then they cannot call it possible. If they accept that conclusion, nothing is possible, even though they have called it possible. — س ره

[^V01-130]: They may say either that God is the agent in an absolute sense, or that His existence is identical with His essence. The first claim is contradicted by names such as “the worshipped” and “the praised,” which are passive forms and are still applied to Him. The second is contradicted by all the beautiful names. Scripture also uses the word “existent” of Him, as in the prayer: “I call upon You, O You who are present everywhere; perhaps You will hear my cry.” — س ره

[^V01-131]: The author's wording in this chapter is compressed and not entirely clear. A later chapter will explain the difference between linking existence and dependent existence, clarify what is meant by a “state,” and set out the important principles that follow from these distinctions. We will return to them there. — ط ره

[^V01-132]: The three modalities—necessity, possibility, and impossibility—are features of this kind of existence. To sum up: there is linking existence and existence stated as a predicate. Linking existence means that one thing is affirmed of another. It is what we mean in “whiteness is present in the body” or “the body is white”; even if we omit the linking word, the connection is still there. This link is not an idea that stands on its own. It is like a grammatical particle: we cannot make it a separate subject of a statement without changing it into existence stated as a predicate. It links parts of affirmative statements; a negative statement denies the link. It is also different from the judgment that subject and predicate are one, which occurs in every statement. This kind of linking existence occurs in affirmative statements with a subject and predicate, but not in simple statements such as “X exists.” The author calls it linking existence, following his teacher in *The Clear Horizon*, to avoid confusing it with dependent existence. Al-Lahiji, in one of his books, called the existence of accidents in their subjects “linking existence” and confused the two. Existence stated as a predicate, by contrast, means that something exists in itself, as in a complete statement such as “X exists.” A thing may exist in itself and for itself, as an intellect or body does; or it may exist in itself but not for itself, as an accident does when it depends on a subject. The first is existence in itself; it is either through itself, as God's existence is, or through another, as the existence of substances that do not inhere in a subject. — س ره

[^V01-133]: That is, they agree in their nature, since existence has no species and is not a universal kind. — س ره

[^V01-134]: They are one in nature and reality, but differ in how we consider them. Existence stated as a predicate lies outside the ten basic categories; the kind set against it is the category of relation. Relation is a second-order idea, and second-order ideas have a weak kind of realization. In that respect, they belong to the same broad nature as existence stated as a predicate. Consider this carefully; it is subtle. — ن ره

[^V01-135]: That is, the essences drawn from the different levels of existence as it unfolds. — ه ره

[^V01-136]: When linking existence is considered precisely as a link, it is not an existence or a thing in its own right. If we call it “existence” in this respect, the word is being used in a different sense; that is the correct account. But when the mind turns toward the link and makes a judgment about it or through it, it becomes existence stated as a predicate. The same happens with grammatical linking words: while they serve as links and tools, they are not complete, independent ideas; when we focus on them and make them the subject of a judgment, they become independent noun-like ideas. What is incomplete becomes complete; what is only potential becomes actual. There is a difference between being a thing and merely having the possibility of being one: possibility, just as possibility, is not a thing in its own right unless considered in another way. The author will explain this further when he discusses matter as an abstract mental idea. — ه ره

[^V01-137]: If their agreement were in some other meaning, that meaning would itself have to be predicated of them, and the distinction would collapse. Perhaps the author means that the difference between them is so great that they nearly share a word only, as in the earlier discussion of how essence is described as existing. Otherwise, this would conflict with what he has established throughout the book: abstract ideas, relations, and absences all have some share in existence. This view also answers a serious difficulty for philosophers who discuss second-order ideas and relational features even though philosophy is supposed to study real things. The author says that links and relations exist in the way relations exist, even if they do not exist as independent subjects. If they did not exist in this way, there would be no difference between true and false statements. Even if linking existence existed only in the mind, that would be enough, since existence has one nature whether it is mental or external, extremely strong or very weak. It is better to understand the author as speaking about how the two ideas differ when considered simply as ideas, and how the realities of linking and dependent existence differ—not as denying that the existences themselves share anything. In existence, what makes one thing distinct is also what it shares with others. The distinction is this: another relational existence attaches to the independent existence of whiteness once whiteness has been established as a real feature. First we establish, in a simple statement, that whiteness is real and belongs to the world outside the mind. Then we consider how whiteness is related to an ivory body, or how the body's existence is related to whiteness. Whether we express this connection by making whiteness or the body the subject of the statement depends on how the mind considers it. — س ره

[^V01-138]: Examples include blackness in a body or for a body; an effect's existence for its cause; and something known as present to the soul. As explained in *The Clear Horizon*, the point of this three-part division is that dependent existence is not limited to accidents. It also applies to forms present in matter, an effect's existence for its cause, the Active Intellect's existence for the soul, and God's existence for the world when discussing final causes. For us, the Active Intellect's presence to the soul is an example of existence “at” something; our perception of particular things is different, since the soul brings those perceptions about, so they are more like effects of a cause. A substance can be independent in relation to things below it, yet dependent in relation to God.
