[^V01-297]: That is, the causes and conditions that must be in place for a thing to come into being. — ه ره

[^V01-298]: Someone might object: if every denial is true of an essence at its own level, then possibility must be true of it there, since possibility includes the denial that existence and nonexistence are necessary. The answer is that this is true, but the denial of that denial is true as well. Just as possibility is not identical with the essence or a part of it, the denial of possibility is neither identical with nor a part of the essence. — س ره

[^V01-299]: The wording seems mistaken, because possibility is itself a denial, and the text says that these denials are expressed in negative statements. Here, the other denials may have been mentioned only in passing. Changing “first” to “second” in the text would not fix the problem, since necessity and impossibility are not negative statements. The wording would make sense if read as “their opposites”: the denials of necessary existence and necessary nonexistence, which together define possibility. I suspect the original instead said “its two parts”—the denial of the necessity of existence and the denial of the necessity of nonexistence—with “first” and “second” reversed. — س ره

[^V01-300]: This explains the exception for possible essences considered in themselves. If the division says that a thing, in reality, is never outside the three categories, then it is exhaustive. But if it says the same of a thing at every level, including its own essence considered just as it is, that is false: at that level, the essence may be none of the three. Even if one category were said to belong to it there, the division would still not be exhaustive. Possibility cannot be identical with the essence, since possibility is a denial while the essence has its own distinct content. Nor can it be a part of the essence, since then the essence would be itself plus possibility. The essence cannot be necessary or impossible; if it is possible, possibility itself would have to be possible, and the same question would arise again without end. — س ره

[^V01-301]: This means the source of necessity. Necessity as a way of relating a predicate to a subject cannot exist at the level of God’s essence; what exists there is its source, the fullness of existence. It is like saying that relational attributes are additional to the divine essence, while what grounds them is the essence itself. — س ره

[^V01-302]: A reader might ask: if possibility is not in an essence at its own level, why do philosophers call it essential? Because there are two different claims. Possibility may be true of an essence without being identical with it or forming part of it. The philosophers who call it essential mean that it follows from the essence itself; this is “essential” in the sense used in the *Book of Demonstration*. The present argument denies only that possibility is a piece of the essence, in the sense used in the *Isagoge*. In other words, something can be said of an essence because of what it is, without being part of its definition. The commentator also distinguishes what possibility is said of from what directly grounds that claim: if possibility comes from the essence itself, the essence is its ground; if it comes from something added, the essence is only what the claim is about. — س ره

[^V01-303]: Here existence is the predicate in a simple statement such as “God exists.” That first kind concerns necessary existence itself; those that follow concern necessary relations between a subject and what is said of it. In a simple statement of existence, we are not saying that one thing belongs to another. Existence is not a link between them. The first necessity therefore belongs to existence itself; the others concern what must hold in a relationship. Another difference is that the author calls necessity “eternal” in the first case and “essential” in the others. You may ask: if a simple statement of existence contains no such relationship, especially when it concerns God, how can necessity describe the character of a relationship? I reply: at this stage we are only setting out the alternatives; the proof has yet to be examined. — س ره

[^V01-304]: Or two contradictories, or two similar things, combined in a way that makes the whole impossible. Neither of two opposites need be impossible by itself; what is impossible is putting them together in this way. You may object: if a combination, considered simply as a combination, is possible, what is impossible here? I reply: as a combination it is possible, but as a combination of these particular things it is impossible. Something impossible in what it means may still be formed as an object of thought. — س ره

[^V01-305]: The discussion relevant here has already appeared. Keep it in mind. — س ره

[^V01-306]: A possible thing can be considered in two ways. First, we can consider its essence as an existing thing whose existence is separate from other things. When we relate it to God, all the other factors that contribute to its existence—intermediaries, causes, conditions, and what prepares it—join with God to make up its complete cause. Second, we can consider its existence as linked to other things, so that it cannot exist unless they do. “Zayd,” for example, may mean the person born to ʿAmr and Fāṭima at a certain time and place, and so on. On this view, his existence is linked to the whole network of causes and conditions, and bringing him into existence means bringing that whole network into being. In this sense, God is his complete cause. Most philosophical discussions use the first way of considering a possible thing. It follows that a possible thing is necessary relative to another only when considered in relation to its complete cause, or to something that shares that complete cause. Otherwise it remains only possible relative to that other thing. A Necessary Being, by contrast, can only be necessary relative to a possible thing, since the possible thing’s existence depends on it. — ط

[^V01-307]: Examples are a human being’s speech and a donkey’s braying. This is true when we consider their nearby causes. If we trace those causes back to the Cause of causes, they are necessary relative to it. — س ره

[^V01-308]: One example is the impossibility of a vacuum considered alongside the absence of whiteness from something that can be white. Here, “because of” should be understood as “in the case of,” as in the Qur'anic phrase “establish prayer at the sun’s decline.” This avoids an objection based on the absence of the First Effect, which is possible in itself, and the absence of God, which is impossible in itself: the relation between these absences is necessity, not possibility. The rule can also be extended to essentially possible things and what follows from their essences, since there is no relation between them and a creator in whether they are brought into being. The answer will be that whatever entails something impossible in itself is itself impossible in itself. On this reading, “because of” means “on account of,” not “at the time of.” — س ره

[^V01-309]: An effect has no independent existence of its own; its existence is entirely dependent on its cause. — س ره

[^V01-310]: That is, the absence of the cause considered in relation to the effect’s existence, and the cause’s existence considered in relation to the effect’s absence. — س ره

[^V01-311]: Someone may object that this does not answer the question about a thing changing from one state to another, since possibility as “lack of necessity” is still part of the objection. The answer is that a thing possible in itself does not demand either side, so it does not conflict with something else requiring it to exist. It is like any subject ready to receive a feature. But a thing necessary in itself does require existence, so another thing could not make it possible: removing its necessity would also remove the existence its nature requires. Similarly, if possibility meant a demand for nonexistence, and something else supplied existence, the two demands would conflict. — س ره

[^V01-312]: There are three relevant kinds of statement. In a simple negative statement, such as “Zayd is not a writer,” we consider the subject and predicate, then deny that they are connected. In an affirmative statement with a negative predicate, such as “Zayd is a non-writer,” we affirm that a negative feature belongs to the subject. A statement with a negative subject and a negative predicate has both kinds of negation. The first statement has four parts in the mind: the subject, the predicate, their possible connection, and the denial of that connection. The affirmative statement with a negative predicate adds a fifth: assigning the negative feature to the subject. In a statement with a negative subject and predicate, both terms are themselves treated as statements. This is why “Zayd is not a writer” differs from “Zayd is a non-writer”: in the first, the denial comes before the connecting verb; in the second, the connection is affirmed and the predicate is negative. The second kind of statement still requires the subject to exist, because it assigns something to that subject. Some logicians deny this and say that “vacuum is nonexistent” does not require a vacuum to exist as its subject. But the proper way to say that no vacuum exists is “No vacuum is existent,” which does not assume a vacuum as a subject. Then the broader claim “Nothing existent is perceptible” would be false. The same issue appears in an argument that says, “A substance is not an accident; whatever is not an accident does not need a subject.” The first statement is affirmative with a negative predicate, not a simple denial. — س ره

[^V01-313]: Three objections are raised. First, if possibility is only a denial, and denial removes the connection between subject and predicate, possibility could not be a way of qualifying a statement alongside necessity and impossibility. Second, if possibility is two denials taken together, it would not be one simple meaning like necessity and impossibility. Third, this would contradict the earlier claim that possibility is the positive statement that both necessities are absent. The answer is to distinguish the essence considered just as it is from the mind’s judgment about it. Of an essence in itself, we make two simple denials: its existence is not necessary, and its nonexistence is not necessary. These denials contain no further judgment. The mind can then restate them as one affirmative claim: the essence is such that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary. That is how possibility is affirmed of the essence. Since this affirmative claim is true of the essence, it requires a basis; and because nothing else is under consideration, its basis is the essence itself. This avoids all three objections. It also resolves the apparent conflict between an essence’s own lack of necessity and the necessity or impossibility it receives through another. The first claim concerns the essence by itself, where there is no demand either way. The second concerns the essence together with its cause. The statements differ in meaning and refer to different circumstances, so they do not conflict. — ط

[^V01-314]: The equal relation between existence and nonexistence follows from the meaning of possibility. The positive statement that an essence is possible is true when the essence exists, either in the world or in the mind. Someone might object that if the essence itself requires both sides to remain equal, the earlier problem still stands, even if that requirement is not the meaning of possibility. The answer is that this requirement is only a requirement not to require either side. — س ره

[^V01-315]: The discussion is about how possibility is predicated of an essence, not the first, mental grasp of what possibility means. The claim that it is true to say that neither necessity applies is mentioned in another work, *The Clear Horizon*, but there too it is not presented as the meaning of possibility, only as something that follows from it. “Being true” is itself a concept. Here, a simple denial means a bare refusal of a connection, which does not require the subject to exist. A negative predicate, by contrast, describes the absence of a feature in a subject and therefore does require a subject to exist. Some writers call this an affirmative statement with a negative predicate. In that sense, the positive statement discussed above resembles it. — س ره

[^V01-316]: This argument is included among the kinds of possibility because someone might object: if possibility is neither the essence nor part of it, then it must be an incidental feature that needs a cause; and if it is caused by something else, possibility would be “through another.” The answer is that, as the author explains, the possible thing has only bare potentiality. Possibility is not something made, and the essence is not a maker. The terminology therefore does not force the conclusion. Also, a feature that needs a cause is one added to a subject; not every feature that can be said of a subject is an added feature of that kind. — س ره

[^V01-317]: This applies to the cause of existence as well, though this existence is like nonexistence because it is pure potentiality: the existence of prime matter. Prime matter is also a co-cause, since a form helps bring matter into existence. The form in question is one separate being. — س ره

[^V01-318]: This is the view of the distinguished philosopher Dāmād: in judgments, nonexistence follows the pattern of existence, unity, and plurality. Just as the identity of an effect’s nonexistence follows the identity of that effect’s existence, the nonexistence of a particular complete cause follows the identity of that cause. The many absences are absences of separate parts and conditions, not multiple instances of the absence of the complete cause—just as the parts of a whole may exist separately without dividing the real whole into separate wholes. — س ره

[^V01-319]: It is contradictory to say that a thing’s possibility in general comes from something else while, by itself, it could still be possible, necessary, or impossible. If its possibility comes from another, how can it have any of these statuses in itself? Also, “allowed” here means “conceivable,” not possibility in itself. — س ره

[^V01-320]: This is disputed. If we suppose the other has no effect, the thing may still be possible in itself, as the first argument says. The two arguments are called groundless for the reason just given, not because they take possibility to mean that the essence itself demands the outcome. The commentator adds that they may be further objections to an earlier proposal, and that some of their problems are too obvious to need stating. — س ره

[^V01-321]: The denial applies to the qualifier. So to say “a human being, considered in itself, is neither existent nor nonexistent” means that existence is not the human being’s own special nature, either identical with it or a part of it. This does not mean that the human being lacks existence altogether, since existence can belong to it in another way. — س ره

[^V01-322]: This distinction does not hold in every case. Sometimes a thing is rightly said to lack both a feature and its opposite when considered in itself, as with features that belong to an essence only on condition that it exists, such as writing or motion. In other cases, when a feature belongs to an essence without that condition, the essence is not free of one side or the other, even when considered in itself. Existence, unity, possibility, and thinghood are examples. So an essence considered in itself is free of features that arise only with existence and of their opposites, but its own essential features are different: the essence is not the source of them, even when one side cannot be denied of it. The rule about where the denial belongs applies to the essence’s own features. If we say “a human being, considered in itself, is not existent,” the denial is about existence in any form, which would wrongly make the essence entirely without existence. That is not the same as denying a feature that can be absent at the essence’s own level, as explained earlier. — س ره

[^V01-323]: The best answer may be that possibility is a simple denial, expressed by “is not” in the incomplete sense, and this kind of denial cannot itself be denied by another simple denial. The denial that is denied in the phrase “the denial of the denial of both necessities” is instead a negative feature used as a predicate. Denying that feature does not remove possibility. — ط

[^V01-324]: This is part of the opposing speaker’s argument, which makes its weakness even clearer. — س ره

[^V01-325]: The author seems to be responding to an earlier objection: if possibility is only a denial, it cannot be a way of qualifying a statement alongside necessity and impossibility, since a denial removes the connection between subject and predicate, while a qualification describes that connection. He replies that possibility, though negative, is a positive state of the subject; therefore, the statement is affirmative with a negative predicate. But earlier he said that the division into the three categories is really two divisions: first, between what must exist and what need not; then, among what need not exist, between what must not exist and what is neither necessary nor impossible. In that second division, the negative is already being used as a predicate. The author’s claim that a simple negative statement merely removes a connection, rather than affirming a negative connection, also makes it hard to explain how a negative feature can be positively assigned. — ط

[^V01-326]: This seems to conflict with what was said earlier: possibility is the essence’s lack of demand for either necessity, not its demand that both necessities be denied. Perhaps the earlier passage explained possibility in itself, while this passage explains what it means to say, in a division, that an essence that exists in the world or in thought is possible. The statement is affirmative with a negative predicate, even if possibility itself is a simple denial. When a subject exists, it can be described as having that denial. In this sense, being described as possible, though it belongs to a level prior to existence, works like being described as existent. — س ره

[^V01-327]: Another answer is that possibility is the denial of both necessities from all eternity. The familiar distinction is between “the possibility of the world’s eternity,” which is false, and “the eternity of its possibility,” which is true. The denial in the objection is a denial that begins at some point, not an eternal one. If possibility came from another, it would not be eternal. — س ره

[^V01-328]: The same objection also applies to the author. Earlier he said that dividing an essence into the necessary, the impossible, and the possible amounts to two divisions, each built from a thing and its opposite. On that account, the two denials are separate in thought and cannot be one unless they are considered in another way, such as as an affirmative statement with a negative predicate. This also shows the weakness of the earlier attempt to make possibility such a statement. Neither answer fully resolves the objection. If the claim “the essence is possible through another” is true, it is an ordinary claim about the essence, not part of its definition. But the argument would then imply that the essence exists without a cause of its existence or a cause of its nonexistence. That is impossible in reality, because it would make the essence neither existent nor nonexistent—not merely “neither” when considered at the level of its own essence. — ط

[^V01-329]: This does not answer the objection. The absence of necessity still needs a cause; if the essence is not its cause, something else must be. That would leave two absences caused by something else, which is precisely possibility through another. — ط

[^V01-330]: “Added in the world” describes these things; it does not mean that what is added is an object beyond the thing it describes. The following words—“but they are added in the mind”—make this clear. — س ره

[^V01-331]: The author earlier tried to reconcile the positions by saying that these concepts have dependent existence, not existence in themselves. This works for the three categories, but not for existence and unity—unless “existence” here means the act of affirming that something exists, or the verbal concept “to exist.” — س ره

[^V01-332]: This argument assumes Suhrawardi’s view that every whole made of parts exists as one distinct thing in its own right. — س ره

[^V01-333]: The example is light. For him, light has the same underlying reality whether it exists on its own or as a feature of something else. Later, in the discussion of God, he explains that knowledge, power, will, and similar things may be qualities at one level, independent realities at another, and necessary in themselves at the highest. — س ره

[^V01-334]: You might object that being caused is different from being known. But whatever makes it true to say that a thing is caused—whether that basis is real or something recognised by the mind—must also make it true to say that God knows it. Otherwise something would escape His knowledge, which embraces all things. This is even clearer for simple realities, from which things made of parts ultimately arise. — س ره

[^V01-335]: If “the disputing group” means the followers of the First Teacher who accept the reality of possibility, the point is clear. If it means theologians, as the wording suggests, the argument is a proof, not a debate framed in their own accepted premises. It uses assumptions they would not accept, such as the existence of an intellect and the claim that the First Effect is eternal and created directly. It also assumes that coming into being means having been preceded by nonexistence in one’s own being, whereas they say it means being preceded by another; and that possibility is what makes a thing need a cause. It also assumes that one source can produce many things only if it acts in different ways. — س ره

[^V01-336]: Someone might ask: could the Necessary Being produce possibility first and the First Effect afterwards, so that He would not be producing two things at once? No. Possibility cannot exist on its own, and a feature cannot cause the very thing to which it belongs. Besides, this would mean that the First Effect was not really first. — س ره

[^V01-337]: This dependence is what is meant by causation; other kinds of dependence mean only that two things cannot be separated. A feature belongs to an essence in itself because it belongs to it when considered just as it is, without regard to whether it exists in the world or in the mind. It would belong to the essence even if the essence could be considered apart from both kinds of existence. But an essence considered apart from its relation to a creator is, by agreement, only an idea. What belongs to it in that way is all the more clearly only an idea. — س ره

[^V01-338]: One of the two descriptions is a mental state—the lack of necessity—while the other is an actual state. There is no contradiction between an actual existence and a mental nonexistence. — س ره

[^V01-339]: The description belongs to existence and nonexistence. Some copies use a feminine dual form, but that reading is incorrect. — س ره

[^V01-340]: That is, for the description to apply to things in the world, it would need dependent existence there, as explained several times above. — س ره

[^V01-341]: This applies even to impossibility. The impossibility of being made of stone applies to a human being as a dependent description in the world. But the impossibility of a partner to God or of opposites being joined is only assumed in thought, since these subjects do not exist as definite things. — س ره

[^V01-342]: To describe something as having a feature in the world, the thing must exist there; the feature need not exist there as a separate thing. The same applies when we say that something is true of a subject. We must also distinguish the ideas discussed in general philosophy from the ideas studied in logic: they do not describe things in exactly the same way. — س ره

[^V01-343]: The same applies to individuality. It means that the very idea cannot be thought of as true of many things; but thought is a second-order concept. A natural individual—the thing to which individuality applies in the world—is not a logical or mental individual. If “individual” means a thing made distinct, which is existence itself, then it is more fully real in the world than anything else. — س ره

[^V01-344]: One could say this follows from the author’s view that logic is part of philosophy and that the subjects studied by logic have some kind of reality outside the mind. He will return to this later. — س ره

[^V01-345]: One possibility cannot differ from another simply by being possible: possibility has one meaning. Nor can matter make them different, since matter, considered in itself, has no distinctions. And the future things to which they refer cannot distinguish them either, since those things do not yet exist. If each possibility is said to differ only because it is a different possibility, the argument goes in a circle.

    This argument also seems to apply to readiness in matter, even though that readiness exists in the world; so the proof would wrongly make it only mental. It also applies to any number of possibilities, not only an unlimited number. The answer to the second objection is that the author means that a multiplicity of possibilities in themselves cannot be conceived. The first objection is answered by distinguishing readiness from possibility as such. Readiness, considered merely as possibility, has no reality for the author. Those who say it exists mean that it exists as a readiness or feature of matter, which is the subject prepared to receive something. The author later distinguishes two kinds of possibility: possibility in itself, where an essence can be considered without contradiction as existing or not existing; and readiness for a particular way of existing, which arises only when the conditions are in place and obstacles removed. These differ in their subjects, as will be explained in the discussion of potentiality and actuality.

    The author says elsewhere that readiness means removing an obstacle or its opposite, either fully (near potentiality) or partly (remote potentiality). Even if we grant that readiness has real existence because it is the very state of the prepared thing, it exists in relation to what it is prepared for, and as a weak existence of that thing. Prime matter itself exists only as a deep potential. The author’s descriptions of readiness as nothing, as a quality, or as a relation can be reconciled: it is “nothing” when viewed as potentiality in itself; a quality when viewed as a weak form of existence; and a relation when viewed as something that necessarily points to what the thing is ready to receive.

    A further objection to the claim that possibility exists in the world is that it would make nonexistent essences real. Possibility in itself belongs to an essence considered just as it is. If it were a real feature, it would have to exist before the essence exists, even though it is not a substance. Also, if possibility were real, an endless chain would follow, since possibility itself would be possible. One cannot say that possibility is possible through itself: if it were a real possibility, it would be an essence under one of the ten categories, with existence added to it, and their relation would itself have to be qualified by possibility. Saying that possibility is possible through itself merely repeats the word; the question is how existence relates to it. — س ره

[^V01-346]: The reasoning is that if the possibilities were distinct in the world, our ability to recognize their differences would follow those real differences. But the argument being considered says that their differences come only from the mind. The claim that the possibilities exist in the world would therefore arise only because we assumed they were already different there. — س ره

[^V01-347]: This wording also allows for the case where each half gains a limited number of new possibilities. That case is covered by the later argument that the total would then be limited. Together, the possibilities can be grouped by whether they are unlimited or limited, and by whether they are already present or newly arise. The author’s five cases are: the same unlimited set in both halves; new unlimited sets; new limited sets; two already existing unlimited sets, each described as half the whole; or two limited sets already present. The source later addresses the fourth case. The argument resembles proofs used to show that a body’s active powers cannot be unlimited. — س ره

[^V01-348]: Someone might say that an unlimited set can still be smaller or larger than another unlimited set, as an unlimited series of tens is smaller than an unlimited series of hundreds. The first series is one tenth the size of the second, so each half could contain an unlimited set that is only half the total. — س ره

[^V01-349]: If these infinitely many parts cannot be divided, that is the view of al-Naẓẓām, who held that bodies are made of indivisible parts. If they can be divided, there would be an unlimited number of parts in fact, which would imply an unlimited size. A similar problem follows from some of the earlier possibilities, but the author gives a separate difficulty for each. — س ره

[^V01-350]: This objection seems to apply both to what is possible in itself and to something being ready for a change. The reply is that possibility, considered just as possibility, is an idea in the mind, even when the readiness for a change has some reality. The preparedness in an embryo to become human relates to the embryo; in this respect it is called readiness, and we say that the embryo is ready to become human. It also relates to the human being who may come to exist; in this respect it is called “possibility through preparation,” and we say that a human being can come to exist in the embryo. In this second sense it is only an idea. Also, even if readiness is real, whether considered as a state of the prepared thing or as a relation, a real feature need not have a real relation or a real thing at the other end of that relation. The author will discuss this later. — س ره

[^V01-351]: The Arabic word used here means a basin where water collects. It can also mean a plot of land someone takes for themselves or that a ruler assigns to them. Some copies instead read *ijāda*.

[^V01-352]: These are the two sides often called the side of light and the side of darkness, or the side turned toward God and the side turned toward the soul. — س ره

[^V01-353]: The claim “everything possible in itself is made of parts” and the claim “everything made of parts is possible in itself” each need their own proof. We cannot prove the second simply by turning the first sentence around; it is like separately proving that every immaterial being understands and that every being that understands is immaterial. — س ره

[^V01-354]: The difference from the earlier examples is that there the parts conflict with the composite: the parts are supposed to be necessary or impossible, while the whole is possible. In these two examples, the conflict is within the composite itself: it is impossible as a joining of contradictories, yet possible as a composite idea. The same applies to a composite of opposites, if we take each opposite together with the feature of being joined to the other. — س ره

[^V01-355]: This argument is answered by considering the First Effect. It is possible in itself, yet its nonexistence would entail the nonexistence of God, which is impossible. — س ره

[^V01-356]: The broad claim that follows—whether the consequence is necessarily existent—shows that the phrase “between a possible thing and something impossible” should be left out. This wording comes from the learned Dāmād’s *The Clear Horizon*: “The possibility of the antecedent belongs to it in itself, and it entails that the consequent is possible relative to the antecedent itself, not possible in itself. What follows from the link is only that the opposite of the consequent is not necessary relative to the antecedent, because the consequent is necessary relative to itself, whether it is necessarily present, necessarily absent, or neither when considered in itself.” This version is clearer. — س ره

[^V01-357]: That is, when one claim necessarily leads to another, the opposite of what follows cannot be necessary in relation to the first claim. This is a general possibility that can go with the consequent’s necessary existence, necessary nonexistence, or lack of necessity in either direction. This possibility too is relative to the antecedent, not to the consequent considered in itself. — س ره

[^V01-358]: The First Cause, considered in relation to the First Effect, is possible in the sense that it does not, by itself, require that the effect exist or not exist. The author sees this as close to a view expressed by al-Dawānī. — س ره

[^V01-359]: A further argument can be made. If causality is necessary, it is either identical with God’s essence or separate from it. Either way, the author’s conclusion follows, even without considering the impossibility of there being two necessary beings: if causality were separate, its effect could be absent while causality remained, unlike the First Cause, which is necessary. If causality is possible, it must itself have a cause, because possibility requires a cause and incidental features need an explanation. This leads either to an endless chain or to the same difficulty again. — س ره

[^V01-360]: The difficulty arises because something impossible through another must ultimately rest on something impossible in itself. Yet what is impossible through another is only possible in itself, so a possible thing appears to entail something impossible in itself. This would also destroy reasoning by contradiction, which infers that an assumption is impossible because it leads to an impossibility. The author’s answer is that the thing that entails the impossibility is not the possible essence itself, but its nonexistence. That nonexistence is not possible: it is necessary, while existence is impossible for it. The problem is therefore resolved, and reasoning by contradiction remains sound. — ط

[^V01-361]: “Necessity” here means absolute necessity in itself, timeless and unqualified.

[^V01-362]: This is also evidence that existence itself is what is real, including in the act of bringing things into existence. Those who say that essence is what is real still have to answer the argument. — س ره

[^V01-363]: One of the author’s contemporaries avoided saying that the First Effect’s existence is necessary through the necessity of God because he failed to distinguish three claims: necessary in itself; necessary because a Necessary Being exists; and necessary because that Being makes it so. He wrongly thought the second claim meant the effect was necessary in itself. The First Effect’s nonexistence is impossible because of the impossibility of God’s nonexistence, not because its own essence cannot be absent. Its existence is necessary through God’s necessity, not through itself and not because God separately imposes necessity on it. It remains through God, not through itself or a separate act of preserving it. This describes the world, where things are mostly equal in their own nature. God, by contrast, is necessary and lasting through Himself. — س ره

[^V01-364]: That is, someone might say this. — س ره

[^V01-365]: If “the thing” means the First Effect’s essence, it has no necessary link to the source. If it means its existence or nonexistence, its existence is necessary through the source and its nonexistence impossible through the source, so again no link has been shown. The reply is that “possible” means the essence, but the entailment does not come from the essence itself; it comes from the state of existence or nonexistence that belongs to it. More generally, overlooking the reality of essence causes many rules to be overlooked. Or “possibility” here may mean need and dependence. — س ره

[^V01-366]: The issue is that existence or nonexistence through another rests on a corresponding necessity or impossibility. Yet what is impossible through another is possible in itself, so a possible thing seems to entail something impossible in itself. That would undermine reasoning by contradiction, which uses the impossibility of a consequence to disprove its cause. The answer is that the thing entailing impossibility is not the possible thing itself, but its nonexistence. Nonexistence is not possible: it is impossible, while existence is impossible for it. The problem is resolved, and reasoning by contradiction remains sound. — س ره

[^V01-367]: This example is different from the previous one. There, a condition beyond the essence and its existence—such as coldness in a paralyzed hand that cannot feel or move—makes something impossible. Here the impossibility comes from the thing’s own level of existence, as with a human form existing in the mind, which cannot be material in that way. In the present case, the requirement of nonexistence may be distinct from the essence, but it is part of its very way of existing. “The nature of reality” means the particular kind of existence that requires matter and time; “the real” is broader. The wording moves from a particular case to the general rule, while the preceding line moved from the general rule to a particular case. — س ره

[^V01-368]: The author is referring back to the earlier argument, though he will soon discuss further objections to reasoning by contradiction and answer them. The next objection is different: how can an assumption entail what conflicts with it, as when an unlimited distance is said to entail being bounded? — س ره

[^V01-369]: That is, in those proofs by contradiction. The possibility that may entail an impossibility is possibility in itself. The possibility used in those proofs is possibility in reality: what can occur without contradiction. If something’s being possible in reality entails an impossibility, that proves only that it is not possible in reality. It may still be possible in itself. If it is not possible even in itself, that requires a separate proof. — س ره

[^V01-370]: This refers to the later necessity, one of the two necessities that surround every possible thing.

[^V01-371]: This refers to the earlier necessity, expressed by the rule: a thing does not exist until it has become necessary. — س ره

[^V01-372]: The careful critic takes “inborn preference” in a different sense: just as necessity and impossibility mean that existence or nonexistence must apply to a thing, so the opposing view says that one side is more fitting for a possible thing, without any cause or demand in its essence. Arguments about a thing’s own causal power do not disprove this version. — ه ره

[^V01-373]: This answers the careful critic’s point. If we say that a possible thing’s own essence causes the preference, then either the possible thing has no reality at all, so it cannot cause anything, or the cause’s effect fails to follow from it. But if we say only that one side fits the thing better, those arguments do not directly apply. Even necessity in itself is not “causation” in the ordinary sense, since the cause and its effect are one. It means that one side fits the thing so fully that it becomes necessary. The claimed preference would be similar, but would stop short of necessity. — س ره

[^V01-374]: This refers to an inborn preference strong enough to make a thing actual and close off its need for a Creator. Preference may be inborn or come from another, and either kind may or may not be strong enough to make the thing exist. On close examination, all these views fail, though some fail more plainly than others. — س ره

[^V01-375]: Al-Fārābī’s claim is limited to preference, since that is the topic here. His words “without necessity” cover both a thing coming to exist while existence and nonexistence remain equal, and a thing coming to exist because one side is preferred but not necessary. He does not mention that existence might come about with no preference at all, as that is already included in the first case. — س ره

[^V01-376]: The first case concerns preference strong enough to make the thing actual. This case concerns a preference too weak to do that. The thing would then occur without being brought about by its essence or by anything separate, since the argument assumes an existence sequence without necessity. — س ره

[^V01-377]: This is another reason the second case is worse. The existence of a possible thing is not its essence and therefore needs a cause. If the essence makes existence preferred, it is the cause of the thing’s being described as existent. The thing could still fail to exist, however, because the preference does not make existence necessary. Its nonexistence would then be possible even while its essence—the alleged cause of existence—remained. The argument is a proof, not a debate that depends on the opponent accepting the author’s premise: the opponent has already assumed that the thing exists without any cause. — س ره

[^V01-378]: There are three possible states. In the view defended here, the less-favored side is always impossible and the favored side necessary in itself. In the opposing view, the less-favored side has only a non-necessary disadvantage and can still occur; the favored side has only a non-necessary advantage. The third state is that the favored side has a non-necessary advantage while the less-favored side is impossible. The author argues that only a necessary disadvantage could make the less-favored side impossible, but the opponent has assumed a mere preference. — س ره

[^V01-379]: Someone may say that this changes the assumption, since a preference short of necessity has become an impossibility, even if not an impossibility in itself. The reply is that the impossibility applies to nonexistence only when it is qualified by being less favored. It does not apply to the essence by itself. The essence remains possible, and the impossibility that belongs to the added description comes through something else. — س ره

[^V01-380]: Someone may object that the less-favored feature depends on the essence, and what depends on something also depends on the thing it depends on. The answer is that the preference does depend on the essence, as does the preference for existence. But neither preference is necessary in itself; each can be absent. So the impossibility and necessity that arise from them can also be absent. There is no contradiction. — س ره

[^V01-381]: “Some possible things” means certain possible essences. The phrase continues the opening of the next argument. — س ره

[^V01-382]: Copies differ here: some say “before the commentary on philosophy,” while others say “before philosophy matured.”

[^V01-383]: This example differs in no important way from the one just given. That is why the author answers it, and the next claim, together by saying that both are false. — س ره

[^V01-384]: This means stable things, such as substances. — ه ره

[^V01-385]: In other words: if you accept this for cause and effect, accept it also for an essence’s supposed preference for existence. — س ره

[^V01-386]: These are the two mistaken claims: the one about things that pass away, and the one about a cause that waits for conditions before bringing about its effect. — ه ره

[^V01-387]: A clearer way to put the point is: necessity gives a thing independence, and impossibility does the same in its own way. A thing needs something else because neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary for it. If origination—either as a condition or as part of the reason for need—were added to that reason, it would still be considered only for something possible in itself. A necessary or impossible thing would already be independent. So the argument finally returns to possibility. This proof also shows that origination alone cannot even be part of the reason for needing a cause. The next proof applies to all the views. — س ره

[^V01-388]: The word means “of the relation.” — س ره

[^V01-389]: If origination is a condition, it comes one step later still, because a condition must itself be in place before what depends on it. — س ره

[^V01-390]: Possibility is the way the imagined idea of existence relates to an essence in the mind. This is why we can call an essence possible before it exists. Origination, by contrast, means that the existence given to an essence was preceded by nonexistence. It therefore comes after the act that gives the essence existence.

[^V01-391]: Many copies read “preference,” but “being preferred” is the correct reading. The word “preference” is used only to echo the earlier wording. — س ره

[^V01-392]: Some copies omit the phrase “in relation to.”

[^V01-393]: The examples of the two cups, two loaves, and two roads were used by al-Ashʿarī to argue that one equal option may be chosen without a reason. But a few examples cannot prove a general rule. Perhaps the point was only to argue against an opponent, not to establish the general claim. Also, for al-Ashʿarī, God acts and people are compelled; so any reason for the choice must lie with God, not with the person choosing. The same is true for those who hold that God creates the act while people still have some role in it. Demanding a reason only from the person’s point of view fits the view that people act independently. The author’s reply is that God may have hidden causes in creation: He may know, for instance, that the second road leads to a pit or a wild animal, and direct the person toward the first to protect them. Even when people act, they may in some nearby actions be instruments through which God or an angel acts. — س ره

[^V01-394]: Their argument is that the same cause would apply equally to both matching things, as would their essence and anything that follows from it. Any separate factor would also seem to apply to both. If the differing factor were itself separate, the same question would arise again, leading to an endless chain. The reply is that an endless chain of changing conditions does not imply that the chain has always existed. One thing may be prepared by earlier conditions in its own matter, while the other is prepared by different conditions. If we ask what explains the difference between those conditions, the answer points to still earlier conditions in their respective materials, and so on. There is no endless chain of things existing all at once, because material conditions change. Or the material itself may be the factor that makes the two outcomes differ. If someone asks why one material is prepared one way and another differently, the answer is that each material is part of what makes the thing that particular thing. Without those differences, the two would not be two separate things. The commentator notes that the argument’s use of “matching things” is itself questionable if there is truly no difference between them. — س ره

[^V01-395]: This is mistaken: “being essential” is not the whole essence. It is a general, incidental idea in the mind. — س ره

[^V01-396]: The point is that what is known depends, in one way, on God’s knowledge: the fixed forms of things are known by Him. God’s knowledge, which is one with His single essence, follows those forms in what they require of themselves; in that sense, the forms are truly described by their own essential features. His knowledge, however, is too exalted to be described by them except in a dependent way. The forms and realities are likewise described by existence, knowledge, and other perfections only in a dependent way. So divine knowledge is, in one respect, dependent on what it knows and, in another, the source on which those realities depend. — ن ره

[^V01-397]: “Other than His essence.” — س ره

[^V01-398]: One could explain it this way: the world’s existence is “by chance” in the sense that it exists through another, not through itself. Everything returns to God; “everything perishes except His face.” “O You who are, You who are nothing but You: everything apart from God is false.” — ن ره

[^V01-399]: This is the existence itself. How, then, could existence be what comes about only incidentally, rather than directly? Earlier the author reported Suhrawardī’s view that existence is only an idea, as are necessity through another and similar concepts. He did not accept this for existence or for necessity through another. Perhaps here “necessity through another” means the way a relation is qualified, not necessity itself. — س ره

[^V01-400]: The author will later explain that saying things happen by chance conflicts with necessary links in existence. It works only if one denies necessity and impossibility altogether: if a necessary link existed, one thing would depend on another through that link, and chance would disappear. The debaters’ appeals to “producing what already exists” and “joining opposites” overlook this point. — ط

[^V01-401]: The author does not answer the supposed problem here because “while” is taken to mean that cause and effect exist at the same time. There is no problem with the cause and its effect existing together. — س ره

[^V01-402]: This would put the cause’s action and its effect at the same level in the order of what things are. But that cannot be right. The cause acts on what the thing is, considered in itself; at that level the thing has no separate identity that could stand beside the cause as an equal. Considered as existing or nonexistent, it comes after the cause’s existence or nonexistence. — س ره

[^V01-403]: The point is that saying “the cause acts on the essence as it is in itself” does not mean that the essence itself is directly made. It is the place where the effect appears, or is called the effect in another sense. The author explains this in *The Divine Witnesses*, when he divides existence into the real, the general, and the limited. The essence is like a footstool or an image of existence. — س ره

[^V01-404]: Origination means that existence is preceded by nonexistence. So this view places the cause’s action in the interval between the time of nonexistence and the time of existence, not in either state. It is a difficult view because it does not apply to things created directly, on their account, but only to the natural world as a whole. — س ره

[^V01-405]: They choose the view that the cause acts while the effect does not exist, then say that no opposites are joined because the cause acts in the first moment and the effect exists in the second. This is simply mistaken: it makes the time before the effect exists the cause’s time of action. — س ره

[^V01-406]: Yes, but this is a simple negative statement; or we can say, “The human being no longer remains.” — س ره

[^V01-407]: The correct wording is “or the relation being described as existent.” — س ره

[^V01-408]: That is, through the cause. — س ره

[^V01-409]: That is, a simple, undivided thing, like the undivided knowledge of God. They mean the simple reality named by “being described as existent,” which the mind analyzes into parts. — س ره

[^V01-410]: They missed the case where being described as something is not an independent thing, but is not itself noticed as an object. This is suggested by their claim that being described as something is itself an essence, though it is not really an essence. It is simply an essence being described as existent. It is like saying that a thing’s coming to be is itself a thing that has come to be. — س ره

[^V01-411]: The difficulty is this: if existence alone is real in its own right, then every true statement that matches neither the outside world nor our minds considered as mental states would be impossible. One example is “the effect’s absence is caused by the cause’s absence.” This statement is true, even if nobody happens to think it. But it does not match anything in the outside world, since absence is nothing and has no external reality.

    The usual answer is that such truths correspond to “reality as such” (*nafs al-amr*), rather than to the outside world or the mind. Philosophers say that “reality as such” includes everything in the outside world, and overlaps with what is in the mind while also reaching beyond it. Some explain it to mean the thing itself: saying that a thing is such-and-such “in itself” means that the thing itself is such-and-such; the wording puts “the thing” in place of “it.”

    But this explanation does not solve the problem. If “the thing itself” means its real existence, the original difficulty returns. If it means the thing’s essence, distinct from its existence, that cannot be right either, because nothing besides existence is real. Others explain “reality as such” as the World of Command: a universal, immaterial intellect containing the forms of all true statements. But if those forms are direct knowledge—things present to that intellect—then they are just the external realities themselves, and would not match a statement such as “the effect’s absence is caused by the cause’s absence.” The problem remains. If they are ideas in that intellect, there is no reason to posit them, since similar ideas already exist in our minds; and again the problem remains.

    The better answer is this: what is real in its own right is actual existence, and it is what truly exists. Every true fact belongs to it. Essences are ways existence appears to our rational minds. So the mind is forced to extend the idea of “existence” to essences as well, then make whatever true judgments it must about them. In this way, the concept of “existence” or “being” comes to apply more broadly, both to real existence and to essences.

    Then the mind is forced to take a further step: it applies the bare idea of being real to every abstract concept it has had to form, such as nonexistence, unity, action, and potentiality. It also accepts the judgments about these concepts that reason requires. The place the mind imagines for reality in this broadest sense is what we call “reality as such.” The author will return to this later, God willing, in the discussions of mental existence and other topics. — ط

[^V01-412]: Rather, the essence is established as an object of the mind’s consideration, and so becomes possible. — س ره

[^V01-413]: That is, the “natural universal,” another name for an essence. — س ره

[^V01-414]: Existence’s need for a cause is essential to it, as the author says. What is essential in this way is not itself explained by a cause. The claim that possibility is the cause of need applies to essences. Here, “cause” means a step in the explanation, and the need belongs to the essence indirectly. If we mean the need that exists in dependent beings, then “possibility” means dependence or poverty, and the point returns to what we have said: this need is essential and has no further cause. — س ره

[^V01-415]: That is, a body is finite in general, and each of its particular forms of existence is limited in its own way. — ن ره

[^V01-416]: Here, “eternity” means only a dependent, derivative kind of permanence, not existence that is eternal in itself or independently. God is far above having a partner. The reality described as eternal in this way belongs to the World of Command, not to the created world. God has real attributes of perfection that are identical with the depth of His essence, and relational attributes that lie beyond that depth. Their being “additional” in this relational sense does not conflict with saying that His attributes are identical with Him in every respect. Complete devotion to God’s oneness denies any attribute added to Him, whether relational or real. Consider this carefully: the point is subtle, and few grasp it fully. — ن ره

[^V01-417]: Existence is the relation itself, not a thing that has a relation. It cannot be separated from this relation, just as a thing cannot be separated from itself. — ن ره

[^V01-418]: This refers to the earlier discussion, where the author first established an aspect of permanence for some possible existences—those belonging to the World of Command—then denied it. — ن ره

[^V01-419]: The example is imperfect because, in the case under discussion, there is no fixed thing like a body that receives a manifestation of God as a body receives the sun. Things are manifestations of His light and displays of His beauty and majesty. Nothing is already established before this manifestation; there are only its levels and forms. — ن ره

[^V01-420]: Some effects have one cause for coming into being and another for continuing to exist. A building, for example, comes into being through construction, but lasts because its material is dry and firm. Other effects have the same cause for both, as when a mold gives water its shape. The world, in relation to God, belongs to this second kind: God is necessary in Himself and necessary in every respect. The world does not belong to the first kind. So anyone who says that, if God could cease to exist, the world would still continue without Him should be silenced outright. — س ره

[^V01-421]: This excludes mere preparatory causes. Their role is called causation only in a loose sense; it is accidental, not genuine causation. — ن ره

[^V01-422]: This can mean one of two things. First, the soul may become able to do without the body and its use once it has reached full development. This is the natural end of life. Or the body may lose its ability to receive the soul before the soul has reached full development, because of some outside accident. That is a violent or untimely death. — ن ره

[^V01-423]: What the builder directly causes is the movement of his own body: his soul moves and sets his limbs in motion. The exact joining of parts, such as bricks and stones, into a particular form happens only as an indirect result of his powers. This kind of indirect influence is called chance or coincidence. — ن ره

[^V01-424]: That is, in terms of kind or type. — ن ره

[^V01-425]: As you can see, the sea of matter runs out because there is no matter that exists separately on its own. God’s words of existence do not run out, because His giving of existence never stops, He never withholds His mercy, and He cannot be silent. The same applies to the seven seas. — س ره

[^V01-426]: At that point, the supposed deciding factor is still equally related to both sides. So what seemed to be a preference is, in truth, an equal relation. Think carefully. — ن ره

[^V01-427]: You may ask: if existence already has the advantage, how can the two outcomes still be equally open? I answer: even a cause that will eventually make one outcome necessary leaves both outcomes open until it has done all that is needed. A cause that merely favors existence has not ruled out every way the effect could fail to exist. The preference, considered without the final purpose or condition that settles the outcome, has left both possibilities open. To claim that the preference already belongs to existence is to confuse what the mind considers with what has actually happened. The thing does not yet exist. As we have seen, possibility is not a separate state alongside the thing's existence or nonexistence; nor is a mere preference.

    Consider the argument another way. If a preference truly fixed one outcome, that outcome would be necessary—contrary to the assumption. The preference is itself something that may occur or not occur and therefore also needs an explanation. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif objects: why should the greater weight supplied by an outside cause not suffice for the favored outcome? What is obviously impossible, he says, is for two equally balanced outcomes to occur without a reason, or for the less favored one to occur. I reply that if the favored outcome actually happens, the supposed mere preference has given way to what makes its occurrence necessary. Beforehand, necessity is something we understand; when the possible thing exists, it exists through the necessity supplied by its cause. Its actual existence reveals that the cause made it necessary.

    You may reply that, for us, existence reveals necessity, but for those who accept mere preference it reveals only preference. We mean by necessity nothing more than what makes the thing truly exist. If you choose to call that 'preference,' our disagreement is only about a name; you might as well call it 'possibility.' But how could actual existence, which excludes nonexistence, show only a preference that still allows nonexistence?

    To say that a possible thing comes into existence through a preference that has not reached necessity is like saying that a person reaches a rooftop merely by thinking about it, deciding to climb, setting up a ladder, and stepping on every rung except the last one. The final part of the complete cause is still missing. However many incomplete conditions have been met, they do not settle whether the person reaches the roof. Even endlessly many such preferences would not explain why the cause brings about existence rather than leaving the thing nonexistent. That would still be choosing one outcome without what decides it. I have explained this at length because the distinction is easy to miss. Do not let it escape you. — س ره

    Saying that the sides cannot be equal because the preference points towards existence confuses what the mind considers with what exists outside the mind. Existence has not yet occurred in the outside world, so the possible thing’s existence is no more actual than its nonexistence. As explained earlier, possibility applies only when we consider the thing in itself, not to its actual absence or to its actual existence—whether outside the mind, in the mind, now, or in the future. Preference, too, has meaning only at that level. It is not yet an actual state.

    Another way to put the argument is this: if the preference is not equal and truly belongs to one side, then that side has become necessary through its cause. But the claim under discussion assumes that no necessity has been reached. Also, preference itself is one of the things the mind can consider; it too may occur or fail to occur. Its own occurrence would therefore need a preference.

    A later commentator raises this objection: Why can’t the favored side occur simply because an outside cause has made it more likely? This does not seem obviously impossible; what is obviously impossible is that one of two equally likely sides, or the less likely side, should occur. The answer is that when the favored side actually occurs, this goes beyond mere preference. How is it different from saying that the cause made it necessary? In the mind, necessity is distinct from existence and is considered before it. Outside the mind, necessity is the existence itself. So when we know that a possible thing exists, we know that its cause made it necessary.

    Someone might reply: “That is your view. Those who accept mere preference without necessity say that existence shows only that the cause favored it.” We answer that by “necessity” we mean whatever grounds the judgment that the thing exists. If you call this “preference,” then we disagree only about the name. Call it “possibility” if you wish. But how could actual existence, which cannot be absent, show a preference that can fail to occur, even if its absence is less likely? Existence and necessity cannot fail to be; mere preference can.

    To say that a possible thing can exist through a preference that falls short of necessity is like saying that someone can reach a roof by imagining the result, deciding to do it, wanting it, setting up a ladder, and climbing every rung except the last. The result would occur even though the final part of the complete cause was missing. Having many conditions and incomplete causes in place does not remove the equal chance of reaching the roof or not reaching it, when the outcome is considered in relation to the person who acts. Those conditions are only being considered in the mind. Even infinitely many weak preferences would not settle what the person brings about. For the person to produce existence rather than nonexistence would still be a choice without a reason. The author expands the discussion because it is easy to misunderstand. — س ره

[^V01-428]: Calling the concept “existent” an essential feature of a real instance of existence is slightly imprecise. That is why the author adds that it must be true as long as the reality exists. As explained earlier, existence is not a species, a general kind, a dividing feature, a universal, or a particular. The real point is that the concept of existence is an abstract idea the mind draws from descriptions; as a concept, it has no reality outside the mind. If it did, existence, whose very nature is to be outside the mind, would itself exist in the mind in the same way it exists outside. It would then have one nature in the mind and another outside it, and would become an essence equally open to being and not being. That is impossible. — ط

[^V01-429]: The argument is that if nonexistence were possible while the thing exists, opposite claims would be true at once. That is impossible in itself. Whatever entails something impossible in itself is also impossible in itself. So existence would be necessary in itself. — س ره

[^V01-430]: For this speaker, the condition is the essence’s relation to its maker. — س ره

[^V01-431]: This answer works if the condition is part of what we call the subject. The claim that a cause must exist for its effect works differently: there the cause explains why the effect exists. The reply to the earlier scholar changes the objection rather than answering it directly. The author says 'even if the argument were complete' because it is not. Possibility and impossibility concern existence and nonexistence in general, not some special kind of either. Motion, for example, can exist, but not as something fixed and unchanging. A thing impossible in itself must be nonexistent, not merely absent in one particular way. Yet the other scholar speaks of 'nonexistence while the thing exists,' which is a special case. Moreover, he treats 'while it exists' as a condition on the denial of existence. It really qualifies the subject, for the subject is already 'the existing essence.' Adding the condition to the denial repeats what the subject already says. An essence considered as existing cannot, while it exists, be nonexistent. Its opposite—existence—is therefore necessary. — س ره

    There is another problem. The phrase “nonexistent while it exists” makes “while it exists” sound like a condition on the claim that the thing is absent. But it is really a condition on the subject: it means the essence is being considered as existing at that time. So adding the condition to nonexistence repeats the same idea. An essence that exists at a given time cannot be absent at that time; its opposite, existence, must hold. — س ره

[^V01-432]: This can be so when the opposite side is nonexistence; when the opposite side is existence, it may be impossible. — س ره

[^V01-433]: The essence considered by itself can receive existence, and existence belongs to it in that respect. The opposite claim, nonexistence, concerns the essence under the condition that it exists. This reading fits the view of the Imam and is also suggested by the author’s later words. — س ره

[^V01-434]: In the second way, the difference comes from applying a condition. Here, the difference comes from the condition itself. A difference made by adding a condition is weaker than one made by the condition itself, though both involve a condition. — ن ره

[^V01-435]: This is a proof, not just an argument meant to trap the other side. So it does not show that the author rejects the view that existence is real in itself. — س ره

[^V01-436]: This rule is very useful. If a possible thing exists at one time, it cannot be absent at that time, since it must exist while it exists. It cannot be removed from another time when it was never there. Nor can it be absent from reality altogether: for reality as a whole to lack it, it would have to be absent at every level, which is not the case. This is why things are said to remain fixed in relation to the higher sources, and even more so in relation to the First Source. Each thing is present to Him at its own level, with no fading or loss. One of God's beautiful names addresses Him as 'You from whose treasures nothing is diminished.' God's knowledge does not change. This concerns an essence insofar as it has become real. As for a particular real existence, nonexistence cannot belong to it: a thing cannot receive its own opposite, and existence has no separate underlying subject on which its contrary could arrive and replace it. Understand this. — س ره

[^V01-437]: This is an important principle with further consequences. For example, every material being implies the existence of a corresponding being that does not depend on matter, is of the same order, and oversees it. Why? If the material being has a place in reality as a whole, it cannot be lost from that whole; and in that respect it cannot undergo any change. Every change involves some loss of what was there. Yet every material thing, precisely because it is material, can change in some way. So at every level of material beings there must be a corresponding being free from matter, loss, and change.

    Some Western students of nature, noticing something of this principle, supposed that a thing might eventually cease to need a cause. They reached that conclusion because they considered only causes made of matter. They overlooked two points. First, a material being's relation to reality as a whole does not do away with the relations among material beings themselves. Second, not every cause is a material cause. There is also the cause that acts and produces an effect, which anything that depends on another for its existence still needs. We shall establish this later. — ط

    This idea led some Western scientists to wonder whether the need for a cause might end if “cause” meant only a material cause. But they missed two points. First, the relation between a material thing and reality as a whole does not cancel the relations between material things themselves. Second, causes are not only material; there is also the cause that brings a possible thing into being, and no possible thing can do without it. This will be proved later. — ط

[^V01-438]: Here, “reality altogether” means reality in general, without limiting it to one level or a particular set of levels. — ن ره

[^V01-439]: On the view that each kind has a higher, guiding reality, every essence has one kind of possibility in the realm of intellect, but may have two in the material world. According to this view, the higher realities of kinds are each represented by a single individual, while in the material world a kind may have many members. The difference comes from matter and the further conditions it needs. — س ره

[^V01-440]: This is a hidden point that few understand. The movement at issue is a thing’s passage from potential to actual. This passage must ultimately rest on a simple reality that changes from within itself, not because another thing changes it. Otherwise, the chain of changing things would go on without end. This simple, ever-flowing present is the timeless order that connects what changes with what does not. Time measures ordinary motion: the gradual change of something that receives new actuality from an active source. Time is the very reality of this changing thing as it passes step by step from potential to actual. A sequence of events in time leads, in one direction, to the timeless order, which joins the eternity beyond time. The active source remains; what receives its action begins and ends. So we speak of the source’s continuous giving, not of the world as a product that has continued forever. — ن ره

[^V01-441]: Some things brought into being through direct creation are joined to time and place without themselves changing gradually. The heavenly spheres, for example, are living beings whose matter is formed by souls that have no parts of measurable size. A sphere's nature and its soul are one in existence, though we can consider them separately. Its measurable parts belong to its body insofar as its body is matter, not insofar as it belongs to a general kind. Such a being is alive by its nature and does not die through the usual process in which one bodily form replaces another. It may cease to appear, but that is not the same as dying. Disappearance is broader than decay, just as existence is broader than coming into being. A link with time and place that does not involve gradual change can end without one thing being destroyed by another. Existence itself cannot be destroyed, for that would require a change in God's knowledge—far be it from Him. On the day when the heavens are rolled up like a scroll, their disappearance is the drawing back of what was spread out; what seemed mixed is no longer mixed, and what comes into view does so in a new form. Consider this carefully. — ن ره

[^V01-442]: Some copies read “or things that are desired.”

[^V01-443]: All this follows from the view that existence is a real, graded reality, with levels ordered by completeness and lack. The highest level is God. — ط

[^V01-444]: Some copies read “two opposing things.”

[^V01-445]: If 'possibility' here means being dependent on another, the comparison is clear: dependence stands to necessity as lack stands to completeness. Dependent existences are described as luminous because their very reality consists in being connected to and supported by another; that connection is not something added to them. But if 'possibility' means neither existence nor nonexistence being necessary, or means that both remain equally open, then we are speaking of a feature of an essence, not of an existence. Since it is not the same kind of thing as necessary existence, we can call it a lack only in comparison with sheer nonexistence and nothingness. — س ره

[^V01-446]: The discussion is about readiness, not about the sperm as the thing that has readiness. The sperm is only an example. A readiness-quality depends on its subject. So it is actual in one respect and potential in another. Basic possibility, by contrast, is pure potential: its subject is not actual, whether in existence or nonexistence. — س ره

[^V01-447]: This is not the same as saying that something is possible because its occurrence would involve no contradiction. — ه ره

[^V01-448]: On this view, readiness is only a relation. The mixture in a sperm is a bodily quality, and a courtyard is a space. Neither the quality plus its relation to a future form nor the space plus its relation to the number of people it can hold exists as a separate thing. What remains is the relation alone. — س ره

[^V01-449]: Here, “coexist by chance” means that they happen to accompany one another, without any necessary connection. — س ره

[^V01-450]: The difficulty is that comparing something with another thing requires the first thing to be visible and distinct to the person making the comparison. That cannot happen in the situation being described. — ن ره

[^V01-451]: If the explanation were as stated, then all impossible things and all complex forms of absolute nonexistence would be known and could be discussed. What, then, would remain of the claim that absolute nonexistence and what is impossible in itself cannot be known or discussed? The real question is how we can form a concept of something that has no distinction, knowledge, or report about it at all, and then make claims about it. — ن ره

[^V01-452]: What we know and judge at that point is not absolute nonexistence itself. It is the concept “absolute nonexistence,” which applies to itself as an idea and is present to the mind. We are saying that if this concept pointed to something outside the mind, as a picture points to the thing it represents, then no judgment about the concept could pass over to that outside thing. But it does not point to an outside thing now; it is only an idea. If it did point to such a thing, it would no longer name absolute nonexistence. This is a subtle point. — ن ره

[^V01-453]: To say that absolute nonexistence cannot be judged means that the concept cannot be used to make a claim about something outside the mind. It has no real-world form for the claim to apply to. — ن ره

[^V01-454]: The word “some” matters because not every concept fails to apply to itself as a real thing. The concepts “thing,” “universal,” and “essence,” for example, can also apply to themselves in that sense. All concepts apply to themselves in the first, basic sense—as ideas. — س ره

[^V01-455]: This expands the brief point made earlier. The author could have left it out there. — س ره

[^V01-456]: Here is how a circular dependence leads to an endless chain. Suppose A depends on B and B depends on A. Then A depends on itself. But what something depends on must be distinct from the dependent thing. So, on this supposition, A and “A itself” must be different. Yet A itself is nothing other than A. We can repeat the argument, replacing A with “A itself,” then with “the self of A itself,” and so on. This produces an endless chain on both sides of the original circle. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif presents the argument this way in his notes on *al-Mataliʿ*; the details can be found there.

    I can give a shorter and firmer explanation. On the assumption of circular dependence, A depends on B, B on A, then A on B again, then B on A, without end. None of these steps establishes that A or B actually exists. They are like a chain of conditions: “If B exists, A exists; if A exists, B exists; if B exists, A exists...” We never reach the point where we can say, “But B exists, therefore A exists,” or the reverse. Nothing establishes the first condition, so the chain cannot stop. — س ره

[^V01-457]: An accidental conditional can connect true claims: “If a human being speaks, a donkey brays.” Both may happen, but one does not require the other. The cases at issue here are false claims, such as “If a human brays, a horse speaks,” “If two identical things cannot be together, neither can a vacuum,” or “If Zayd does not exist, the phoenix does not exist.” We cannot treat such pairings as true just because both claims are false; at most, they can be supposed together. — س ره

[^V01-458]: A universal “if … then” statement covers every possible way the first claim may be assumed. So “whenever two is a number, this follows” includes the case where two is assumed to be odd, as in the example. — س ره

[^V01-459]: The author first denies that existence is added as something separate, then denies that it is attached to the essence as a feature. — س ره

[^V01-460]: Rather, conceiving something is an act of relation, as the Imam al-Razi holds. — س ره

[^V01-461]: Not so. Those thinkers too sought to show only that existence and essence differ in our understanding, as we saw earlier. Al-Tusi says as much in *Tajrid*: existence is added in our mental representations.
