There may be exceptions among some followers of Aristotle who hold that existence joins essence outside the mind, and among the Muʿtazilites. — س ره

[^V01-462]: The note clarifies the alternatives. Existence and essence cannot be identical in meaning yet distinct in reality, since one essence has only one existence. If they are called “the same” only in meaning, this does not rule out their being distinct in reality. If they are the same in reality as well, they must be identical in meaning, one must be part of the other, or one must be added to the other. — س ره

[^V01-463]: This is how the argument appears in *Sharh al-Maqasid*, but there is a difficulty. The collection of all these added existences has no property beyond the properties of its individual members; nor does it have a separate existence of its own, as we shall explain when we discuss endless chains. Each added existence would have to rest on another existence already present, which would itself be added to the essence. The same would be true without end. We would never reach an existence identical with the essence. — س ره

[^V01-464]: This critic rejects the claim that an essence must already exist before existence can belong to it. He says that essence may come before existence in what it is, just as it comes before unity, individuality, possibility, and other features that belong to thinghood itself. — س ره

[^V01-465]: “Essences” here means the things the mind distinguishes from existence. In thought, they are ideas attached to other existences; in ordinary speech, they are themselves called existences. Or the author may mean that they are existences in reality, not merely in thought. Either way, the point is that essence and existence are one outside the mind; otherwise, the view would be al-Ash‘ari’s. — س ره

[^V01-466]: The things we understand in our minds are reflections of existences first brought into being directly. The word “forms” most likely refers to the general forms that higher realities reflect into the reasoning mind. Another possibility is that their light appears to us and we see those forms directly or become united with them. On this reading, “by reflection from higher realities” concerns nearness and distance from God; “the light of existence appearing within us” concerns how ready or unready we are to receive it. Consider the sun. One person grasps only the ordinary idea of a bright heavenly body; another knows its full nature through the causes on which it depends. The same distinction applies elsewhere. — س ره

[^V01-467]: This knowledge does not come merely by drawing an idea from things, as people commonly suppose. A Persian verse says: “Free yourself from matter to see what is free of matter. To see anything, this is the condition.” The Qur'an says, “In God's Messenger you have a good example,” and, “Follow their guidance.” It is also reported from the imams: “Our affair is difficult, exceedingly difficult; none can bear it except a messenger sent by God or an angel brought near to Him.” This is what is meant by intercession at the beginning and the end of the journey.

    Following their example fills the heart with light and purifies one's inner life until the person reaches the intended goal: knowing things as they truly are through direct experience. While this work prepares the seeker, it is called the path; when it achieves its aim, it is called the reality, and people reach it to differing degrees. I have explained as much as space allows of the subtle meaning suggested here, but few fully attain it. Do not suppose that this contradicts the earlier statement that existence is added to the essences of possible things. — ن ره

[^V01-468]: Al-Ash‘ari means “existent” in the sense of what is actually real, but for him this reality is the essence itself after a maker brings it into being. He denies that existence has a separate instance, in the mind or outside it, that makes “existent” apply to an essence. The author also grounds the claim that something exists in a kind of union, but he means that the concept “human being,” for example, is united with a particular reality of existence. — س ره

[^V01-469]: This note challenges the view that existences differ completely in reality. If they do, how can one shared idea be drawn from them? If it can, then the earlier proof that there is only one Necessary Being would fail. — س ره

[^V01-470]: Calling “existent” an idea formed only when we think about other things seems to conflict with the claim that what it names is a reality in its own right. An idea of this second kind is usually understood not to point directly to a thing existing outside the mind. How, then, are we to understand the claim here? It is no answer simply to give the word “secondary” a new meaning unlike the one these thinkers ordinarily use. — ن ره

[^V01-471]: The note objects that the concepts divided into primary and secondary are general ideas, not real existences. — ن ره

[^V01-472]: The soul is existence without an essence beyond it because every description we imagine for it—such as “the first perfection of a body,” “the ruler of the body,” or “a substance separate in itself but not in its actions”—is different from the soul itself. None of these ideas is what we mean by “I” or “my self.” The soul is not beyond substance because it is less than substance, but because it is a reality of existence. The note also says the soul has no fixed limit to its growth; it can always go beyond what it has reached. Scripture says that human beings were created weak and are deeply unjust and ignorant. Existence with no limit has no essence beyond itself. Concepts such as God’s knowledge, will, and power do not describe a limited existence, so they are not essences. An essence is an idea that describes existence with a limit. The same applies to the intellects. — س ره

[^V01-473]: Here “pure existence” means existence not joined to anything else. “Necessity” means standing on one’s own, as the Shaykh holds of the soul. — ن ره

[^V01-474]: To claim that only qualities can be stronger or weaker is to make an assertion without proof. Existence itself differs by degrees; other things, such as qualities, are called stronger or weaker because of their relation to existence. The reality of existence ranges from fullness to lack, from independence to need. — ن ره

[^V01-475]: The Shaykh calls existence one and simple because he believes that a shared idea can be part of what a thing is, while still applying by degrees. If it is part of what things are, then the unity of the idea in the mind reflects unity in reality. The philosophers in Aristotle’s school reject this, since they say that only an added feature can apply by degrees. They therefore think that the same idea in the mind does not prove that the realities themselves are one. The Shaykh also calls existence a “kind” because, if something can apply by degrees and still be the nature of the things it applies to, then existence itself can be that one nature. — س ره

[^V01-476]: The point is that the general idea of existence is not part of the essences of particular things. It is a mental idea, but in a way it stands for those things as their nature does: it applies to them from the outside without adding another feature to them. If this is so, the one idea reflects a shared reality. Particular existences have no parts, either in the world or in thought, so what they share is also what makes them different. — س ره

[^V01-477]: The note explains why a particular thing needs the general idea: if that idea were absent, the particular would also be absent. The reverse does not always follow. If a cause is absent, its effect is absent; but if a condition is present, the thing that needs it does not have to be present. The author’s wording sets out two related points, rather than repeating one point twice. — س ره

[^V01-478]: If they mean the general idea of existence, their view makes the Necessary Being nonexistent. If they mean an all-pervading existence present in every thing, it makes every existent—including filth—the Necessary Being. The first follows if “absolute existence” means a concept; the second follows if it means something present in all instances. I would add: if they mean the reality of existence without any limit, even the limit of being called “absolute,” there is no problem—provided they mean the reality that encompasses all things. — س ره

[^V01-479]: The absence of everything is not impossible in itself. It is impossible only because it would also remove one thing that cannot be absent in itself—the Necessary Being. The same is true of denying all causality: that would remove a particular kind of causality that cannot be absent. — ه ره

[^V01-480]: Calling existence in general a secondary idea seems to conflict with saying that it has one real instance, God, or many real instances. The same issue arises when the author says that a general concept has real instances. But “secondary idea” here means only that existence in general, as a general idea, has no reality outside the mind. That is clear enough, though this is not unique to secondary ideas: no general idea, even a basic one, exists outside the mind in its general form. The note says this will be explained later. — س ره

[^V01-481]: The same observation appears in *Sharh al-Maqasid* by al-Taftazani. — س ره

[^V01-482]: This means the general, self-evident idea of existence. — س ره

[^V01-483]: “Shares” here means manifestations of existence. A share in a concept differs from the concept only through a relation or condition, which is itself only an idea. Outside the mind, a manifestation is existence appearing in a particular essence that is absorbed in it. The philosophers call this an “illuminating relation.” In one respect, a name is the thing named; in another, it is different—just as the image of a thing in the mind is that thing in one way, but not in every way. — س ره

[^V01-484]: “Shared” may mean that existence is universal because it encompasses all things. One could also say it is particular, if “particular” means that it is distinct in itself—not that it is a general kind surrounded by features that make it individual. — س ره

[^V01-485]: Perhaps the author says existence applies by degrees because its real instances have different levels. The difference among them is then attributed to the general idea of existence. Otherwise, we would have to say that ideas themselves apply by degrees. The note says the author seems to allow this in some later discussions. — ط

[^V01-486]: These views bring together the main points made from the beginning of this book, as an alert reader will see. — س ره

[^V01-487]: If existence itself differs by degrees, then it has many levels. These levels differ in relation to one another: one may lack something that another has, and one may be less complete than the other. Yet they all share the same basic reality. We can divide existence into mental and external, potential and actual, many and one, then say that existence itself is external, actual, and one. This is what the author means when he says that existence in itself is simply real and actual. — ط

[^V01-488]: This note clarifies the words “even though.” — س ره

[^V01-489]: The phrase “existence is the things themselves” may mean that existence is what is most real in each thing. Given the words that follow, it may also point to a higher vision in which the forms of things fade from view and only the light of God remains. In this vision, the traveler sees the All-Hearing and All-Seeing rather than an animal; the Subtle and All-Aware rather than a spirit; the Holy and Pure rather than an angel; the Ever-Living and Exalted rather than the heavens; and the Greatest Name rather than Adam. The note quotes the saying, “My knowledge of the luminous is knowledge of God,” and connects this to the Qur'anic words “When God’s help and victory come,” and to the saying, “The height of sincerity is to deny attributes of Him.” In this vision the cycles of outward appearances end and the divine names come into view; it goes beyond even seeing the Named, where the names themselves fall away. The note compares the passage to a Persian line in al-Tusi’s *Aghaz va Anjam*: “Praise belongs to God: all beings begin from Him and all return to Him—indeed, all are He Himself.” It presents this as another possible way to understand the author’s words. — س ره

[^V01-490]: Essences and fixed realities are forms of God’s names, attributes, and their effects. In the level of divine oneness, they share one existence with the names and attributes, since they are realized through the One named, though their meanings differ. — س ره

[^V01-491]: The names and attributes follow from existence in meaning, but in reality they are one with it. Later, the author will show that life, knowledge, will, power, and other perfections follow existence wherever it appears and are joined to it. — س ره

[^V01-492]: This points to God’s all-sustaining presence, and to His being first in reality while all else comes after Him. — ن ره

[^V01-493]: These words are reported from Ali, whose speech is described as God’s speech: “With everything, but not by being beside it; different from everything, but not by being apart from it.” In another place: “Within things, but not by mixing; beyond things, but not by separation.” Elsewhere: “He is not inside things by entering them, nor outside them by leaving them.” — س ره

[^V01-494]: “Within things without mixing, beyond them without separation” means that God is not inside things as one thing is inside another, nor outside them as one thing leaves another. The difference is in His quality, not in being cut off from them. — ن ره

[^V01-495]: The note names six levels of divine self-disclosure: oneness, divine unity, the world of power, the world of spirits, the visible world, and the all-comprehensive human realm. It says that the six days during which God’s light is hidden correspond to these levels, as in the Qur'anic account of the creation of the heavens and the earth in six days. — س ره

[^V01-496]: Al-Saduq says in *The Beliefs* that souls and spirits remain after death; some are blessed and some punished, until they return to their bodies at the resurrection. The commentator says this does not conflict with God ending things at the first trumpet by hiding them when the light of oneness shines and they fade from view. This is a deep divine mystery, not what the words may seem to mean at first. — ن ره

[^V01-497]: This means that essences appear in detail in the outside world, while in God’s all-encompassing knowledge they were already present without names or distinctions. The note quotes the mystic poet Jami: “The world’s essences, beyond how and why, were hidden from both knowledge and sight. No mark of their being was written on the tablet of knowledge; they had not yet drawn strength from the gift of existence.” — س ره

[^V01-498]: This follows the author’s view that the soul creates forms, drawing them from hidden and unseen states into visible levels. — س ره

[^V01-499]: The author’s qualification “when thinking of them as images” answers a possible objection. Someone might say that mental images can cause things: without an imagined building or fire, no building or fire would be made outside the mind. Or that they can be affected, since they have essences that can receive forms. Or that they can be stable, since imagined forms—and even more so intellectual ones—are more stable than material things. The answer is that the author means images considered as tools for viewing external things. From this point of view, they are appearances of those things. He is also explaining their special status: they are not active like separate intellects or receptive like material forms. — س ره

[^V01-500]: Mental existence is defined by contrast with external existence: an external thing has its characteristic effects, while a mental thing does not. But mental things have effects of their own: they remove ignorance, have a distinct form in the mind, and can produce reactions such as blushing from shame or turning pale from fear. In these respects, they are real in the mind. Every mental thing is measured against something outside the mind; whatever has no counterpart outside the mind has no mental form either. And things whose very nature is to be external and to produce external effects—such as existence in its pure external sense and the Necessary Being—cannot be present in the mind in that way. — ط

[^V01-501]: Anything present to another thing must first exist in itself, and its presence removes one kind of nonexistence from that other thing. This is what we mean by a feature or quality: it is present to something after the lack of it has been removed. So everything present to another is a feature of it in this broad sense, though it belongs to the other only at the level where it removes that lack. An effect is present to its cause in this way: it removes a lack in the cause at the level where the cause’s action is complete. The note says this gives a clue to how God’s active attributes arise, a matter to be explained later. — ط

[^V01-502]: The soul is not always weak in itself. Its weakness here comes from its role as a mirror for the images of particular things. — س ره

[^V01-503]: The author says “estimation,” not “imagination,” because the estimating faculty directs the brain’s powers and grasps particular meanings such as love, fear, wishes, and hopes. Each of these has its own image. For example, intense fear in a dark graveyard or wilderness may make the imagination form a frightening shape, perhaps a demon or monster. Intense love and longing may make a lover imagine that the beloved is present. Through wishes, hopes, fears, and desires, people form images of what they want, dread, or love. Most people attend either to the things themselves when they are present or to the images their minds create when they are absent. Only the most devoted attend to God, the Creator of all these forms. The philosophers say that simple intellects create the detailed forms of intellect. — س ره

[^V01-504]: “Knower” may mean someone who knows realities in detail, someone able to act in existence, or someone with both abilities. Here it means the second or third kind. — س ره

[^V01-505]: “Outside the place of imagination” means outside the knower’s own imagination. This distinguishes true creation from magic or sleight of hand, which may show images outside the magician’s imagination but only by influencing the imaginations of the audience. — ه ره

[^V01-506]: The five realms are the divine realm, the realm of power, the realm of spirits, the visible human world, and the all-encompassing human realm. The human realm itself can contain and preserve the ordered, unseen realms above the world of meanings and fixed realities. — س ره

[^V01-507]: The word “and” begins a new sentence here. It does not describe a state or join this point to the previous one, which would make the passage contradict itself. — س ره

[^V01-508]: The passage through “the forms preserve one another” describes the knower’s awareness of all the realms. The following passage describes the fact that a knower must always be present to at least one realm. Every thing that exists outside the mind passes through all the levels of knowledge before appearing. One form can preserve the others because a form in a higher realm is the cause, spirit, and meaning of the forms below it. A lower form reveals its higher cause, since an effect points back to its cause and an image represents its meaning. — س ره

[^V01-509]: This means that no one is entirely inattentive—not ordinary people and not the special few. Ordinary people also witness a display of reality, though they may not know what is appearing through it. — س ره

[^V01-510]: A person creates and preserves things through resolve, but even when the person creates an act, God is the true Creator. “There is no power or strength except through God, the Most High and Mighty.” — س ره

[^V01-511]: The note says the reply as given is not quite right. If the mental form is simply the reality of the known thing, with no difference between the two, then there is no distinction between a thing and its mental counterpart; this seems to deny mental existence. The philosophers mean that an essence remains the same while its existence differs, which would allow a counterpart and bring back the original problem. The reply’s phrase “shadow-like appearance” may mean only that the mind is related to the reality known. But if it means a separate existence for the form, then the same question arises about the essence shared by different kinds of existence. The better answer is that each thing has a counterpart suited to its own nature. For a nonexistent thing, the counterpart is precisely the lack of any external reality. Its mental form is also an idea of absence, not a different object. The mistake is to assume that a counterpart must always be something that exists.

[^V01-512]: Knowledge of nonexistent things was explained earlier by distinguishing a thing’s basic meaning from the fact that it is absent. Absolute nonexistence is absent in its very nature. — س ره

[^V01-513]: The supposition itself is real as a thought, but “flies” is stated as an actual feature. So the subject must have some actual existence. — س ره

[^V01-514]: A universal statement concerns whatever falls under a general title in reality, whether its examples exist outside the mind, are only possible, or do not exist at all. If the statement is to apply to those real or possible examples, it cannot be limited to actual external things. Since the subject understood in this way is not present outside the mind, it must be present within it. — س ره

[^V01-515]: The shared idea exists in the mind, but we do not have to consider it as existing there. Its commonness comes from the mind’s way of considering it. In many places, the author holds that commonness comes from existence itself—specifically, a dependent mental existence—rather than from essence by itself. This may be what he means when he says that the point will be explained later. — س ره

[^V01-516]: “Applies to them” does not mean that the mental universal is literally predicated of external individuals as one and the same thing. The proof concerns an idea in the mind. The essence considered only as a kind, apart from its material features, can be said to be the same as the individuals; but mental existence and universality cannot be separated from the essence in the mind. Here, “same” means that the idea shares the individuals’ basic nature. The universal term that can truly be applied to each person is the nature “human being,” considered without a condition. — س ره

[^V01-517]: The word 'natural' is unnecessary here and would be better omitted, as the author’s later words make clear. A thing’s nature, considered by itself—not even as the subject of a general idea—exists outside the mind. The error is to confuse that nature with the general idea of it in our minds. — س ره

[^V01-518]: This is true: the idea that applies to many is the natural kind, which is indistinct from its individual examples in its basic meaning. The argument still works, as the author says. — س ره

[^V01-519]: This argument assumes that anything that exists for something else must exist in the same place where that relation applies. Some philosophers instead say that a relation’s being true of a thing requires only that the thing it describes exist, not that the relation itself exist in that same place. The author may mean that ideas drawn from things, though they do not exist outside the mind, still have a real standing. For example, being Zayd’s father or owning a horse is not an external object; these are relations we understand in the mind. The note says this point, despite its qualifications, belongs to the first method. — س ره

[^V01-520]: Ali is reported to have said, “I tore down the gate of Khaybar through God’s power, not through bodily strength.” A Persian poem makes the same point: “The power and action of God rose through him; he uprooted Khaybar’s gate by a force beyond his own. And what is Khaybar? Even the fortress of heaven would have been weak before that hand.” — س ره

[^V01-521]: Knowledge, like life, will, and other perfections, accompanies existence wherever it is found. Indeed, these perfections are one with existence itself. Natural beings have existence, though it is incomplete and mixed with potential and lack. They also have a weak kind of knowledge and life. The Qur'an says, “There is nothing that does not praise Him, though you do not understand their praise.” This awareness is basic knowledge, not the power to feel through touch. Otherwise, plants would be animals, since an animal can sense and move by choice. A thing in nature does not reach sensation until its powers of movement have developed, as the stages of life require. There is also another answer: natural things act under the direction of higher powers that know the ends toward which they are directed. A shot arrow moves toward a goal, but the archer knows the goal, not the arrow. In the same way, natural things may be directed toward ends that are known by the powers directing them. — س ره

[^V01-522]: This meaning differs from the previous one. The previous one was “what exists as existing,” meaning existence itself. This one is an essence that actually exists. It differs from the last meaning because it includes actual existence and the condition “not in a subject,” while the last meaning includes neither. — س ره

[^V01-523]: The concept of something existing in a subject—which is what an accident is—cannot be a broad category for the nine kinds of accidents. That would conflict with the philosophers’ view that these nine are the highest categories. al-Muhaqqiq al-Damad does say that substance and accident are two broad categories. But the better view is that “accident” describes how these things exist in relation to something else. An essential feature belongs to a thing without reference to anything outside it. In truth, an accident has a dependent kind of existence: its existence in itself is the same as its existence in the subject it depends on. Even if most philosophers leave relation out of their definitions, they agree that it belongs to the way these things exist. Since being an accident means having a relational existence, and existence is not part of a thing’s basic nature, being an accident is not essential to it. — س ره

[^V01-524]: This means considering something with a condition, or without one. By “taking the universal where the particular belongs,” the author means treating the general idea as if it were the particular magnet. — س ره

[^V01-525]: Earlier in this commentary, the natural universal was explained as a nature that can be considered in several ways: by itself, joined to other conditions, or separated from them. It is even more open-ended than an unrestricted nature, since it can take on many conditions that cannot coexist. This is what the author means when he says it can be joined to incompatible conditions. Other writers use “natural universal” for a nature considered without any condition; the author calls this an intellectual universal. al-Taftazani writes in *The Refinement of Logic* that its subject is natural. Some copies read, “as the essence described as universal is called an intellectual universal.” On that reading, the meaning is clear. — س ره

[^V01-526]: Many things do not fall under the ten categories, such as particular possible existences, which are not necessary existents, and simple distinguishing features. These are either particular existences, as the author holds, or simple natures that do not belong to any category, as other philosophers hold. Even some qualities, such as a point or unity, do not belong to the nine categories in their view. — س ره

[^V01-527]: The first problem was answered earlier. The second and third are these: a general idea is universal as an idea, yet it exists in a particular mind, and its subject is one of the things that makes it particular. How, then, can it be both general and particular? Also, in their view, knowledge and the thing known are one. Yet knowledge of blackness belongs to the knower, not to blackness itself. God’s knowledge of things is identical with His being, but the things He knows are not. The commentator then explains the view with a mirror example. Imagine a person standing before a mirror, with his body reflected in it. There are two images: the person’s natural image, which is not in the mirror, and the reflection on the mirror’s surface, which depends on the mirror. The view says that the mind works like a mirror. For each thing we perceive, it posits three forms: the external thing, known indirectly; a mental form, which is present to the mind but does not depend on it; and a form that depends on the mind, which this view calls the external thing. Each form has its own subject. — س ره

[^V01-528]: This view combines two positions. It says that the form in the mind is like the external thing in its nature and features, while the form that depends on the mind is its shadow because it is a quality. The actual external thing, meanwhile, belongs to another category. Or else it invents a third position by claiming there are two forms: those who say the mental form is a likeness, and those who say it is a shadow, each speak of only one form. No one spoke of two. — س ره

[^V01-529]: The point is to show the flaw in saying that what exists in the mind, apart from the mind, is general and immaterial. Generality and being free of matter depend on its existence for the mind. This also supports the author’s claim that there must be a causal link: the mind must be one of the causes of what exists in it. — س ره

[^V01-530]: Just because a thing exists for another in the same way it exists in itself, it does not follow that it must exist inside that other thing. The claim cannot simply be turned around. But here the point is that a mental form cannot exist for the mind in the way that something produced exists for its maker. The mind, especially when it is only potentially able to understand, receives forms passively. So this particular kind of existence for the mind must mean that the form depends on the mind. — س ره

[^V01-531]: That is, the mental form is not in matter and is not covered by material features. The author says that, if this form did not depend on the mind, it would have to be particular and perceptible, not general and intelligible. The author is showing that the other view leads to a contradiction, as his words “we assumed it was intelligible” make clear. According to that view, the mind frees forms from matter by removing their material features. But that process depends on the forms existing for the mind. If the forms do not depend on the mind, they remain material, whatever names one gives them. — س ره

[^V01-532]: This is the position he takes on mental forms to answer several objections.

[^V01-533]: This objection will arise in two forms later, in the section of this book on the intellect and what it knows. — س ره

[^V01-534]: Someone might say that the reverse must also follow. The answer is that there is no quality in the mind, as we will explain when discussing God’s knowledge and the beings that govern the kinds of things. All these forms exist through the soul’s existence. Their concepts, of course, can be applied to themselves in the basic, definitional sense. — س ره

[^V01-535]: The phrase “their relation to bodily kinds” can be read as referring either to the intellectual forms themselves or to the forms together with the ideas drawn from them. On the author’s view, and on Plato’s, the objects of intellect are the intellectual realities seen from afar in the creative world.

    The author distinguishes the soul’s perception of sensed and imagined forms from its perception of intellectual forms. It brings the first about through its own activity, but reaches the second through an illuminating connection. Why? Individual forms are marked by size, shape, change, and limits. So the author often says that the soul perceives them by making them. He sometimes describes this as union, since these forms are the soul’s own lights and appearances, not separate things. As a saying about the appearance of the First Reality puts it: “All are expressions; You are the meaning, the magnet of hearts.”

    General forms, by contrast, are marked chiefly by unity, freedom from matter, and their reach across the subtle details of imagined and natural things. They rise above both worlds and both regions. So the author says that the soul knows them by becoming one with them. This is what he means by an illuminating connection and by direct, present knowledge. Such knowledge can occur through union or through causation. Causation does not fit here, though some writers sometimes say that the simple intellect or soul creates detailed intellects and forms of knowledge. The author has reasons for rejecting this, including his reply to al-Qushji. So union is what remains.

    If you ask what he says about general ideas that have no separate intellectual beings as their source, he says they too represent the sources of existing things, but they are labels that do not accurately fit them. Even an inaccurate definition points toward the thing it is meant to define. To see how this can happen, consider how the light of existence reaches even its opposite, nonexistence, including absolute nonexistence, and an essence considered apart from existence. We can understand universal existence—the most obvious and wide-reaching thing—by seeing from afar the light of existence itself, which is brighter and wider than any light or shadow. In the higher world, a quality and the thing it belongs to are one, just as the scent of musk and the musk itself are one; otherwise, potentiality would follow.

    Many minds find the idea that knowing a general form means seeing the source of a kind unsettling. The author discusses the reasons elsewhere. Most come down to two. First, people treat a concept as if it were the whole reality and overlook existence itself: its unity includes all its levels and details, so it can both know and be known. Second, they treat the general idea only as a mirror for looking at particular things, instead of turning it around and seeing what the idea itself reveals. — س ره

[^V01-536]: This does not mean a limited kind of existence, such as the existence of water, fire, or other natural things. It means another, form-like and luminous existence for these natures, unlike their dark material existence, which cannot support knowledge. The author means that the existence of natures in the mind—in the signs within the soul—is like their existence in external things—in the signs of the world. Just as external existence is God’s sacred outpouring and illuminating act, not a substance or quality in itself, so knowledge is an existence that flows from the soul and is lit by it; in itself, it is neither a substance nor a quality. The natures themselves are substances, quantities, and qualities in the basic, definitional sense, not in the ordinary sense. This distinction between the two ways of applying a term matters to the argument that follows. The reply rests on two points: things in the mind are themselves in the basic sense, not in the ordinary sense; and the forms are truly qualities, not merely called qualities as a figure of speech. The reply accepts the familiar philosophical principles; the author has already offered other answers that do not depend on them. — س ره

[^V01-537]: The author says “in our view,” even though everyone agrees that a nature considered by itself is neither existent nor nonexistent. The reason is that those who treat a nature as a real thing are, in effect, saying that it exists in itself, though they may say it exists only through its relation to its maker, as the author says of existence. They accept the point in words, while the results of their view imply it. As Imam al-Razi says, the claim that a nature is not made follows from the question of what a nature is in itself. — س ره

[^V01-538]: At first, this seems to conflict with the author’s earlier claim that universality comes from intellectual existence itself. But intellectual existence is so wide that it extends evenly across all its details. In the section on the soul, he says that the generality and individuality of an intellectual form are not two separate things. How, then, can its nature be general? Perhaps he means that generality comes from the nature’s lack of individual features and its great openness, as he suggests here. Its ability to apply to many comes from being seen from afar, with its inner reality not fully grasped. “They forgot God, so He made them forget themselves.” Or perhaps he means that the nature does not resist being general, as something able to receive that feature, though it does not require generality by itself. The discussion of the soul makes this point clearer. — س ره

[^V01-539]: This is the standard definition of a human being, though it can be challenged. A definition may tell us what truly makes a thing what it is, or it may merely help us tell that thing apart from others. Here we need the first kind. So the definition should include each level it passes through: its material and mineral form, its ability to have dimensions, growth, the senses, the powers that prompt and carry out movement, voluntary movement, and reason both as a capacity and in use. A thing cannot reach a higher kind until it has all the conditions of a lower kind. If “mineral form” is included under “able to have dimensions,” then growth and sensation should be included too. Otherwise the definition does not show all the essential parts. It is not enough simply to distinguish humans; the words “rational” or even “laughing” would do that. A full definition would be: a human being is a substance that can have dimensions, has an elemental and mineral form, grows, senses, moves by choice, and reasons. — س ره

[^V01-540]: This follows the common view. The author will discuss later whether it is a quality only incidentally. — س ره

[^V01-541]: Ordinary predication concerns the shared existence of subject and predicate, and existence is incidental to an essence. The second kind of predication is different. — س ره

[^V01-542]: Predication requires a difference in one way and identity in another. When a definition is said of the thing it defines, the difference is between the general and the detailed meaning. For example, “human being” is “animal that reasons.” The two are the same in nature, but one is the full definition and the other is the thing defined. The phrase “human being is human being” can also have meaning if someone has first suggested that a human being can be separated from itself. The reply says that the human being whose existence you question is exactly the human being whose existence cannot be denied. Similarly, when philosophers say that a human being, considered just as a human being, is only itself, they mean that it is neither existent, nonexistent, nor anything else beyond its own nature. This is not empty repetition: it says that the two meanings are identical, not merely that they share an existence. — س ره

[^V01-543]: “Essence” here means the actual thing or example. If two concepts are identical, they share an existence; but the reverse does not always follow. Primary predication is about identity of meaning. The existence in question may be actual, mental, or merely assumed. Claims such as “nothing is nothing” or “contradictions are contradictions” use this kind of predication, even though they have no actual existence. — س ره

[^V01-544]: For example, “a laughing person is a writer” and “a laughing person is not a writer” can both be true in different senses: one may be a writer in actual existence without being one by nature. The concept “laughing person,” which is shared by all people who laugh, is “laughing” by primary predication but not by ordinary predication. — س ره

[^V01-545]: The author means natures considered without any condition—the natural universals discussed before the two kinds of predication. He does not mean “intellectual universals” in the usual technical sense. This is clear from his argument, especially since he treats intellectual universals as the real sources of kinds, seen from a distance. On that view, they are substances just as an individual is an example of a nature. Here, “universal” means the nature’s indeterminacy; “intelligible” means the concept as it exists in thought. — س ره

[^V01-546]: The author’s view is that particular mental images are produced by the soul, while general forms are reached when the soul sees separate intellects from a distance. In the first case, the soul brings the forms about. In the second, it is a place where higher realities appear. If these forms exist in the soul as qualities, that is because they are features of the soul; their intelligible, general nature is not itself one of the categories. By themselves, the general forms are separate substances. As features of the soul they are qualities; as ideas they are meanings of the categories, not the categories themselves. — ط

[^V01-547]: Existence makes the hidden features of essences appear. But existence itself is neither a substance nor an accident, so how could it be a quality? Another way to put it is that existence makes an essence actually show a quality, as the sun makes water hot or darkens a face. It is not like a passenger’s movement being attributed to a ship that moves. — س ره

[^V01-548]: The soul is a place where general intellectual forms appear, but it produces particular sensory and imagined forms. — س ره

[^V01-549]: The argument rests on the view that mental concepts are not examples of categories in the ordinary sense. Natures as general ideas are only ways of considering things; an actual example comes from existence. A concept of substance or quantity, considered apart from its particular existence, is true of itself only in the primary sense. So it would have been enough to say that the mental idea of substance does not produce the effects of substance. The author adds that even an intellectual universal does not become an example of itself by being universal. Since a concept exists through the soul, it is not an individual example of the category it names. — س ره

[^V01-550]: The author makes the effects of a category the test for whether something is an actual example of it. On this test, even an image in the imagination would not be an example unless the effects of the category were present. — س ره

[^V01-551]: The author says this because he is still completing and strengthening the argument, not because he thinks the proof has failed. — س ره

[^V01-552]: This also shows that the author denies that natures, by themselves, are examples of categories—not only that intellectual universals are. The same reasoning works whether one follows the usual view of universals or the author’s view that the soul sees separate intellectual forms from a distance. Some might say that a particular image in the imagination, such as a human being, is a human and a substance in the ordinary sense. The author’s reply is that even an external human being is an individual because of its particular existence, not because of its nature alone. The imagined human image exists through the soul’s existence, especially if knowing is the soul’s union with what it knows. One simple existence can give rise to both general and particular ideas without dividing. Every imagined form is a light or appearance of the soul. Another way to say this is that mental forms are above the categories, like the soul, not below them. The author discusses this in the section on intellect and what it knows. — س ره

[^V01-553]: The author has established that mental ideas are not categories in the ordinary sense, though they are categories in the primary sense. He now adds that they are qualities only incidentally, not by nature. The source of the difficulty is that he does not explain fully how this incidental quality works. Existence itself is not a quality, and the nature of a thing is already the category of the thing known. If the connection to the soul is an illuminating relation, then it is existence, not quality. If it is ordinary relation, the forms would be related to the soul, not qualities of it. The commentator’s answer is that the author follows the common view that mental forms exist in the mind as qualities. The forms are present in the mind, and this presence is what we call knowledge; the forms themselves are qualities only because they exist in the mind. — س ره

[^V01-554]: “Quality” and “power” may refer to one thing. “Power” can mean an accidental faculty, as discussed later. Or “quality” may reflect the view that imagination is an accident, while “power” reflects the view that it is a substance, like a substantial form. — س ره

[^V01-555]: Physical forms exist outside the senses and have physical effects on the sensory powers when the senses meet them. At that stage there is no awareness. The soul’s awareness accompanies them and makes the forms appear as particulars or as general ideas. These two kinds of forms appear to the soul in two worlds free from matter: the greater or smaller imaginal world—the philosophers disagree on which—and the world of universal intellects. The three worlds of matter, imagination, and intellect correspond to one another. — ط

[^V01-556]: This prepares for the claim that the image in a mirror is not in the eye, and leads to the claim that it must exist in the imaginal world. Suhrawardi treats these images as mirrors that let us see particular material things, not as objects we look at for their own sake. He explains their attractiveness and beauty by the body’s needs, but may confuse the body’s role with the image itself. Without the liver’s heat, for example, cold water would not be so desirable. — س ره

[^V01-557]: The author does not also say that the image is not in the mirror itself because the same argument applies there. He has shortened Suhrawardi’s reasoning. Suhrawardi first rejects the ideas that vision happens through a ray from the eye or through an image stamped into the eye. He then argues that the image is not in the mirror, since it looks different from different viewing positions. The author combines these arguments: the first prepares for the second, which supports the existence of the imaginal world. Suhrawardi gives a Persian riddle: “I found a mountain inside a cottonseed; can you guess what it is? I found an ocean inside a kohl pot; can you guess what it is?” The eye and brain are not containers for a huge image; they are surfaces through which it appears. — س ره

[^V01-558]: That is, the imaginal world, also called the world of meanings. — س ره

[^V01-559]: The soul cannot know anything until it exists for the soul. So whatever it knows, whether particular or general, must exist within the soul’s own being. This would mean that each soul has its own image, distinct from the general imaginal world, since the soul’s particular nature changes what it perceives. The same happens when the senses distort what they see, or when mirrors change an image by their shape. The same argument should apply to intellectual forms: what the soul knows must exist within its own being. — ط

[^V01-560]: In my view, the author should say about imagination what he says about understanding: the soul sees the sources of kinds from a distance. Ugly images may be distortions caused by the surface through which they appear, and the same kind of distortion may happen in intellectual ideas. I agree with the author about imagined forms, but about understanding I hold that the luminous soul sees reflections of divine Forms that differ from those Forms in level. The soul’s imagined world is its smaller imaginal world, and its intellectual forms are its smaller world of intellect—not the greater intellect itself, unless the soul is absorbed into the Active Intellect. — س ره

[^V01-561]: The images do not exist as real beings in the higher spiritual world. They have only a shadow-like existence: they are reflections that depend on the things they copy. A reflection or shadow is not the thing itself. It is like a mirage beside the realities of the natural world: we see it, but it shows us the appearance of a thing, not its true nature. This is a strong argument that an image corresponds to what it represents. Many spiritual writers use reflections, shadows, and echoes to explain this relation. One mystic writes: “Everything but Him that appears to you is a second image seen by a squinting eye.” The point is that things seem to exist separately in their own right, though they depend on existence itself. — س ره

[^V01-562]: The Persian verse in the main text says that the Beloved plays music behind the veil and begins a new note at every moment. Here the melody means the outpouring of existence, also called the Breath of the Merciful or God’s word “Be.” The echo means the natures of things, which reflect the different modes of existence. Jami uses the same image: “One sound reaches your ear in two ways: sometimes you call it a call, sometimes an echo.” Elsewhere he writes: “An echo of your call entered the sanctuary, and the people of Arafat answered with a hundred cries of ‘Here I am.’” The second line of the verse quoted by the author also suggests that God’s words never run out: God is never silent but continually makes truth known. The author connects the image of existence and essence without the earlier verse, which speaks of love. Read together, the verses show that God’s true love flows through every kind of love, just as His beauty appears in every reality. His love is the call; all other loves are its echo. In perfect love, the echo returns to its source. — س ره

[^V01-563]: The main problem is not simply that one thing would be both an individual and a general idea. The real problem is that every bodily kind would need an immaterial individual of its own. One kind would then have a material individual, an immaterial one, a quality, and a substance. Being free of matter is a higher state than being a substance or quality. The claim that one thing is both particular and general is a secondary difficulty, not a separate objection; the author already answered it while addressing the first objection. — س ره

[^V01-564]: This explains why the objection says that every bodily kind must have an immaterial individual of its own. — س ره

[^V01-565]: If the idea retained those material features, it could not apply to things that lack them. It would no longer be general or truly apply to many things. — س ره

[^V01-566]: These are the two claims made by the objector. The author rejects both, as he will explain when he speaks of those who accept the higher spiritual world. — س ره

[^V01-567]: If we remove the features that make something particular, whether in the outside world or in the mind, what remains is its nature, which is neither general nor particular. This is another philosopher’s answer. The author’s own view is that generality comes from the wide reach of intellectual existence, as explained earlier. — س ره

[^V01-568]: Mental forms count as qualities only when we consider them as features of the soul and as forms of knowledge it has. Compared with things in the outside world, they are concepts, neither substances nor qualities. — ط

[^V01-569]: Existence applies to all things in one meaning. In the Necessary Being, existence is not joined to an essence; in other things, it is joined to one. If you ask what belongs in the definition of a human being, the answer is that “body” must include both natural bodies and imaginal bodies, even if the latter are shadow-like. “Rational” must include both actual reason, such as the active intellect, and reason as a capacity, such as the possible and passive intellect. “Sensing” and “moving” must include both the source or power for these acts and their actual performance. “Knowing” includes direct, present knowledge. “Growing” includes both the power to grow and actual growth. “Feeding” includes feeding in the imaginal world. The life of the plant soul is also present in the human soul in a higher and simpler way. — س ره

[^V01-570]: The author’s first reply followed his own view: the soul makes the images it imagines. They arise through its activity rather than entering it and changing it. Here, however, he adopts Suhrawardi’s approach. He focuses on imagined images, though the objection also applies to intellectual forms. On the author’s account, the soul does not contain intellectual forms as separate features; it knows them by joining with them and rising toward the higher world. In that world, forms and the things they belong to exist as one. No thing there can be a subject without its qualities, or a quality without its subject, because that would require matter and potentiality, which do not exist in that realm. The sweetness of sugar and sugar itself, for example, exist there as one. The answer is that the forms do not exist in the soul as separate qualities. This applies to intellectual forms as well, so the author did not need to discuss them separately here. The first answer applies more directly to imagined forms, the second to intellectual forms, and the third to both. — س ره

[^V01-571]: Someone may ask: if the mental forms were not in the soul at first and then came to be there, is that not a change in the soul? And is change not a kind of being affected? The terms “passive knowledge” and “active knowledge” also seem to support this. The reply is that the author denies the soul is affected by the real material things themselves—the actual forms that exist in the physical world—not that the soul changes in any sense when it knows. The higher causes contain knowledge of all worldly things but are not changed by their bodily features. They contain these forms as their causes, not as things they receive. The forms in the soul are prepared either to flow from a higher source, as the philosophers held, or to be formed by the soul itself, as the author held. If we grant that mental forms exist in the soul as qualities, their presence there still need not mean that the soul is passively affected by them. The measure of being affected is that a form comes from something else and is received through matter, not simply that it appears in a subject. — س ره

[^V01-572]: This point is explained later. The real existence of evenness is the state of a thing that can be divided into two equal parts. This applies to an even number, such as four, whether it exists outside the mind or in it. It does not apply to the soul simply because the soul has an idea of evenness. The philosophers who say that abstract ideas exist through the things from which we draw them accept this much. — س ره

[^V01-573]: The author could also agree that mental things exist in the outside world in one sense: the mind itself is an outside thing, and the mental form exists as a state of the mind. It is “mental” only in relation to the thing outside the mind that it represents. A spoken name or written mark is also an outside thing in its own right, while representing a person named Zayd. — س ره

[^V01-574]: The sciences build proofs around real subjects and the features that truly belong to them. They do not need to discuss every general or accidental meaning. So a word can have one shared meaning in everyday speech but several separate meanings in a technical discussion. The words “in the mind” and “the mind in the outside world” sound alike, but “in” means something different in each. In technical language the word works like two different words, not one word with one shared meaning. — ط

[^V01-575]: There is another important objection, the seventh after the six in the main text. If mental ideas are only reflections of things, each idea must have a real thing outside the mind that it reflects. Then the soul could not imagine what is impossible, what does not exist, or any simple idea with no matching thing outside. An answer based on supposition and statements that do not assert actual existence seems to assume what it is trying to prove: the very act of supposing gives a mental existence to something with no external example, which is the problem raised by the objection. A full answer depends on the later account of how ideas arise from their examples, and on the difference between concepts that state what a thing is and other ideas that simply serve as mental names or labels. — ط

[^V01-576]: This note applies to statements about both impossible things and the Necessary Being. The author’s phrase “when no nature has been formed at all” refers to impossible things; “or in the mind” refers to God. It is strange to place statements about the Necessary Being among non-assertive statements, since a claim is plainly true when its subject exists in reality, and non-assertive when the subject exists only as an assumption. The Necessary Being is the deepest reality; everything else depends on it. One possible reply is that an ordinary, unconditional statement says: anything that is an example of this nature is such-and-such. That requires both an actual example outside the mind and a concept in the mind that lets us consider it. Impossible things have no actual examples, while God has no nature that can be formed in the mind, even though God truly exists.

    Someone might object that if the mind cannot grasp God’s full reality, then statements about any outside thing would also be non-assertive, because its actual existence cannot enter the mind without changing into something else. The answer is that a possible thing has a nature that can be fully understood and is shared by its mental and external forms. God has no such nature. The concepts “Necessary Being,” “pure being,” and “pure existence” are only ways of pointing toward God. They act like a mirror: they direct thought toward God without making God an object pictured in the mind. A concept can be true of itself by essential predication, while the reality it points to remains beyond the mind. This is how we can make true statements about the Necessary Being without grasping God’s full reality. — س ره

[^V01-577]: Some people attribute the copy-and-shadow view to the ancient philosophers as well. — س ره

[^V01-578]: Many thinkers have said that the name and what it names are one. The clearest examples are the philosophers’ view that God’s attributes are identical with His essence and the mystics’ view that a true name is absolute existence considered together with one of the highest attributes. The same idea applies here in a broad sense: a spoken or written name, as the way a thing appears and is considered, is not wholly separate from it. That is why a judgment about the thing can also be made about its name or written form. In this respect, neither is entirely separate from the thing. — س ره

[^V01-579]: The commentator asks how the scholar can say that existence comes before a thing’s nature while also saying that existence is only an idea, has no example outside or inside the mind, and does not even exist as a feature of the nature. The answer is that “the existing thing” that comes first means the thing as produced by its maker. “Nature” means the thing considered simply as what it is; that nature is an idea, a point on which the philosophers agree. The scholar says that everything outside the mind after it is made, and everything in the mind, is some nature. What we point to as a nature is itself the thing made and existing. The idea of “existent” does not name an extra feature joined to it, because existence is the thing’s being real, not something added to it.

    This is close to Mulla Sadra’s view that two things do not exist here except in thought: the human being, for example, is real by being one with a mode of true existence. No separate thing corresponds to the idea of “existent” to make that unity impossible. The scholar likewise says that the idea of “existent” corresponds to the nature itself. A possible thing has a nature that can be described as either existent or nonexistent; the Necessary Being can only be described as existent, never as nonexistent. The scholar interprets the philosophers’ claim that God is “pure existence” to mean that God is “purely existent,” since God cannot be neutral between existing and not existing. The commentator rejects this account of God, but says that it is not the issue being discussed here. If being produced is real, it must be real existence; if it is not, it cannot rule out nonexistence. Mulla Sadra considers the account close to the truth because it agrees with some principles discussed earlier. — س ره

[^V01-580]: The objector has taken “becomes” to mean that one thing changes into a different thing. The right reading is a simple change: something comes to exist. It does not mean that one already existing thing turns into another. The scholar’s second answer amounts to this. — ن ره

[^V01-581]: The priority is at the level of existence in general, not at the level of a definite nature such as human being or horse. The “existent” in the second answer is not a specific thing that first appeared. — س ره

[^V01-582]: This kind of identity is true of real existence. But for the scholar discussed here, there is only a concept and the nature that gives rise to differences of kind and broader kind. What, then, is this “one thing” that is supposed to remain through the change? It seems to be no more than the general idea of nature or thinghood, a second-order idea. — س ره

[^V01-583]: If no real feature is shared by two natures, we should not insist that one can turn into the other. Why say that the sky has become the earth? In this scholar’s view, distinct essences are what make things different, while existence is only an idea. There is no real principle that joins one essence to another. A vague idea of “something” does not supply one. It is a second-order idea, not an essential part shared by the two things. The proposed common ground is only something the mind imagines. But two genuinely different things do not become one because we choose to think of them together. In ordinary change, some real basis remains through the change; without it, there is no one thing in the first state and the second. — س ره

[^V01-584]: Some copies of the text add: “How can this be, when some things known by the mind have no subject or container at all?” — س ره

[^V01-585]: This is the point the objector intends. It does not apply to the copy-and-shadow view, because its supporters do not say that the external thing changes into its image. They say that its image is not the thing itself, and they avoid claiming that the two are identical. — س ره

[^V01-586]: This explanation does not work unless there is something real that remains through the change from A to B. Without that, the word “change” itself cannot connect the two. This objection does not apply to the copy-and-shadow view, for the reason given in the previous note. — س ره

[^V01-587]: The comparison with prime matter is misleading. Prime matter is undetermined only with respect to the forms it can take; its own nature and basic kind are still fixed. The general natures proposed here are different. Every possible nature, whether a kind or a broader kind, can be understood by the mind. So what is the one reality called “water” that is supposed to remain the same in a physical body and in a mental quality? If it is a real part of both, then simple things such as qualities and intellects become compounds made of parts and must fall under one of the basic kinds. If the shared part is only mental, then it is a broader kind, not something simple; the highest categories would no longer be simple. If it is merely a feature added to each, then the two are not the same nature but only share an added feature. And if it is only a general idea, it cannot make two different things one.

    Mulla Sadra can speak of one existence appearing at different levels—as divine, intellectual, spiritual, bodily, or even spoken and written—because real existence is what unites these levels. The natures and concepts mark their differences. But the scholar discussed here accepts only natures and denies real existence as a distinct reality. What, then, could unite the different forms of water for him? The commentator says they are as far apart as flint and a fragrant flower, or a lamp and the sun at noon. — س ره

[^V01-588]: This passage concerns pure existence itself, not the vague general nature discussed here. Pure, simple, luminous existence cannot be pointed to as one definite thing, though it is the basis of identity. Our question concerns the general nature considered together with existence. Particular natures are already ideas; a wholly vague general nature is even more plainly a second-order idea. There is a difference between something that cannot be pointed to because it has no reality and something that cannot be pointed to because it is too full and real to be limited. So the claim that the nature is wholly undefined has no real subject. — س ره

[^V01-589]: This is a second meaning of “the essential features remain.” Earlier it meant that a nature stays the same when we consider it with existence in general. Here it means that the external nature’s essential features also apply to its mental image when we use that image to think about the outside thing. For example, the mental idea of water is a quality of the mind, but we can consider it as water outside the mind and apply to it the features of external water. — س ره

[^V01-590]: This means the wide, all-embracing intellectual existence of water, of which particular waters are partial reflections. The general idea of water is its nature, since every possible thing includes both a nature and existence. This wide existence includes particular waters in a higher and simpler way; they are its appearances, while it represents them more fully. This account fits Mulla Sadra’s view, but not the view of the other scholar. — س ره

[^V01-591]: The passage up to “Here is the right way to understand it” uses direct experience to show that knowledge is a real quality and to set out the problem. — س ره

[^V01-592]: To resolve the problem, there would have to be something in addition to each mental image’s nature and its existence in the mind: another nature, with its own existence, joined to the nature of the thing known. Only then would a real quality be present. But where is this added thing? The account itself says that when we look within, we find only the image. Simply calling knowledge a quality at one point and the thing it describes at another does not solve the problem; nothing has been added to the image.

    The comparison with Zayd or a body is not exact. We call Zayd “white” or “laughing” because a feature has been added to him. The subject and that feature do not exist in the same way, so their combination is only a union in thought. Here, by contrast, there is nothing beyond the image itself, which belongs to the same basic kind as the thing known.

    When people say that a quality and the adjective that describes it are one, they mean that the quality, considered simply as belonging to something, can be said of that thing. In that statement, the quality and the thing described share one reality: the quality is not separate from the thing but belongs to its existence. This does not mean that exactly the same mode of existence belongs to both. If it did, the basic kinds of qualities would disappear, because one existing thing cannot be both a substance and a quality. — س ره

[^V01-593]: In the example of Zayd, his existence and the existence of his features are distinct. In the case discussed here, the thing known and knowledge share one existence, as the main text explains. — س ره

[^V01-594]: This seems to assume what it needs to prove. Without a separate feature added to the image, there is no basis for calling it a quality; qualities are usually features added to a subject. The same objection applies to two similar claims made later, unless the argument adopts the philosophers’ view that qualities exist in a subject. — س ره

[^V01-595]: Since a quality is a feature that exists in a subject, the earlier example of Zayd and whiteness fits better. The author also holds that relations have their own kind of existence. If the case discussed here worked in the same way, knowledge would belong to the basic kind called relation. — س ره

[^V01-596]: The author has already explained how a quality and the thing described by it can be one without making the basic kinds of qualities disappear. That is what he means here. The Sayyid takes a different view. The author’s account works: it preserves both quality and substance without adding a separate feature, as explained earlier. The Sayyid’s account of their unity does not work on its own. — س ره

[^V01-597]: The opening of this chapter draws on an earlier distinction between existence in itself and existence in another thing. Some beings have no independent existence at all, such as links between things. If a link had any independence of its own, it would become one end of the link, connected to another end; that contradicts the assumption that it is only a link. Since everything that exists outside the mind has at least some independence, a pure link can exist only together with an existence that supports it. It is not separate from that existence but belongs within it. A link between two things therefore joins them, and both are present in some way within that relation.

    This also means that linking existence and existence in itself differ in kind; there is no shared idea that covers both. A pure link cannot itself be named or used as a subject or predicate, or called general or particular, because it has no independent existence. All this concerns the first part of the argument.

    At the end of the chapter, the author says that all possible beings are links in relation to God’s existence, and that God supports them and watches over every soul. This means that an essence considered by itself has no status, either independent or dependent. What matters is the existence that supports it and accompanies it. The same essence can be viewed as a complete, noun-like meaning, or from another angle as an incomplete, relation-like meaning. This is a useful idea for understanding degrees of existence, God’s knowledge, and other questions. — ط

[^V01-598]: A compound statement does not mean that the subject and predicate point to the same thing, as some theologians mistakenly think. It means that one thing is affirmed of another. — س ره

[^V01-599]: The author will later say that a predicate, simply as a predicate, has no existence in itself. So here “predicate” means the link between the terms, not an ordinary thing that is said of a subject. The objection that one thing cannot be said of another unless it first exists does not apply to this link. Nor does the existence of the first predicate in a compound statement create the alleged endless series. The series arises only if we mistake the link for a separate thing that exists for another and then needs a further link. The link is not an independently existing object; it is the fact that something is established of another, not a separate thing that is established. This is the difference between linking and dependent existence. — س ره

[^V01-600]: Here “subject” means the subject-term in logic, not the thing in which a quality exists or the whole subject-predicate pair. In this sense, the questions of a science are predicates linked to their subjects. This link is what the author calls linking existence. — س ره

[^V01-601]: The earlier thinkers either treated essence as real in its own right, dividing reality into two kinds—existence and essence—or held that each existence is distinct from every other, as the philosophers in Aristotle’s school appear to have done. Either way, a possible being has an existence of its own; it is not a pure link. Mulla Sadra, by contrast, says that existence alone is real and that essences are ideas. What is related and the relation itself are both existence, at different levels: limited existence, absolute existence, and true existence. The possible being is pure connection, complete need, and dependence. — س ره

[^V01-602]: Saying that a quality has existence in itself, like a substance, does not conflict with saying that it is one level of the substance’s existence. The author says this elsewhere. As explained in an earlier note, a quality’s existence in itself means that the mind can understand what the quality is without also thinking about its subject. Yet its actual existence in itself is the same as its existence for that subject. This differs from a pure link, which cannot be understood without both things it connects. — ط

[^V01-603]: The point is confirmed by the fact that the simple, luminous reality of existence cannot itself be an idea, whether of the first kind or the second. It is the reality to which an idea refers. At first it may seem strange, if existence is real in its own right, to call the abstract idea “existing” a second-order concept. Concepts such as human being, horse, water, fire, white, and black are first-order concepts because they refer to things outside the mind. The concept of existence also refers to real things: God’s existence and the existences of possible beings. These are its main referents, since essences exist only indirectly.

    There is a difference, however, between the actual individuals of a natural kind and the different modes of existence. A human nature has individuals both in the mind and outside it; the same nature is found in both places. But the various modes of existence outside the mind are not individual examples of one shared nature called “existence.” There is no common essence shared by general existence and its particular modes. As we explained earlier, general existence is a mental idea, not a part that makes up its individual instances.

    It is possible to distinguish the abstract idea “existence” from the idea “being existent,” just as Persian distinguishes *hastī* from *hast būdan*, and “whiteness” from “being white.” That distinction has some basis, but it does not help to make it a separate philosophical issue, since the author does not keep the two senses apart in many places.

    The word “thingness” is also an abstract noun. It means what can exist—the nature that answers the question “What is it?” It is a second-order concept because the special natures of human beings, horses, cows, whiteness, and blackness have no shared feature called “thingness” over and above their own differences. If they had a shared essential feature, the highest kinds would not be highest. If it were an added, nonessential feature, particular things would count as things only after that feature was added, as a body would be white only after whiteness was added. That is plainly wrong. Possibility and necessity, which describe how one thing relates to another, have been explained earlier. — س ره

[^V01-604]: It is better to say that mental existence is “not part of” a second-order concept, rather than saying that it is “not a condition” for one. There is no problem in saying that mental existence is a condition for a logical second-order concept to apply, as when universality applies to the idea of human being. Some philosophers define a second-order concept in this way. Perhaps the author means that the logical concept applies to the nature itself, while its existence in the mind is only the setting in which the concept applies. On that view, the statement is about what holds whenever the nature is in the mind, not a conditional statement. — س ره

[^V01-605]: This conflicts with the accepted rule that each science studies the features of its own subject, while a higher science establishes the subject and its basic principles. For example, the study of matter and form belongs to the highest science; physics treats them only as principles. Perhaps the author means that a lower science defines a thing’s nature before proving that the thing exists. But defining a thing as it actually exists belongs to the higher science, because a thing’s nature depends on its existence. This is why definitions before a statement that something exists are only verbal definitions; after its existence is established, they become real definitions. — س ره

[^V01-606]: Existence is applied to a natural kind through its individual examples, as we attribute a ship’s movement to the person sitting in it. To say that a natural kind exists is to say that one of its individuals exists. Those who deny that natural kinds exist and those who say that essence is what truly exists take opposite extremes. The truth lies between them: a natural kind exists as a reflection or shadow of existence. It has no separate thing corresponding to it, yet it has some share in real existence through the individuals that embody it. As we said earlier, a natural kind is real in the mind’s ordinary judgment, but is only figuratively real from the viewpoint of direct insight and philosophical proof. The different ways that existence can be attributed are relevant here. — س ره

[^V01-607]: “Particularity” here means the logical feature that applies to a particular instance of a natural kind: a specific nature together with the features that make it an individual. Sometimes “particularity” means individual existence or being distinct. In that sense, it is a kind of existence, not a mental feature or second-order concept. — س ره

[^V01-608]: The point is that Zayd is particular in the mind’s view of him. Logical particularity means that a concept cannot be thought of as applying to many things. This mental feature applies to the Zayd in the mind—that is, to the idea of Zayd—not to the person outside the mind. Particularity does not simply mean being unable to be shared. At most, it is a philosophical second-order concept, not a logical one. So why should logic study it? — س ره

[^V01-609]: There are four objections to the scholar’s account. First, it reverses the author’s argument, as he explains later. Second, it assumes the point at issue: the scholar defines being described one way, but his opponents mean that the subject and the feature both exist in the setting where the feature is attributed. Third, if a subject can be described without the feature existing, there would be no difference between true and false statements. “Zayd is a father” is true, though fatherhood does not exist as a separate thing in Zayd; but then the same claim could be made of a wall. Fourth, this account would erase the difference between essential features and added features. The commentator has discussed these points earlier. — س ره

[^V01-610]: I do not think this account is right, because it would overturn many accepted philosophical principles. The author himself does not follow it consistently. For example, a feature being true of something depends on the subject’s existence, not on the feature’s existing as a separate thing. This is clear from negative descriptions such as “Zayd is blind.”
