    It would also make relations into real things. If a relation existed as an independent substance, that would plainly be impossible. If it existed as a feature like whiteness, it would have to exist in a subject. But existing in a subject is itself a relation. If each relation were a separate real thing, it would need another relation to connect it to its subject, and so on without end. The chain stops if relations exist through the things from which the mind draws them, rather than as independent things.

    The same problem arises with a lack, such as blindness. If a lack existed outside the mind without the thing it was a lack of, it would stand against the positive feature as one contrary stands against another. Yet these thinkers say that lacks exist. For them, “exists” must therefore mean two things: either that something has a real thing corresponding to it, or that it has a basis from which the mind can draw it.

    The author is right that being described is a relation, but a relation can depend on existence on one side and on a nature on the other. As we explained earlier, natures are features of existences, and possibility is a feature of existence. Another scholar’s explanation of this point is weak, even though the conclusion is right.

    The sound argument is this: being described means predication, and predication means that subject and feature are one in existence. This unity is possible when one existence—the subject—supports the statement. The subject side is considered as the thing itself; the predicate side is considered as a concept. The predicate therefore does not need to exist in its own right. If it exists, it does so for some other reason. To be said of a subject, it must also be considered without restriction. So when something is described, what matters on the predicate side is only the concept; existence is required on the subject side, not the predicate side. We can see this in ordinary statements too: “Zayd is blind,” “Zayd is ignorant,” and “Zayd is possible” are all meaningful even though their predicates do not exist as separate things. — س ره

[^V01-611]: This is plainly right. A linking relation exists only together with its two terms, and both terms must exist in the setting where the link holds. A statement cannot have one side only in the mind and the other outside it, or one side real and the other merely figurative. — ط

[^V01-612]: Relations exist as links, not as independent things or as containers. Other features, such as powers and capacities, exist potentially. Potentiality has existence too, though it is weaker than actual existence and depends on it as a shadow depends on what casts it. Perhaps this explains how the two views can be brought together. — س ره

[^V01-613]: Even without the author’s main principle, these philosophers can answer the objection. Relations are drawn by the mind, but they are not imaginary fictions: they have a real basis. A relation exists through the thing from which the mind draws it, so studying relations is still studying real things. Second-order concepts are also features of real things. Universality, for example, applies to the mental idea of human being, whose nature is the same as that of human beings outside the mind.

    Things in the mind are real in their own right; they are “mental” because of their relation to the mind. Relations guide the mind and help it reach what it does not yet know, producing real effects. This answer works for those who regard logic as part of philosophy. For those who do not, there is no problem. — س ره

[^V01-614]: This is a key and very useful question, especially for understanding God’s oneness. Some thinkers regard it as self-evident; others have proved it. It is discussed in the commentary on *The Wisdom of Illumination* and in the metaphysics section of this book. So the claim that the philosophers never proved it is false. As we have seen, it is self-evident. — س ره

[^V01-615]: The proof begins by asking what “good” means. A thing is good when it is preferred to other things; that preference gives rise to desire and choice. Some things are wanted for their own sake, others for something connected to them. The things wanted for another reason ultimately lead to something wanted for its own sake. There must be a good that everything seeks and every goal leads back to. That good can only be existence: nonexistence has no reality of its own, and essence is not an independent reality. So existence is good, and since goodness belongs to existence itself, existence is good in its own right. Evil is nonexistence.

    This proves two of the chapter’s three claims: that existence is good and nonexistence evil, and that good has degrees matching the degrees of existence. The third claim—that existence can be evil in relation to something else—is explained in the next chapter. Evil in this relative sense occurs only in the material world, not in the higher world. The question of how this kind of evil enters the divine plan is taken up later. — ط

[^V01-616]: Someone may object: later, in the discussion of causes and effects, the author will say that essences have some reality. How can evil and deficiency belong to essences if evil is only nonexistence? The answer is that assigning evil to an essence does not conflict with assigning it to nonexistence. Without an essence, nonexistence could not be attributed to a possible thing. Existence cannot accept nonexistence at the same time, just as whiteness cannot accept blackness, or connection cannot accept separation. There must be something that can take either side. For colors and other changing features, that is matter; for existence and nonexistence, it is essence. — س ره

[^V01-617]: One might ask: if prime matter has no completed form of its own, and is only the capacity to receive one, how can it be what catches the heavenly souls? If the text means “by means of it,” the answer is that matter makes change possible and brings new pleasures. Without it, the elements could not become bodies ready to receive souls. Forms that belong to the world of images do not undergo that change from a lower state to a higher one, because they are free of matter. If the text means “within it,” the image is clear: the rational souls are heavenly birds held in the cages of the elements. — س ره

[^V01-618]: How can the reality of existence have a counterpart? One of its deepest consequences is that it cannot be absent. As the previous note explained, one opposite cannot be present where the other is. When one opposite enters a thing, it removes the other: blackness removes whiteness, cold removes heat, and separation removes connection. — س ره

[^V01-619]: If the opposites truly existed in relation to existence, the first problem would follow; if they could exist there only potentially, the second would follow. — س ره

[^V01-620]: They can come together in thought when we consider them apart from their opposition. This point appears again shortly. — س ره

[^V01-621]: Later, in the discussion of opposites, the author will explain that the standard definition is two positive features that take turns appearing in the same thing and differ as much as possible. If two features take turns appearing in the same thing, one cannot exist within the other. The standard account also says that opposites must belong to the same nearest kind. This rules out opposition between a substance and one of its features, since they do not belong to the same closest broad kind.

    People do sometimes say that one feature belongs to another. They mean either cases where the features do not share a nearest kind—for example, when properties specific to quantities are applied to them, or when relations are applied to other features—or cases where their nearest kind includes more than two subtypes, as when a geometrical body, a surface, and a line are described in relation to one another. The standard account also says that there can be only two opposites. The author disagrees with the standard view on most of these points. He will discuss them fully later, if God wills. — ط

[^V01-622]: Do not take the author’s claim that the mind can imagine every idea to mean that ideas such as nonexistence and absolute nonexistence have a reality of their own, which the mind discovers just as it discovers other things. That would be wrong. If they had a reality of their own, they would be essences outside the mind. As explained in earlier notes, saying that a concept is real in itself does not fit the view that existence is what is real. Saying that it is present in the Active Intellect—the higher intellect in this account—does not solve the problem of what real thing the concept refers to.

    These ideas have no reality outside the mind. The mind forms them, but does not make them into independent things; if it did, they would be things, not ideas. Rather, it forms them as ideas that point beyond themselves, as ideas of essences do. They can therefore be applied to the outside world and to what is treated as outside it. We say, for example, that Zayd exists outside the mind, or that Amr does not exist outside the mind. Since these ideas are not truly present outside the mind, the mind places them there only as assumptions. This is what the author means when he says a few lines later that such a statement is made as an unconfirmed claim, with the force of a conditional whose two sides are both false.

    Earlier, in the discussion of things existing in the mind, we showed that what produces effects by its very nature—the real existence of things—or what is by its nature devoid of effects—nonexistence—cannot enter the mind. In the first case, its effects would have to appear; in the second, there would be no effects at all. The ideas of existence and nonexistence, and the other ideas the mind forms, are therefore not drawn directly from anything established outside it. The mind forms them by making assumptions.

    To explain: the mind can give one thing the idea or feature of another. It may suppose a horse to be a rational animal, which would make it a human being. Or it may suppose a horse to be a human being, and then say it can laugh and wonder. By using this habit of attributing one thing to another, the mind can suppose one relation to be like another and form a new idea that is not taken directly from anything real outside the mind. For example, the mind can imagine something related to outside natures as light is related to something in darkness: it brings it to light, lets a searcher find it, and makes its effects appear. The mind calls this “existence.”

    The mind can also imagine something related to a nature or to existence as the removal of a thing from the place where it was, the removal of clothing from someone wearing it, or the absence of something from view. This gives it the idea of “nonexistence.” The same applies to other ideas the mind forms in this way.

    The mental act that gives rise to these ideas has two kinds of cause. The first is stable and constant: it always leads the mind to form the idea. This is the cause behind ideas such as existence, nonexistence, unity, and multiplicity, which can be established by proof. The second is temporary and depends on circumstances. It gives rise to social ideas such as leadership and being led, mastery and service, as well as metaphors and poetic images. There is much more to say; some of it will appear later, in the discussions of essence and other subjects, if God wills. — ط

[^V01-623]: From what we said in the note to the previous chapter, it may seem that the idea of nonexistence and other ideas formed by the mind are made up of parts, rather than being simple. But the author denies only that they have parts in their own definition. The earlier note means that the things these ideas apply to can have parts, not the ideas or words themselves. The same is true of what the ideas “sentence,” “speech,” “ten,” and “many” refer to. — ط

[^V01-624]: Everyone agrees that what does not exist is not a thing, and that we cannot make claims about it or point to it as a thing. That is why the author uses it as the comparison. Also, “nonexistent” has a broader meaning: it can mean nonexistence itself, or an essence that does not exist. — س ره

[^V01-625]: Do not think the author means that a person first understands the idea of absolute nonexistence, then forms each particular absence by attaching that general idea to a positive thing. The mind can form a general idea only after it has encountered particular cases to draw it from. Rather, the author means that people first become familiar with some particular absences and with nonexistence in general. If they later want to think of particular absences, they can form them by adding the relevant relation. This is like how we first see Zayd, Amr, and Bakr, then form the general idea of being human, and later distinguish tall people from short people.

    The real process is this: we notice many distinct existing people, such as Zayd and Amr, and compare them. When we focus on Amr, Zayd is no longer present in our thought. The mind mistakes not finding Zayd for finding his absence. From Amr’s presence, it forms the idea of Zayd’s absence; from Bakr’s presence, the idea of Amr’s absence. These particular absences are like separate examples. The mind then forms the general idea of nonexistence from them, as it forms a general kind from its examples. — ط

[^V01-626]: This is like numbers that can always be counted higher, not like the endless succession of events. That succession is real; it does not exist only because someone thinks about it. An absence is outside the mind only in the sense that the existence it denies would have been outside the mind. — س ره

[^V01-627]: Once we understand this, we see that everything outside the mind and in the higher and lower levels of thought is a real instance of existence. Nothing is an instance of what opposes existence in meaning, except the idea itself, which applies to itself only as an idea. If the opposite of existence did not enter reality in any way, reality would not have different forms or levels. That is why philosophers, including the author, have worked hard to study nonexistence and discover what it is. — س ره

[^V01-628]: Examples include ideas such as contradictions existing together, identical things existing together, circular cause, an endless chain of causes, emptiness, and the idea of nonexistence itself, which applies both to itself and to the absences of possible things. Forming these ideas gives nonexistence a basis as an idea and lets us understand possibility, which leaves more than one outcome open. What these ideas refer to is not an existing thing but the absence of the thing they suppose. Call it the nature, name, or example of the impossible: it exists only as impossible. Every real example must fit the nature of what it is. If it did not, the thing itself would disappear, and the claim would contradict itself. For example, if a real example of motion were fixed and unchanging, it would not be motion. The same applies here. — س ره

[^V01-629]: Here “cause” means a cause that prepares the way rather than producing an effect directly. The absences connected with events follow the same order as the events themselves, and causes among such events prepare the way for one another. This kind of preparation applies to absences that follow events, but not to absences that precede them. Earlier and later absences are not like parts of a continuous line. The later absences, considered toward the future, are endless and not ordered among themselves. The earlier absences, considered toward the past, are without a beginning and not ordered among themselves. Since these absences are described as eternal, this seems to conflict with the rule that whatever has existed from eternity cannot cease to exist. The answer is that the rule applies to things that exist and have existed from eternity. — س ره

[^V01-630]: This follows from the mind’s way of forming these ideas, as we explained earlier. The mind assumes nonexistence itself and gives it a place in thought, just as it does with essences. It then applies to it the judgments used for things that exist: it can be a kind or broader class, be said to belong to something, or be treated as an opposite. In the same way, the mind assumes the idea of existence and gives it features of essences, such as being general, applying to many things, or being said of something. — ط

[^V01-631]: The point is that the mental idea of nonexistence lets us treat it as a kind, while what the idea names lets it be treated as an opposite. More precisely, just as existence exists by itself, nonexistence does not exist in itself. The absence of nonexistence is existence itself, not a kind of nonexistence or its opposite, just as the existence of existence is existence itself. But the absence of a person, for example, is the opposite of that person, just as that person’s existence differs from them in meaning. — س ره

[^V01-632]: To say that God never reveals Himself in the same form twice is to say that each appearance is new: each day He is at work anew. This concerns the forms through which He appears. But if we consider the divine reality itself, apart from those forms, there is no repetition: it is one simple reality, with no past or future, no beginning, and no passing away. Nothing is lost and then renewed.

    Think of existence itself. Apart from the natures that receive it, existence is not a substance or feature, quality or quantity. It has no size, and so no time, no decay or coming-to-be, and no measurable parts. It does not change. Time and change belong to the material forms and natures that receive existence. This is the inner meaning of the issue; it is not limited to this world or the next. — س ره

[^V01-633]: Since there is no individual thing before or after itself, and we have explained that absences become many only when the things they are related to are many, nonexistence itself is not multiple. — س ره

[^V01-634]: By “imagination” here, the author means that the mind takes the general nature of a thing in place of its individual identity. The human nature found in Zayd can be spoken of before and after his life; Zayd himself, as this individual, cannot. But we can still speak of a thing’s earlier or later absence, because what applies to the general nature can apply more broadly than what applies to an individual. The mind expects the individual to last, then mistakes its absence for something that arrives and replaces it. It does not see that each temporal thing exists only in its own time; each has its appointed term.

    Nonexistence contradicts existence only when both apply at the same time. If a thing exists at one time and is absent at another, they are not opposites in the same respect. Its earlier or later absence does not remove an existence that was present in its own time. That existence has already excluded absence. The later and earlier absences come from the times when the thing does not exist. Each existence is a sign of the One who has no equal. Existence itself does not set or pass away; only forms and natures have a past and a future. If someone looks only at existence and ignores the forms and natures that receive it, there is no morning or evening, no coming or going. The soul is subtle: it takes on the form of whatever it attends to, whether meaning or image, idea or form. — س ره

[^V01-635]: If this is so, the coming-to-be of events is a spreading of the light of existence, while their absence is its drawing back. It is not that one thing is added to, or removed from, a fixed subject. This is a rare and subtle point, and few understand it. — ن ره

[^V01-636]: The objection is: why can’t the difference be that one time is earlier and the other later, without leading to an endless chain? The reply is that if “earlier” and “later” belong to the very nature of the two times, then the times differ in nature, contrary to the claim that they are the same. Even if time’s nature has degrees, being earlier is essential to one point in time and cannot be separated from it. If that point returned, it would still be a beginning, even while being assumed to be restored; it could not be restored as that very point. The only remaining difference is that one point is earlier and one later, which leads to an endless chain.

    The author’s objection is not answered by saying that restored time has lost its status as a beginning and is only a restoration. If restoration means that it exists in a second time, then that time needs another time, and the chain continues without end. If it means that it is later by its very nature, then it is not the same time that began in its own nature. It has not been restored as itself. — س ره

[^V01-637]: The author is referring to the idea that an individual could remain itself in a higher form of knowledge, such as God’s knowledge or the Preserved Tablet. But the commentators he criticizes have missed a point: knowledge by representation, in which an essence is present without its effects, cannot exist beyond souls—in God or in other high immaterial beings. This will be explained later. — ط

[^V01-638]: Every mental image, considered in itself, is general. Whatever details it contains, the mind can still suppose that it applies to more than one individual. The mind rules out several instances only when some further reason requires it, such as the impossibility of two exact duplicates. So if a mental image first exists outside the mind and then exists there again, the second instance is a different individual from the first, because nothing preserves its individual identity. A sensory or imagined image is individual only through its connection to something outside the mind: by sensation, or, in imagination, by both the mind’s assumption and its connection to the outside. If you picture Zayd, who has died, and set aside what you know of his past life, then look closely at the image itself, you will find that it could apply to many people. — ط

[^V01-639]: Prayer and the remembrance of God are among these practices. Justice rests on temperance, courage, generosity, and wisdom. In short, the righteous train the practical mind through religious law and spiritual practice; those brought near to God train the mind that knows. The training of the practical mind mentioned here—polishing the mirror of the reasoning soul—means cleansing it of bad actions, poor character, and the distorted opinions of the debaters. These opinions will later be named among five veils; the mystics call this kind of knowledge the greatest veil. Here the author mentions only cleansing, while elsewhere he speaks of both cleansing and adorning the soul. His aim here is to train the mind that knows directly and the practical mind indirectly. Cleansing is a negative process and can go together with gaining knowledge. Adornment is different: practicing courage or generosity, for example, can distract from gaining true knowledge of faith. — س ره

[^V01-640]: That is, by adding a feature that distinguishes the restored thing from the thing at its first beginning. The result would be that one accident had to exist in another accident. — س ره

[^V01-641]: These are accidents tied to time: when the particular time has passed, they pass as well and cannot be restored. This differs from an enduring accident, which is not bound to a particular time. — س ره

[^V01-642]: Perhaps their reason was that if an accident could be restored through a human being, it would have to be brought back by that person, since it is within human power, and not directly by God—especially on the Muʿtazilite view. Then the person would have to repeat the evil acts and sins in the next world, which is meant for reward, not action. The theologians allowed God to restore what lies within His own power. The commentator says these views would be better left out. — س ره

[^V01-643]: What his words seem to mean is that the early philosophers divided statements into different parts according to the kind of statement. A simple affirmative statement has three: subject, predicate, and judgment. It has no separate linking relation, because it says that the subject exists, not that some added feature belongs to it. A simple negative statement has only the subject and predicate; it has no affirmative judgment. It denies the judgment and removes the subject’s existence. Nothing outside the mind corresponds to that removal as a separate thing.

    A compound affirmative statement has four parts: subject, predicate, the link between them, and the judgment that affirms the link. A compound negative statement has the subject, predicate, and link, but no affirmative judgment. That is the structure of the statement itself. If we also consider its status—necessary, possible, or impossible—the early philosophers treat the status as a quality of the affirmative link. The judgment affirms that qualified link in positive statements; in negative statements, negation removes it. A necessary negative statement therefore denies that the predicate necessarily belongs to the subject; it does not affirm that the predicate necessarily does not belong to it. Otherwise, statements would not contradict one another in the right way. Contradiction is between affirming a judgment and removing that judgment, not between affirming a judgment and affirming its removal.

    Most later philosophers say that every statement, whether simple or compound, affirmative or negative, has four parts: subject, predicate, link, and judgment. They claim that negative statements have a negative link just as positive statements have an affirmative one, and that negative statements also contain a judgment. They base this on what seems to be the ordinary meaning of statements. For example, they take “A human is an animal, necessarily” and “No human is an animal, necessarily” to affirm opposite relations, rather than to deny the necessary affirmative relation.

    The early philosophers’ view is correct, but one point needs care. Judgment—what we call assent—is not a feature in a category of things, nor is it a picture in the mind. It is an act of the soul: the mind makes the subject and predicate one in its judgment. This act does not require the mind to picture a linking relation. In simple statements, it can judge by considering only the subject and predicate. Assent itself does not change between simple and compound statements; it does not sometimes require a link and sometimes not. The link is something the mind pictures alongside the statement, not a part that makes the judgment what it is.

    We can see that the mind uses the idea of a link in simple statements and negative statements too, just as it does in compound affirmative statements. But it generalizes this idea by mistake. In compound statements, the predicate exists in the subject in a dependent way, so the mind has to picture how they are connected. It then wrongly extends this to every statement. In short, an affirmative statement joins subject and predicate in its judgment; a negative statement does not. — ط مده

[^V01-644]: Words such as “connected” and “separate” are also used of negative statements by comparison with affirmative ones. A nature that has taken a step into existence reflects existence and its features. What, then, should we say of nonexistence, which is sheer denial? The realms of absence, evil, and darkness, and the world of deception, cold, heat, and other harsh conditions, are made only indirectly. They are not fundamental realities like the first forms of essences and the lower levels of possibility. — س ره

[^V01-645]: The relations in the main text are reversed. Necessary existence means that nonexistence is impossible; impossible existence means that nonexistence is necessary; possible existence means that nonexistence is possible. — س ره

[^V01-646]: In the first two cases, the definition uses a broader idea, since lasting existence is broader than necessary existence. In the third, it uses a narrower idea, since the opposite of a broader idea is narrower than the opposite of a narrower one. But the definition is only meant to explain the words, and the three statuses are clear in themselves, so this is acceptable. — س ره

[^V01-647]: “Status” here can mean the status expressed in words or the status understood by the mind, so it covers the statement as conceived. The difference between the stated status and the actual one applies only to false statements. — س ره

[^V01-648]: In the statement “No human is an animal, necessarily,” necessity describes the affirmative relation before negation is applied: “A human is necessarily an animal.” The word “not” is then applied to that claim. — س ره

[^V01-649]: That is, an exception is made from the general rule. — س ره

[^V01-650]: The author’s claim that necessary negation means that the affirmative relation is impossible seems to answer the problem. But if the three statuses are qualities of relations, as some philosophers say, the problem returns. The statuses would then be relational meanings attached to the links they modify, and impossibility would become a kind of relational nonexistence—the very idea the author rejects. This supports the earlier note: the mind imagines negation as a thing, like existence and affirmation, then gives it a status. That is one of the mind’s fictions, and it turns the statement into a different kind of claim. This may be what the author means by his reply, especially in light of the next chapter. — ط

[^V01-651]: The general unqualified statement is different. It is one of the kinds of statement with a status. When compared with another kind, they may differ without contradicting one another, since both can apply at once. The unqualified kind is narrower than possibility but broader than the other qualified kinds; a broad category and a narrower one can both apply. — س ره

[^V01-652]: The point is that a negative statement is easy to apply, and can be considered in two ways. As a denial, it does not require its subject to exist outside the mind. But as a judgment made by the mind, it does require the subject to be present in thought. So there is no case in which a negative statement is valid but an affirmative statement with a negative description is not. It is not true, as people commonly say, that a negative statement can be valid when its subject does not exist at all, while those affirmative forms cannot. The subject must be present to the mind, whether in a higher or lower level of thought. Thus the affirmative forms are valid in that same case. — س ره

[^V01-653]: This is true even if the existence is only assumed or hypothetical, as in “A partner to God is impossible.” — ن ره

[^V01-654]: We can say that what is wholly nonexistent is not a thing and has nothing, because it has no nature or reality that could have something affirmed of it. We can deny its own identity and features, even nonexistence or impossibility. This is why it is possible to deny something of itself while it is absent. If you object that denying nonexistence of what does not exist would mean it exists, you are mixing two meanings of “is.” Denying nonexistence and affirming existence are different claims. Even if existence follows, it follows because reality cannot be empty of both sides of a contradiction, not because denial itself produces existence. In fact, what does not exist has neither existence nor nonexistence, neither possibility nor impossibility: there is no thing here for any of these to belong to. — س ره

[^V01-655]: The word “also” is misplaced here. As written, it suggests that an affirmative statement does not require its subject to exist except because of the link between subject and predicate. That conflicts with the author’s earlier point. The word should go with the following clause. — س ره

[^V01-656]: “In reality” is one of the philosophers’ ways of speaking about what is true in itself. The commentator will later question whether ideas that exist only as knowledge in the mind can exist above the level of souls. — ط

[^V01-657]: In a statement such as “All G is B,” the subject means every thing that is found and described as G. A statement about a kind as a whole does not make a claim about each individual example in the same way; a statement about one particular thing has that thing itself as its subject. — س ره

[^V01-658]: Since the “logical universal” does not fit here, the universal referred to by G is the idea as understood by the mind. G itself names the shared nature, not its realization in any particular thing. This makes the distinction work. — س ره

[^V01-659]: A “non-substance” taken as absolute nothing cannot be the subject of an affirmative statement, since it does not exist. So an affirmative claim such as “Every non-substance is non-animal” cannot become true just because its subject is absent. A negative statement, by contrast, can be true when the subject itself does not exist. — س ره

[^V01-660]: Some copies read “in statements with a negative predicate.”

[^V01-661]: The better reading, as in *Al-Ufuq al-Mubin*, is “in an affirmative statement with a negative predicate,” not “in negative statements.” The author discussed this point earlier in the section on possibility. — س ره

[^V01-662]: This grouping is not sound. A statement with a negative predicate may first deny a link, and in that respect it does not require the subject to exist. But it then makes a second link—a link that says the denial applies to the subject—and that does require the subject to exist. — س ره

[^V01-663]: The first distinction is about how many things two ideas apply to, or whether they apply to the same number; examples include life and speech, or humanity and speech. The second is about how two descriptions are related in a statement, as with “animal” and “rational,” or “human” and “rational.” The reply means that a claim such as “Everything that is no thing is not broadly possible” can be made affirmatively if the idea is present, even if only as something the mind supposes. The mind can form a positive statement that denies a description, or denies the subject, or denies both. The negative statement is broader only in the way the mind considers its subject. — س ره

[^V01-664]: The two cases are: one side or the other must be true—existence or nonexistence—or neither side must be true. These cases cannot both apply, and one of them must apply, because existence and nonexistence are opposites. But *Al-Ufuq al-Mubin* reports a different account: the two cases cannot both fail, though they may both apply. On that account, one case is that nonexistence is not necessary, as with the Necessary Being; the other is that existence is not necessary, as with what is impossible. Both can apply to something possible in the strict sense. The author’s wording here, that denying broad possibility falls outside the two opposite sides, is clearer than the wording in that other book. — س ره

[^V01-665]: This is what the copies of *The Four Journeys* say. The correct reading, found in *Al-Ufuq al-Mubin*, is “what is not broadly possible is nothing,” and the same correction applies to the next phrase. — س ره

[^V01-666]: The point is that “broader” and “narrower” refer to how many things an idea can cover, not to what can be said of a subject in a statement. The word “with” appears in both cases, which confirms this reading. — س ره

[^V01-667]: Here “most people” means most logicians, in contrast with the earlier philosopher. The commentator explained the different meanings of possibility in an earlier section. — س ره

[^V01-668]: If “impossible” means that one side is necessary without any further condition, then something necessary on both sides would also count as impossible. That would conflict with the claim that every impossible thing lacks necessity on its unrealized side. But if “impossible” means that one side is necessary without regard to whether the other side is necessary too, then the claim applies to every impossible thing, including one necessary on both sides. — س ره

[^V01-669]: An existence that is in the timeless realm, or is a self-disclosure of God, or belongs to His unchanging knowledge, cannot be removed. “What you have will come to an end, but what God has will remain.” God’s storehouses never diminish. This point appeared earlier in the discussion of why a nonexistent thing cannot be restored and in the discussion of possibility. — س ره

[^V01-670]: Someone may ask how there can be a combination if nonexistence is sheer nothing. That question misses the point: a combination requires two kinds, and what could be farther from existence than nonexistence? A combination involves existence and absence, having and lacking. Where there is only existence, as in “existence and existence,” the shared reality remains one, so multiplicity disappears in some sense. In the end, multiplicity comes back to existence and absence; even an essence refers to absence. This is all that is meant by saying that the simple reality contains all things that exist. The point will be explained more plainly later. — س ره

[^V01-671]: This principle says that all existence is gathered in one, even while there is multiplicity within that unity. It also implies unity within multiplicity: existing things are flows from divine existence. There must be a shared nature between God and what comes from Him. He gives existence because He has it; He is its source, its beginning, and its end. — س ره

[^V01-672]: The reply is flawed because it repeats the claim that whatever has no earlier temporal absence is independent of a cause. If they mean only that time does not need a cause for one aspect of its existence, while its basic existence still depends on a cause, that does not make it necessary in itself. — ط

[^V01-673]: This brings back the earlier problem: making absence necessary seems to create a negative relation between absence and its subject, which the author has rejected. — ط

[^V01-674]: “Seeking” includes both natural tendencies and deliberate choices, so it covers the different kinds of motion. A thing’s capacity to seek something is not itself a separate thing. The author will also say later that motion is a process of change, not an independent thing; what exists is what is changing. The same is true of existence: it is the being and reality of an essence, not another thing added to it. If we consider existence on its own, apart from that essence, it is simply one of the ideas we can think about. — س ره

[^V01-675]: Indeed, what depends on another cannot be impossible in itself. Whatever is caused is possible in itself. Anything made necessary or impossible by another is possible in itself. The author phrases it this way because he is answering an objection about something impossible in itself. His deeper answer is that impossibility in itself belongs to the impossible thing through its own nature; it does not come from a separate quality or from a dependence assumed only for the argument. — س ره

[^V01-676]: The words “just as there is no entailment” appear in the copies we have seen, but they are probably an addition, since the same point has already been made. — س ره

[^V01-677]: The point is that something real does not entail something opposed to it in reality. In these proofs, the opposing claims are only supposed by the mind. Two opposed ideas held together in thought are possible, as the author says. Also, one of the opposing claims, when combined with other conditions, may lead to the other. — س ره

[^V01-678]: Some copies add the phrase “because the conclusion is not the name of anything that exists among possible things.”

[^V01-679]: This wording includes both what is necessary in itself and what is possible in the strict sense. — س ره

[^V01-680]: If “simple” means not made up of external parts, that does not mean a thing cannot be defined. A definition may use conceptual parts, and that does not conflict with the thing’s being simple in the world. Accidents, for example, are simple in the world but can still be defined. If “simple” means simple in every sense, that claim is denied. — س ره

[^V01-681]: In the second case, the writer also fails to distinguish between a judgment applying directly and one applying only indirectly, and assumes that it carries over in every case. The author’s point is twofold: he rejects the inference in the proof, and he points out a contradiction in the claim that simple things can only be described through their properties. If those simple things are known through their aspects—that is, their properties—then the simple things themselves are what define them. Their properties are only the means by which we consider them. — س ره

[^V01-682]: The commentator explains why the author lists these ways of knowing separately. Knowing by definition can give a full grasp of a thing’s nature, and direct awareness can also be complete. The first contrast is with direct awareness; the second is with description. “Not by its full nature” means not through a matching mental representation, as in acquired knowledge, but through direct and immediate awareness, without first learning the thing’s parts as one does in a definition. “Not by definition” means not through a broader kind and a distinguishing feature, but through properties and what follows from the thing. “Not by its full nature” can also mean not through complete direct awareness; “but through direct awareness” can mean at least partial immediate awareness. The soul, for example, is directly aware of itself both when fully developed and when still limited. — س ره

[^V01-683]: It should be clear that things made of parts can be known both through their definitions and through descriptions. Al-Razi himself accepts both methods. Al-Razi uses both methods to challenge the opposing view; he does not say that we know composites only by knowing all their parts. The author reads al-Razi as saying that composites cannot be known by description either. If so, knowledge of their parts would be the only route, and the contradiction would follow. — س ره

[^V01-684]: The indefinite wording “one aspect” points to further questions. Saying that real existence cannot be known could mislead readers: real existence is the subject of the highest science, so how could it be unknowable? There are three kinds of knowledge of real existence. First is acquired knowledge of existing natures as they exist; through the mental forms by which we consider them, we learn about the different kinds of real existence. This is why definitions correspond to levels of existence. Second, also acquired, is knowledge of existence in general through universal descriptions that truly apply to it: that it is what the general idea of existence refers to, true unity, identity, light, life, will, love, knowledge, awareness, and the like. Third is direct awareness of existence, which has two forms. One is the soul’s direct awareness of itself, which does not fully encompass it; since the soul is a real existence, this gives a general awareness of existence. The other is the direct awareness of the reality of existence by souls turned toward God: the awareness of one who is absorbed in what is known. What the Shaykh says, even if read as a statement about existence, needs more explanation. This is turning into a long sermon; there will be time for it. — س ره

[^V01-685]: The Shaykh’s statement is true in part, but should be limited to complete, detailed knowledge through definition. Otherwise, the claim that things have a mental existence means that we do know their natures in some way, since the same natures are present in both mental and external existence. Denying that knowledge is possible would amount to denying knowledge altogether. A sound account of knowledge requires us to say that we know the natures of things to some degree, as a little reflection shows. With God’s help, we will return to this in our discussions of essence and knowledge. — ط

[^V01-686]: Once we distinguish knowing a thing in one respect from knowing it through one of its aspects, the examples become clear. If we know a substance as something that, when it exists in the world, is not in a subject, then we know it through that property; how can it still be unknown? Likewise, if we define a body as a substance in which three intersecting dimensions can be conceived, then we know what a body is, since that possibility is the starting point of its form. We also understand “substance” in the specific sense used in that definition. The same applies to the other examples. Since Avicenna’s words, taken literally, would be false and would conflict with his own books, the author explains what Avicenna meant. Even on the view that existence is fundamental and essence is a mental consideration—a view Avicenna also accepts—whatever the intellect uses to represent an essence, its constitutive grounds, and its first position belongs to that essence and expresses its reality. So there is no problem in knowing the thinghood of an essence, and no need to overturn the many principles that would otherwise be affected. — س ره

[^V01-687]: This refers to the discussion of whether simple things can be known. The statement that Avicenna’s words are almost direct evidence for the author’s view refers to Avicenna’s claim that human beings cannot grasp the true natures of things. — س ره

[^V01-688]: “Possible for something else” here means possible to exist in something else in the strict sense. The next division distinguishes things whose own possibility is enough for them to come from their cause from those that need further conditions. Things that must exist in something else—forms in matter and accidents in a subject—are not possible in it in the strict sense, though they are in a broader sense. A garment or a book may belong to Zayd in the strict sense. So there is no contradiction in saying that forms and accidents must exist in something else while the strict kind of possibility remains distinct. The phrase means the ability to be present in, or depend on, something else. Independent substances cannot do this, even though their existence in themselves is the very existence they receive from their cause. — س ره

[^V01-689]: The Necessary Existent is therefore the cause of all things. Every great or small thing, universal or particular, depends on it. All things and their first principles are aspects of it, and existence submits to the Living, the Self-Sustaining. — س ره

[^V01-690]: In the chain of causes, this difference is a difference in possibility itself; in the chain of things receiving existence, it is a difference in their readiness to receive it. — س ره

[^V01-691]: This explains how things can receive existence earlier or later in the chain of causes even when no readiness for existence is involved. Their essential possibility differs indirectly because their actual existences differ. Earlier and later belong to those existences; possibility itself is an abstract idea and cannot vary in degree. This is what the author means when he says he will return to the question later. — س ره

[^V01-692]: The author means that these two kinds of possibility share a meaning in ordinary language. In technical use, their effects and rules differ, so readiness to receive existence must be treated as another meaning of possibility, as the other view says. — ط

[^V01-693]: In his discussion of readiness to receive existence, the author lists many differences between it and possibility in itself, beyond the difference in what they apply to. The opening of this commentary also noted differences in the author’s wording and how to bring those statements together. — س ره

[^V01-694]: This follows from change in the very being of a thing. What changes in its very being is form alone; in one respect, it is the flowing present, which underlies renewal and change in the next world. — ن ره

[^V01-695]: The first phrase continues a new statement. Put another way, simple making takes one object, as in the Qur'anic phrase “Maker of darkness and light”; compound making takes two. Simple making brings about existence by itself—the claim “it is.” Compound making brings about existence as a relation—the claim “it is such-and-such.” The fact that making has these two forms, just as existence does, points to existence as what is made. — س ره

[^V01-696]: The relation here is external. It is like the relation in the mind when we judge a statement: if we attended to the relation itself as the main thing, we would not be making a judgment; we would only be thinking about the relation. — س ره

[^V01-697]: This too is a kind of making, but a mental one, and the mind is its maker. This is the point behind the statement that forming an idea brings the thing itself into the mind. — س ره

[^V01-698]: That is, bringing about the nature of the thing itself through simple making, as the Illuminationists hold. — س ره

[^V01-699]: Do not take the view held by Aristotle’s followers—that a thing’s nature is not made, but its existence is—to mean that the nature’s essential parts can exist apart from existence, or that the thing’s basic reality is unmade because it stands on its own from eternity. This misunderstanding led al-Lahiji to say that natures are made. Once this is set aside, there is no problem in saying that existence is what is made, as explained above. For the Aristotle’s followers, existence comes before nature, as al-Tusi says, and nature is outside the act of making because it is an idea the mind considers. Yet nature is made indirectly, so this relation too would need a maker and would be made by it, though through an intermediary. The answer is that this need is only indirect. — س ره

[^V01-700]: The commentator says the sentence would be clearer if “itself” and “that same” were removed, so it read: “nor by simple making directed at the essential features and necessary qualities.” This would avoid conflict with the later claim that simple making first applies to essential parts. “That same simple act” might mean several acts, each directed at a different thing, as explained earlier. The author rejects this reading because he recognizes one act as primary; the other acts are only indirect. The author’s point is to deny that essential features are made by compound making: a human being is human and an animal by its own nature, not through compound making and not because a maker separately makes its nature. Otherwise, a human being would be human because of a cause, not through itself. — س ره

[^V01-701]: This answers a possible objection: someone might say that we can deny a thing of itself when it does not exist, because a negative statement can be true even when its subject is absent. Since truth and possibility require two terms, if one term is possible, then the other—the thing’s being itself—must also be possible. And if it is possible, and possibility is what makes something need a cause, then it must be made. This would differ from eternal necessity, to which no denial can apply.

    The reply is that even if the possible denial of a thing of itself entails that it is itself, and this possibility requires making the thing’s nature according to the Illuminationists or its existence according to Aristotle’s followers, that does not mean the maker acts on it directly. The dependence may be indirect. The possibility of denying a thing of itself removes eternal necessity, not the necessity that belongs to its own nature; that necessity also removes the need for a cause. So when the author says “no need,” he means no direct need.

    There is a clearer answer. The possible denial applies only when the thing does not exist, and that is a contradiction: a positive statement requires its subject to exist. The argument also proves less than it claims. And the claim “if a thing can be denied of itself when absent, then it can be affirmed of itself in every case” is not a valid inference. It is also wrong to allow this denial in the argument that a thing’s being described needs a maker. “The nonexistent human being is not human” amounts to “what is nonexistent is not human.” The truth is that a thing cannot be denied of itself in any case. Just as existence is distinct from a thing’s nature, so is nonexistence. Once we take the subject to be a human being through its nature, even without its existing in the world, how could we deny its nature of itself? And if we have not conceived any thing at all, how could we identify it as human? Avicenna says, in his discussion of whether the Necessary Existent’s nature is its existence, that whatever nature we suppose is that nature, whether we suppose it to exist or not. — س ره

[^V01-702]: The argument can be challenged this way: if it were sound, it would also show that a thing’s nature cannot be caused. Suppose Zayd comes into existence after not existing. If this does not depend on a condition, then, by the argument above, his existence would continue forever. If it does depend on a condition, and what depends on that condition is his nature, then Amr could also come into existence when Zayd does, since the condition is present and like cases should be treated alike. This does not work for things of different kinds, but even that limited result is enough to refute the argument. — س ره

[^V01-703]: That is, although existence differs according to the natures it belongs to, it remains one reality and is the source of their multiplicity and difference. — س ره

[^V01-704]: The author takes “recipient” in the argument he is discussing to mean a recipient outside the mind, as matter usually is, and raises an objection on that basis. But there is no problem using the word “recipient” even if one holds that existence is primary: a conceptual recipient is also something. A nature could also be called a recipient insofar as it is established in God’s knowledge, as in some Sufi or Mu‘tazilite accounts, where natures exist in higher and lower minds. In that sense, it is reasonable to call a nature a recipient. — س ره

[^V01-705]: What is made directly must be fit to bear the predicate “existent” after it has been made. Natures do not meet this condition. Even if a nature were made, it could bear only the familiar, attributed sense of “existent,” not real existence, since existence does not become identical with the nature or one of its parts. This is a sound point, but it does not prove that the relation of being existent is what is made: that relation is also only a mental consideration. It follows that existence is what is made, and is primary both in making and in reality. Apart from the first argument, these arguments are incomplete. The speaker wants to prove that the relation of being existent is made, but that does not follow simply from disproving that the nature is made. The other two views must also be ruled out, and he has not ruled out the view that existence is made, which is in fact the strongest one. It is telling that the opponent never even argues against it: “They seek to extinguish God’s light with their mouths, but God will bring His light to completion.” — س ره

[^V01-706]: What is made must be something that can truly be called “itself.” This argument is different from the second one: that argument proceeds from existence, while this one proceeds from distinct identity. — س ره

[^V01-707]: In al-Tabarsi’s *Majma‘ al-Bayan*, this prayer is attributed to ‘Ali, though without the words “O who is He.” Sayyid al-Damad used the full wording to open his *Book of Sanctifications*. — س ره

[^V01-708]: The first argument would make sense if “possibility” meant that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary, or that the two are equal, and if this possibility were only a step in proving the need for a cause. It would not, however, establish the conclusion the speaker wants. The argument also works if “possibility” means what the author calls the particular contingent existences, and “causation” means that these existences do not cause themselves: they are intrinsically dependent on God, and what is essential is not caused.

    But if “possibility” means either of the first two things, and “causation” means the real source of need, the argument does not work. Possibility in that sense exists only in the mind, so it would make a possible thing dependent only in the mind. The basis of need would also need a cause, since a cause stands to its effect as the complete stands to the incomplete; this would make the basis itself possible through another, which is false. One could avoid this only by saying that possibility is neither a mental step nor the real source of need, but something like the sun’s relation to the heat of water. The thing that truly needs a cause must also be what the cause is needed for. From this, a discerning reader can see that existence is what is made: it is what needs a cause, indeed it is need and relation itself.

    The saying that “possibility is what makes a thing need a cause” also shows that a nature is not made directly. What is made directly must be intrinsically dependent; if a nature were intrinsically dependent, it would not need a separate cause of its need, since what belongs to a thing essentially is not caused. The thing that needs a cause must be the thing that needs it in reality. If you need someone to build a house, it is you—or the house—that needs the builder, not your nature as such. Everyone agrees that a nature needs an agent in order to exist. So existence is what needs the agent and is made directly; possibility is how the mind sees that need, and nature is how it sees what has been made. In reality, when existence is what is made, the thing that needs a cause, the basis of need, and what needs the cause are one. — س ره

[^V01-709]: In short, a thing’s essential features can be predicated of its nature without a limiting condition or a causal condition; existence can be predicated without a limiting condition but does require a causal one. Existence is predicated of God without anything at all—not even a condition of time. — س ره

[^V01-710]: Not yet having been made is different from being free of the need for a maker, as the author will explain later. Those who hold that existence is primary in both making and reality do not let a nature stand apart from existence, as the Mu‘tazilites do. For them, dependence reaches into the very constitution of a contingent thing; its nature has only a derivative, shadow-like standing because it is considered after existence. “They are only names you and your forefathers have given them, for which God has sent down no authority.” — س ره

[^V01-711]: After a thing has been brought about, existence does not become identical with or a part of its nature. Describing the nature as existent is then like describing something as related to something else in the ordinary, familiar sense. — س ره

[^V01-712]: The argument also implies that the nature would turn into existence. — س ره

[^V01-713]: If the relation to the maker were an ordinary relation between things, it could not make “existent” truly apply, because such a relation is only a mental consideration. Before it is made, a nature considered in itself and apart from its relation to its maker is also only a mental consideration. Adding one mental consideration to another cannot establish reality. But if the relation is an illuminating relation, it is real existence itself. Existence is then primary in making and reality, and nature is an idea drawn from it, as the sound view holds. — س ره

[^V01-714]: The author says “some” to exclude natures defined by their relation to something else. He uses “maker” as a hidden example within the broad class of “other things,” including existence, which is closer to a nature than anything else and cannot be separated from it even in thought. It is as if he said that we can think of a nature without thinking of its existence, its being made existent, or its maker. A particular existence, however, depends on all-pervading existence—the maker’s light, presence, and active support. In one respect, the relation of particular existences to this all-pervading existence is like the relation of a nature’s essential parts to the nature. — س ره

[^V01-715]: This does not mean that a nature is universal in itself. It means that its own nature allows the mind to consider it as universal. If it were already particular in itself, it could not be considered universal. — س ره

[^V01-716]: One might ask: if existence is an idea drawn by the mind, how can it make something particular? The answer is that some say particularity is part of how the mind analyses a nature. A thing’s particular identity is its own “thisness,” not something added to it. It becomes particular through its existence, and its existence through its relation to its maker. — س ره

[^V01-717]: The general nature, whether considered as one individual or as one of many possible instances, has the same relation to its maker. The maker must therefore determine it as one particular thing before bringing it about. This applies when a nature has only one possible instance. Otherwise, its particularity must also depend on differences in matter and readiness. — ن ره

[^V01-718]: The commentator takes the question to mean that the maker causes the thing’s particularity. He does not consider another possible meaning: that the thing becomes particular through its relation to the maker, as some mystics hold. But the maker’s relation to itself cannot make something else particular. The author’s point can also be read this way: a thing can be particular through its maker only if existence is what is made, since existence depends on its maker while a nature can be considered apart from it. — س ره

[^V01-719]: A nature’s necessary result follows from existence, since, in the view of these thinkers, God has no nature apart from existence. A necessary feature of a nature is only a mental idea, because it follows from the nature when we consider it apart from its necessity and its maker. The nature, considered in this way, is itself only an idea. — س ره

[^V01-720]: Suhrawardi says that light is one reality, though some instances exist by themselves and others belong to a subject. Why could existence not work the same way, with some instances—God, the intelligences, and souls—existing by themselves, while others belong to a nature? This seems the best way to understand him. His earlier arguments show that existence cannot be an outside feature added to a nature; they do not show that one instance of a single reality cannot exist by itself while another depends on something else. Nor do they show that existence cannot belong to one nature when it cannot belong to that same nature considered in itself. — س ره

[^V01-721]: Being real is part of what existence is, so it cannot become merely mental. — س ره

[^V01-722]: The point is to show that existence is what is made, and that natures are not. The first argument was that what is made directly must itself be a relation of dependence. This is true of particular existence. It also shows that made things cannot be mere necessary features of natures, since such features remain even when we ignore their maker. But if what is made is existence, it is itself a relation and cannot be separated from its maker. The second argument is that, if everything except the first made thing were a necessary feature of a nature, it would be only a mental idea. The author’s aim is to show that the maker’s effects are not such features. — س ره

[^V01-723]: Since real bringing-about is existence related to God, and true making is existence, the two descriptions point to the same thing. “Equal” here means that neither existence nor nonexistence is prior. Those who allow priority explain possibility as the possibility of either side. The definition by denying necessity, as used in logic, is more exact. However one defines it, this possibility does not apply to particular existence. — س ره

[^V01-724]: A nature can be conceived apart from its existence, which in one sense is its own being, let alone apart from its being made or from its maker. It is empty of everything but itself. — س ره

[^V01-725]: If what is made is existence, what do you think the maker must be? If even existence in general is the basis of causation, then all the more is this true of pure existence—the Necessary Being, beyond every limit of completeness. He alone is the true maker, as the author says. — س ره

[^V01-726]: The source appears to mean “the Second Teacher,” al-Farabi. A copyist may have changed the wording. — س ره

[^V01-727]: Some copies read “compound predication” here instead of “compound statement.”

[^V01-728]: Some copies read “the compound existential predication” here.

[^V01-729]: For this thinker, what is made is the existent thing, not existence itself, since he recognizes no individual instance of existence, either in the mind or outside it. His view comes close to the truth. It differs from that of his contemporary, the scholar al-Dawani: al-Dawani says that a nature is made simply as that nature, while this thinker says it is made insofar as it exists. — س ره

[^V01-730]: If he means that people do not say this in ordinary speech, that settles nothing; philosophical truths are not decided by common usage. If he means that no one says blackness comes from an agent through a compound act of making, who would deny that? But that does not prove his point. If he means that reason does not say blackness comes from an agent through simple making—that blackness itself issues from the agent—then that is false. Many thinkers have held this view. — س ره

[^V01-731]: Every passage quoted from Bahmanyar shows how deeply he understood these questions, how sound his reasoning was, and how thoroughly he had studied philosophy. The student reflects the teacher; like master, like pupil. — س ره

[^V01-732]: Perhaps the author thought Bahmanyar meant that composite natures are made while simple natures are not. Al-Tusi seems to make this point in *The Abstract of Belief*: “Just as a composite needs a maker, so does a simple thing.” The author may be clarifying what Bahmanyar meant. — س ره

[^V01-733]: That is, natures help explain why existences differ, while existences are what make the differences real. So there is no circular argument. — س ره

[^V01-734]: One might object: if each nature is an independent cause, two independent causes would converge on one effect; if the group of them is the cause, then the differences would not belong to the natures themselves. The author points to two ways of explaining the differences. On the first, because natures are ideas, their differences in reality follow from differences among existences, and the differences among existences belong to them in themselves. In that case, “substance is substance by itself” refers to existent substance, and “accident is accident by itself” to existent accident. On the second account, the differences among existences as known by the mind follow from differences among natures, and those differences belong to the natures themselves. Here, “substance is substance by itself” refers to the nature of substance, and “accident is accident by itself” to the nature of accident. A further account says that the natures in this world reflect differences in earlier forms and realms of knowledge, and that those earlier differences reflect the meanings of God’s names and attributes. Those meanings are unmade without God’s essence being unmade. One may also understand “substance is substance by itself” to mean that a thing’s being itself is necessary and needs no cause. This denies compound making, not simple making, as Bahmanyar’s words already suggest. — س ره

[^V01-735]: This means restricting or conditioning the act of making, whether by what is best, by the time of the act, or by some other limit proposed by those who say the flow of existence can stop. — س ره

[^V01-736]: His manifestation is His appearance. The appearance of a thing cannot be separate from it; otherwise it would not be that thing’s appearance. — س ره

[^V01-737]: This is drawn from a saying of the leader of the saints and guide of the pure, Ali. Asked about the higher world, he said: “Forms without matter, free of potentiality and readiness: He appeared to them, and they shone; He looked upon them, and they gleamed; He cast His image into their reality and brought His acts forth through them.” — س ره

[^V01-738]: This phrase belongs with what comes before “be careful”; it is unrelated to what follows. — س ره

[^V01-739]: The author relies on observation because most of his arguments follow the path of studying natures. In philosophical questions like this, someone who follows the path of existence has more room to argue. Existence is a real reality with different levels of strength and weakness. A weaker existence depends on and is constituted by a stronger one. This is possible only if the effect—the weaker level—is a form or unfolding of the stronger level. In other words, the effect must be an image of its cause and a shadow that follows it in existence. — ط

[^V01-740]: That is, every caused thing that has a nature, as discussed in *The Book of Contemplations*. — س ره

[^V01-741]: The “mixture” with darkness is judged with help from the imagination. Strictly speaking, darkness is the absence of light; it is not mixed with light. In any case, the account given by this discerning mystic is subtle, clear, and healing. May God guide us to the right path. — س ره

[^V01-742]: Perhaps the point is to understand the difference between the two kinds of composition. The differences between the two senses of possibility have already been discussed. The author often writes this way; the point is clear enough. — س ره

[^V01-743]: That is, whether the thing exists or does not exist absolutely, as in a simple existential judgment, or exists or does not exist under a condition, as in a predicative judgment. Assenting that fire exists causes assent that heat exists; assenting that heat does not exist causes assent that fire does not exist. Merely conceiving fire or heat does not do this, since a nature remains what it is whether considered existent or nonexistent. The same applies when assenting that the world changes leads to assent that it came into being. Al-Dawani’s objection therefore misses the point. Mental existence of a simple idea does not by itself cause assent to absolute or conditional existence or nonexistence, just as it does not do so in false judgments generally. — س ره

[^V01-744]: That is, the first principles include the truth that affirmation and denial cannot both be true and cannot both be false. Ibn Sina says something similar in *The Healing*, in a chapter on truth and the defense of first principles: “The first of all true statements, to which every analysis leads, is the principle that there is no middle ground between affirmation and denial.” — س ره

[^V01-745]: That is, the kind of dependence in which both the thing that depends and what it depends on belong to the same realm of meaning or nature. The phrase “especially a definition” is therefore well chosen. — س ره

[^V01-746]: As he often says, he follows the philosophers’ approach in the starting points, then parts ways with them in the conclusions. They limit growth and decline in intensity to qualities, and increase and decrease to quantities. This will be explained later, God willing. — س ره

[^V01-747]: The argument also implies that blackness would be made up of parts, even though accidents are simple things in the world outside the mind. — س ره

[^V01-748]: This means that matter may move through substantial forms, even if a nature itself cannot move in existence. — س ره

[^V01-749]: Some copies read “successive instants” here.

[^V01-750]: Someone might object that a void follows only when a thing that can occupy a place is missing from that place, not when a place is missing from a thing. The author does not say that a void follows if a moving thing has no place; he says it follows if the thing has no “where”—a state of the thing that involves a relation to a place. So the argument stands. That is, those imagined instants have no extension or parts. If they did, they would set the measure of motion, and motion would then occur within motion. — س ره

[^V01-751]: The more precise reading may be “instances,” as in the phrase “one temporal instance” that follows. — س ره

[^V01-752]: That is, an instance that exists in reality, not merely a nature or idea. Some thinkers say that motion, taken as a whole, is identical with this one connected temporal instance. This is supported by a later explanation: motion is a thing’s continual renewal, but renewal itself is not a separate thing; it is a relation. What exists is the category in which the renewal takes place. This is like the view that a thing’s existence is its being or coming to be: neither is a separate thing, and neither can be divided in the usual way. — س ره

[^V01-753]: The temporal instance is actual in the way temporal things are: it is neither pure possibility nor complete actuality, like something unchanging. As long as the process continues without a pause, it is one temporal instance, and its continuity gives it the unity of one thing. Al-Dawani’s account of the intermediate state could be understood this way. The author does not read him that way because he thinks al-Dawani means the moving subject never takes on any instance of the category during motion. That was not his meaning: by the intermediate state, he meant an instance that is neither pure possibility nor complete actuality, like motion itself. The “instances” here are the momentary points and temporal parts imagined as divisions, as the author explains. — س ره

[^V01-754]: This refers to the author’s argument that existence itself does not move, and that the moving thing would not remain actual if existence did move. — س ره

[^V01-755]: This question was first raised in logic, in discussions of universals and particulars. A universal may be univocal, applying in the same way to all its instances, or gradable, applying with differences of degree. Since universality is treated as a feature of essence, the discussion of gradation began with essences: philosophers had observed that things in the world differ in intensity and degree. Later, relying on Avicenna’s argument, they said that essential concepts do not vary by degree, only accidental ones. Their reasoning was that an accident has no real counterpart by itself: what exists is the subject and its accident. A derived term such as “black,” formed from blackness as it exists in a body, does not have a separate counterpart in reality, so it can vary. The difference between an accident and a derived accidental term is difficult to grasp, even though neither concept changes in meaning. On this basis, they said that two distinct essences differ either in their whole nature, in part of it, or through something outside it. The author broadens the account to include differences in existence or in thought, so it can also include degrees of existence. — ط

[^V01-756]: The fourth kind is so subtle and important that I doubt you noticed it. Yet it is a sound and solid view. — س ره

[^V01-757]: By continuing with “rather,” the author points to another flaw: the Aristotle’s followers deny the link that their argument assumes. Even if the more complete instance contains something the less complete one does not, it does not follow that the two share nothing essential. What distinguishes them may be the very feature they share, as happens with existence. — س ره

[^V01-758]: This is another Illuminationist argument against the Aristotle’s followers. If two instances of blackness differed through defining features, and a defining feature were outside the essence of the broader kind, then their difference would lie beyond blackness. But we experience the difference as a difference in blackness itself. The Illuminationists conclude that the two instances differ in themselves, not through a defining feature. — س ره

[^V01-759]: The universal nature of blackness itself does not vary; the difference is said to lie at the level of the individual.

[^V01-760]: Do not take this to mean that the concept or essence of blackness itself varies. Here “blackness” means the reality of an individual instance: broader kind and defining feature come together only in the individual. — ن ره

[^V01-761]: This is only an appeal to what seems implausible; it is not a sound basis for deciding what is true. — ط

[^V01-762]: The author attributes this argument in *al-Taqdīsāt* to earlier philosophers, including Avicenna in *The Healing* and others of his school. — س ره

[^V01-763]: The argument is quoted from Avicenna, but the author’s reply does not work. Gradation—difference within sameness—requires one thing to be predicated of another while some of its instances are excluded from others under that same predication. If gradation occurred at the level of essence, where only basic definitional predication applies, there would have to be at least two concepts, each predicated of the other in that basic way and excluded from it in the same way. A fixed concept cannot support this. — ط

[^V01-764]: As the later discussions of knowledge, power, will, good, and purpose will show, there is another kind of difference between two things. It does not fit the rule for gradation given here, nor any of the three kinds of difference listed at the start of the chapter: difference in the whole essence, in part of it, or through something outside it. Knowledge and power, for example, differ, yet each is identified with existence itself. The same is true of other realities called “existential attributes.” Their difference is not a matter of one having more than the other: knowledge is not greater than power. Nor do they differ as two essences, since they are not separate kinds of essence. But the truth is that the broader idea of difference within one reality—where what distinguishes its instances is also what they share—covers more than the rule stated here. Not every difference within a thing’s own reality, without anything added to it, is a difference that can be expressed as “more” or “less.” The philosophers should have discussed this kind of gradation separately, as they did mental and external existence, possibility and necessity, and potentiality and actuality.

    The familiar kind of gradation, by degrees of excellence, requires two simple instances of one reality: the stronger includes all the perfection of the weaker and something more, while the weaker does not include all the stronger has. The weaker is intrinsically related to the stronger, though this is not a relation in the technical category of relation. The mind also sees the weaker as lacking the perfection found in the stronger, even though existence itself excludes nonexistence. This comparison is between two levels at a time. With three levels—weak, intermediate, and strong—there are two comparisons: weak to intermediate, and intermediate to strong. The intermediate is strong relative to the weak and weak relative to the strong. Treating all three as one comparison would require one relation to hold among more than two levels, and would make the middle level contain the shared reality with no increase or decrease.
