That would conflict with the assumed difference between what the levels share and what distinguishes them. So calling the levels “weak,” “intermediate,” and “strong” is not entirely precise. — ط

[^V01-765]: There are two cases to consider. One is a thing changing through stronger or weaker states as it moves from one kind to another—for example, from white to yellow, or from yellow to green. This is different from a weaker green becoming a stronger green. The other case is when stronger and weaker levels exist at the same time in separate things. This second case is clearer, because the levels differ both in how we understand them and in how they exist. — س ره

[^V01-766]: Some who follow Aristotle’s school allow existence to have stronger and weaker degrees, but do not allow existence itself to grow stronger or weaker through change. — س ره

[^V01-767]: This means that the levels are made individual by their own simple identities, while sharing one reality; what distinguishes them is also what they share. This can reconcile the two views. Those who say essential features can vary by degree mean “essential” as existence, the basis of a thing’s reality. Those who deny gradation in essence but allow it in what is accidental to essence mean “essence” as what a thing is, and treat existence as something added to it. — س ره

[^V01-768]: The objector is Sayyid Dāmād, in *al-Taqdīsāt*. — س ره

[^V01-769]: The same explanation would not work for imagined quantities that differ in length, since they have no matter whose readiness could account for the difference—unless one denies that the imaginal world exists. — س ره

[^V01-770]: Some call this mutual opposition. In fact, each intermediate shade is a simple quality and a thing in its own right. The opposition between them is the ordinary, familiar kind; it does not require the greatest possible difference. — س ره

[^V01-771]: Here “blackness” is used in more than one way. When Aristotle’s followers say that blackness is what varies, they mean each individual blackness. When they say that blackness is not what varies, they mean the shared, general nature of blackness. Their statements about the two blacknesses, the bodies that bear stronger or weaker blackness, and the idea of “black” all point to the same view: the feature that accounts for the difference is something other than the shared nature. This fits their claim that the adjective “black” applies to bodies by degrees, while blackness itself does not. — س ره

[^V01-772]: One objection is that a single motion is continuous and has one identity. If the thing it moves through is continuous too, its parts should match the whole in kind and name. How, then, could its stages be different species? The commentator replies that the quality undergoing change is not itself continuous or divisible; continuity belongs to the motion. The usual argument against Democritus concerns parts of continuous bodies, so it does not by itself prove that the levels of a quality are one species. Another reply is that a single motion must occur in one individual thing during that motion. This does not mean the mover stays the same throughout every process: a body can move through places under a series of pulls, and water can change in quality under successive fires. The point is that what one motion occurs in must be one individual thing for that motion, not a series of different species. — س ره

[^V01-773]: The difference in kind here is not between the levels of red themselves: they are all levels through which the motion passes. Red differs from black or white because it is where the process begins or ends. This is a difference in what the quality is, not in the one connected motion. — س ره

[^V01-774]: Some copies read “its arrival” here.

[^V01-775]: The original meaning of “strong” as the power to resist can apply to substances as well as to qualities: one thing can be more able to resist than another. This does not conflict with the technical point in the argument. It conflicts only with the wider meaning of “stronger” in everyday speech. — س ره

[^V01-776]: This refers to length itself, a kind of quantity, and to size, a feature of quantity. The author uses this to show that people do say one line is longer than another. He is not saying that measured quantity is strong in exactly the same sense as a quality; “longer” and “bigger” can simply mean “greater in amount.” — س ره

[^V01-777]: Some copies read “length is the line itself.” — ط

[^V01-778]: The distinction assumes what it is trying to prove. Strength and increase have the same basic meaning: strength that stops at a limit is increase with a limit, while increase without a limit is strength. So this does not separate them. — س ره

[^V01-779]: Both strength and increase can be divided again into forms that have a limit and forms that do not. This is a second division, made after the first division into stronger and weaker. — س ره

[^V01-780]: The examples are being compared in different ways. Five differs in kind from a smaller number such as four, and so differs in its existence as well. But one five differs in existence, not in kind, from another five. Adding five and four gives nine; adding two equal fives gives ten. With length, by contrast, a longer and a shorter measure share the same nature even though their individual extents differ. Another reading is possible: the “equal” part means the amount that matches after the extra part has been added. — س ره

[^V01-781]: That is, the shared broader kind exists in the world as a real thing; “and its existence” explains what is meant by this. — ن ره

[^V01-782]: This disproves the claim that anything that allows degrees of priority or strength must have an opposite. Existence has no opposite, yet it can be deficient, complete, or even beyond complete. — س ره

[^V01-783]: This also answers the claim that anything that admits priority or strength must undergo a process of growing stronger. Existence is a counterexample: its essence does not move or change in this way, as explained earlier. — س ره

[^V01-784]: For Aristotle’s followers, sensation is something that happens to the animal; for the author, it is an action. Movement is an action for both sides. In either case, these are features that happen to a thing; a substance is not made up of them. — س ره

[^V01-785]: Unless we rule out the possibility that effects vary because of different organs, tools, obstacles, or conditions, the objector will not agree that those effects come from the powers themselves. We must show that they do. If the tools include powers that themselves differ in completeness, then a stronger or weaker power in the substance is established. A horse’s power to perceive, for example, is more complete than a mosquito’s, especially if the soul itself has levels of development. If the difference came only from a missing condition or an obstacle, the difference between a horse’s soul and a mosquito’s would have to be permanent. That would mean the power is blocked forever, like saying that an ant can understand general ideas but never does so because a condition is always missing or an obstacle is always present. — س ره

[^V01-786]: The terms “what differs in” and “what makes the difference” are used here in the reverse way from the earlier discussion of degrees. There, the feature that causes the difference was called “what makes the difference,” and the thing that varies was “what differs in.” In discussions of priority, the feature that varies is called “what differs in.” The author is following that usage here. — س ره

[^V01-787]: The word *bi-ḥayth* (“such that”) appears to be a copyist’s error. The correct reading is *bi-ḥasab mā* (“according to what …”).

[^V01-788]: Aristotle’s followers can reply that differences in time belong to existence, not to time’s essence. This does not conflict with their claim that time itself is always passing, since “essence” here can mean either existence or the idea of time, which includes passing and is only a concept in the mind. They can also say that existences differ as separate realities, not by degrees, just as the most general kinds differ. But there is a problem: the author understands their claim about different existences as a difference attached to natures, because they are careful thinkers. If they instead mean that the existences themselves are entirely separate realities, then a single idea would have to be drawn from realities that share nothing. That would revive Ibn Kammunah’s objection and remove the shared ground between cause and effect, among other problems. — س ره

[^V01-789]: The note first states the general rule for things that overlap, then applies it to matter and form. Taken as broader kind and defining feature, they overlap as parts of one essence. Taken as matter and form, they differ, but their priority and posteriority belong to existence. — س ره
